findings.title: Deactivated or downgraded user can refresh tokens and keep old access
findings.description: Entry: packages/server/src/enterprise/middleware/passport/index.ts:230 (app.post('/api/v1/auth/refreshToken')). Attacker: a user who was deactivated (UserStatus.INACTIVE) or removed from a workspace, or whose role was downgraded, crossing the boundary from 'no longer authorized' to 'still authenticated with old privileges'. The path: this route is listed in WHITELIST_URLS (utils/constants.ts:27), so the /api/v1 API-key/JWT gate in index.ts:215-285 never runs; the handler reads req.cookies.refreshToken, checks only the signature with jwt.verify(refreshToken, jwtRefreshSecret) (line 234), then takes the identity from req.user (line 237), which passport.session() populated from the express-session record (deserializeUser at lines 93-95 simply echoes whatever was serialized at login), and calls setTokenOrCookies (lines 260/262) to issue a brand-new auth token. Nothing on the path reloads the user row or the role/workspace-membership row: the refresh token is valid for JWT_REFRESH_TOKEN_EXPIRY_IN_MINUTES (default 129600 = 90 days) and each call mints a fresh JWT_TOKEN_EXPIRY_IN_MINUTES (default 60 min) token, so the stale identity is refreshed indefinitely. Session invalidation only happens on password change/reset (user.service.ts:185, account.service.ts:601); deactivation via updateUser with status=INACTIVE and role changes via updateWorkspaceUser/updateRole never call destroyAllSessionsForUser, so the session and refresh cookie survive. Impact for this application: an administrator who deactivates an employee, removes them from a workspace, or downgrades their role believes access is revoked, but the employee's browser keeps obtaining valid tokens and retains the permissions snapshot captured at login, i.e. full access to the workspace/organization data they were meant to lose. Fix: on every refresh (and on every verifyToken), reload the user, the workspace-user row and the role from the database and reject if user.status !== ACTIVE, the workspace-user is missing/inactive, or the role/permissions differ; and invalidate sessions and refresh tokens whenever status, workspace membership or role is changed, not only on password change.

findings.title: Stale refresh token keeps minting auth tokens after access is revoked
findings.description: Entry: packages/server/src/enterprise/middleware/passport/index.ts:230-262 (refreshToken) reaching setTokenOrCookies at lines 260/262. Attacker: any caller holding a refresh-token cookie from a session that has since been superseded, crossing the boundary of 'which principal the refresh token belongs to'. The path: the handler verifies the refresh JWT signature but never compares the token's own subject (payload.id, and the decrypted payload.meta which encodes user.id + activeWorkspaceId) against the current req.user; it then issues a token for req.user and, with regenerateRefreshToken=false, re-sets the refreshToken cookie straight from req.cookies.refreshToken (line 309). Because the whitelisted route trusts whatever req.user the session provides and never rebinds the new token to the presented refresh token, a refresh token that was never rotated and never revoked remains a long-lived (90-day) credential; after any event that is supposed to end the principal's access but does not destroy the session (deactivation, role change, removal from a workspace), the same refresh token keeps minting valid auth tokens. Fix: in refreshToken, verify that the decrypted meta's user id equals req.user.id and that the workspace still matches, re-check the user's current status/role from the database, rotate the refresh token on every use, and revoke all refresh tokens for a user when their status or role changes.

findings.title: GitHub SSO accepts unverified email, allowing Flowise account takeover
findings.description:
Entry: packages/server/src/enterprise/sso/GithubSSO.ts:73 (GET /api/v1/github/callback, which is in WHITELIST_URLS and therefore unauthenticated).
Attacker: an outsider who controls a GitHub account, crossing into another Flowise user's account (identity takeover).
The GitHub strategy fetches /user/emails with the access token and looks for a verified primary email, but if none is found it falls back to emails[0].email with no verification check (line 47-49). That string is passed straight to this.verifyAndLogin (SSOBase.ts:56), which does readUserByEmail(email) and, if a user exists, logs that user in and mints the session/JWT (SSOBase.ts:80-141). Nothing between the callback and the login re-checks that the email is verified by GitHub, nor that the GitHub account is the same one previously bound to the Flowise user.
Impact: an attacker adds an unverified email address equal to a victim's Flowise email to their own GitHub account (GitHub permits adding unverified emails), or simply has no verified email so the first array element is used; logging in via GitHub then resolves to the victim's Flowise account and issues a valid session/token for it. Full account takeover, including any workspace/org the victim owns.
Fix: require a verified email (reject when no email has verified===true), never fall back to an unverified address, and store/bind the provider subject (profile.id) to the local user so subsequent logins require the same provider identity rather than matching by email.

findings.title: Timing side-channel on unauthenticated basic-auth leaks admin credentials
findings.description:
Entry: packages/server/src/enterprise/controllers/account.controller.ts:128 (POST /api/v1/account/basic-auth), which is in WHITELIST_URLS (packages/server/src/utils/constants.ts:35) so the JWT/API-key middleware does not guard it.
Attacker: an unauthenticated network caller, crossing into the admin basic-auth credential check.
The handler compares user-supplied username/password against process.env.FLOWISE_USERNAME / FLOWISE_PASSWORD with the === operator, which short-circuits on the first differing byte and is not a constant-time comparison. Nothing on the path (no rate limiter specific to this route, no auth guard) prevents repeated probing.
Impact: the administrator credential protecting the deployment can be recovered by a timing side-channel against an unauthenticated endpoint, and the endpoint also confirms whether FLOWISE_USERNAME/PASSWORD are configured (getBasicAuth at line 116), aiding targeted attacks.
Fix: compare with a constant-time function (crypto.timingSafeEqual over equal-length buffers, hashing both sides first), require the credentials to be set before comparing, and rate-limit/audit this endpoint.

findings.title: Forge authentication tokens and sessions via hard-coded default secrets
findings.description:
Entry: packages/server/src/enterprise/middleware/passport/index.ts:33-34 (module-level constants used by every JWT sign/verify) and line 55 (session secret).
Attacker: anyone who reads the repository, crossing into forging authentication tokens and sessions for any deployment that did not override these variables.
The signing secrets fall back to hard-coded literals: jwtAuthTokenSecret = process.env.JWT_AUTH_TOKEN_SECRET || 'auth_token', jwtRefreshSecret = process.env.JWT_REFRESH_TOKEN_SECRET || process.env.JWT_AUTH_TOKEN_SECRET || 'refresh_token', and the express-session secret defaults to 'flowise' (line 55). These literals are committed in source (and mirrored in the .env.example files as 'AABBCCDD...' and 'popcorn' for TOKEN_HASH_SECRET). Because the same defaults are used by every deployment that does not set the env vars, the key is public.
Impact: an attacker who knows the default secret can mint HS256 tokens with the expected audience/issuer for arbitrary user ids, and can sign session cookies, obtaining authenticated access; the default TOKEN_HASH_SECRET ('Secre$t' in tempTokenUtils.ts) also lets them encrypt/decrypt the meta bound into tokens.
Fix: remove the hard-coded fallbacks and refuse to start (or generate and persist a random secret) when JWT_AUTH_TOKEN_SECRET / JWT_REFRESH_TOKEN_SECRET / EXPRESS_SESSION_SECRET / TOKEN_HASH_SECRET are not provided, so no deployment can run on a publicly known key.

findings.title: Unauthenticated login flood pins Node event loop via sync bcrypt
findings.description:
Entry: packages/server/src/enterprise/middleware/passport/index.ts:267 (app.post('/api/v1/auth/login')) which drives the 'login' passport strategy at line 104-111 and calls accountService.login.
Attacker: an unauthenticated caller, crossing the login boundary (no authentication is required to reach the password check).
Path: index.ts:221 treats '/api/v1/auth/login' as whitelisted (constants.ts:26) so no verifyToken/API-key/license guard runs; the request body's email/password reach the local strategy (passport/index.ts:111-123), which calls AccountService.login (account.service.ts:450) -> userService.readUserByEmail (line 460) -> compareHash(data.user.credential, user.credential) (line 469), which is bcrypt.compareSync (encryption.util.ts:38, default 10 salt rounds).
Why nothing stops it: there is no express-rate-limit middleware on the auth routes (the only limiter in the codebase is RateLimiterManager, wired per-chatflow and to /admin/queues, index.ts:327-335), no global limiter is installed on the app, and no lockout/attempt counter exists for an account or source (grep for locked|lockout|failedLogin|attemptCount|maxLoginAttempt finds nothing in the enterprise code). The only reaction to a wrong password is auditService.recordLoginActivity, which records the failure but does not block or delay the next attempt.
Impact: bcrypt.compareSync is synchronous and deliberately CPU-expensive, so it blocks the Node event loop for the duration of each check; an unauthenticated attacker can send a high rate of login requests for a known email and pin the process, delaying or starving every other request on the server (self-inflicted DoS), while also being free to brute-force the credential with unlimited guesses.
Fix: apply a per-source and per-account rate limiter / exponential backoff and an attempt counter with temporary lockout to the login routes (both /api/v1/auth/login and /api/v1/account/login), and prefer the async bcrypt API (bcrypt.compare) so the event loop is not blocked while the limit is enforced.

findings.title: Unauthenticated login attempts cause unbounded audit table growth
findings.description:
Entry: packages/server/src/enterprise/middleware/passport/index.ts:267 (app.post('/api/v1/auth/login')) -> account.service.ts login (lines 457, 462, 466, 470, 486, 494).
Attacker: an unauthenticated caller, crossing the login boundary (the endpoint is whitelisted and needs no credentials to reach the failure paths).
Path: the whitelisted '/api/v1/auth/login' request reaches AccountService.login, and every failure branch (missing credential, unknown user, wrong password, unverified, no workspace) calls auditService.recordLoginActivity (account.service.ts:457/462/466/470/486/494), which creates and saves a LoginActivity row (audit/index.ts:79-85).
Why nothing stops it: there is no rate limit or throttle on the login routes (the RateLimiterManager only covers chatflow API configs and /admin/queues; no global limiter is installed), so an attacker can call the endpoint as fast as the server accepts, and each call persists a new audit row. The attacker controls only the frequency, and the table grows without bound.
Impact: unbounded growth of the LoginActivity table (and the per-attempt DB write cost) driven by an unauthenticated caller, leading to disk/database exhaustion and degraded query performance for the audit views.
Fix: rate-limit the login routes (per source and per account) so the write rate is bounded, and/or aggregate or cap failed-attempt audit records (for example counters per source per window) instead of inserting an unbounded row per failed attempt.

findings.title: Unauthenticated attacker can refresh any tenant's OAuth2 credential
findings.description: Entry: packages/server/src/routes/oauth2/index.ts:307 (router.post('/refresh/:credentialId')). Attacker: an unauthenticated outsider, crossing the login/tenant boundary. The global /api/v1 auth gate in src/index.ts:215-285 skips authentication when req.path startsWith a WHITELIST_URLS entry (src/index.ts:221); WHITELIST_URLS contains '/api/v1/oauth2-credential/refresh' (src/utils/constants.ts:40), and because the match is a raw prefix, the concrete path '/api/v1/oauth2-credential/refresh/<any-id>' is treated as whitelisted, so no JWT and no API key is required. The handler then does credentialRepository.findOneBy({ id: credentialId }) with the id taken straight from req.params (line 309) and never reads req.user or workspaceId; nothing in this file, in the mount (src/routes/index.ts:103) or in any middleware checks that the credential belongs to the caller. Compare the legitimate path: services/credentials/index.ts:130-132 and 172-174 always filter by workspaceId, and routes/credentials/index.ts gates every operation with checkPermission. Nothing on the path stops it. Impact: anyone who can reach the server can refresh any tenant's credential by guessing/obtaining its uuid and receives the provider token response, which the handler echoes back in full via tokenInfo: { ...tokenData } (lines 397-401), leaking the access_token and refresh_token of other workspaces. Fix: remove '/api/v1/oauth2-credential/refresh' from WHITELIST_URLS (or make the whitelist match exact paths, not prefixes), require the same checkPermission('credentials:create,credentials:update') used by routes/credentials/index.ts, and load/update the credential with a where clause that includes req.user.activeWorkspaceId, returning 404 when it does not match.

findings.title: Stored XSS via OAuth2 provider error_description rendered into callback error page
findings.description:
Entry: packages/server/src/routes/oauth2/index.ts:157 (GET /api/v1/oauth2-credential/callback, whitelisted unauthenticated in utils/constants.ts:39). Attacker: a user who can create/update a credential (credentials:create) crossing into the browser session of any other user who runs the OAuth flow for that credential. Path: the handler calls axios.post(tokenUrl, ...) at line 240 where tokenUrl is the credential's accessTokenUrl; on failure it takes axiosError.response?.data?.error_description (line 285-287) and passes it as the 'message'/'details' arguments of generateErrorPage. templates.ts interpolates that string raw into HTML at line 69 (
${message}
), line 70 (${details}), and line 76 (JSON.stringify(postMessageData) inside a escaping). Why nothing stops it: the global sanitizeMiddleware (utils/XSS.ts:5-21) only sanitizes req.query, and this value arrives in an HTTP response body, so it is never sanitized; the error page is sent with Content-Type text/html (line 290-291). accessTokenUrl is a free-form string field (components/credentials/GmailOAuth2.credential.ts:30-34) and createCredential/updateCredential perform no URL validation, so the owner can point the token endpoint at a server that returns a body like {"error":"x","error_description":""} or a breakout. Impact: stored XSS in the Flowise origin: script runs in the victim's authenticated session, can read the session/JWT cookie and call the internal API as the victim, and can exfiltrate credential/token data. Fix: HTML-escape every interpolated value in templates.ts (or use a templating engine with autoescaping), and in the script block escape '<' as \u003c in the JSON.stringify output; do not trust provider response bodies.

findings.title: Unauthenticated SSRF via attacker-controlled OAuth2 token URL in callback
findings.description:
Entry: packages/server/src/routes/oauth2/index.ts:157 (GET /api/v1/oauth2-credential/callback, whitelisted unauthenticated).
Attacker: an unauthenticated caller who supplies an arbitrary credential id as the state parameter, crossing into the server's internal network.
Path: state (line 159, 183-185) is used with no ownership/workspace check to load any Credential row; the credential's decryptedData yields accessTokenUrl which is assigned to tokenUrl at line 213, and line 240 performs axios.post(tokenUrl, ...).
Why nothing stops it: there is no allow-list or private-address (169.254.169.254, 127.0.0.1, RFC1918) block anywhere on this path, and accessTokenUrl is a free-form string credential field (components/credentials/GmailOAuth2.credential.ts:30-34) with no validation in createCredential/updateCredential (services/credentials/index.ts:13-31,169-192). The callback requires no authentication because it is whitelisted (utils/constants.ts:39), and the credential lookup uses findOneBy({ id: state }) with no workspaceId filter, unlike the credential service which always scopes by workspaceId (services/credentials/index.ts:127-135). The request body carries the credential's client_id and client_secret (lines 228-234), so a credential owner can also aim the server at an attacker-controlled collector to harvest those secrets, and the attacker can trigger the request at will.
Impact: server-side request forgery — the Flowise host can be made to POST to internal services or cloud metadata endpoints (SSRF), and the configured client_secret is sent to whatever host is configured.
Fix: require authentication and workspace scoping on this route, and validate/allow-list the token URL (reject non-https, localhost, and private/link-local IP ranges) before calling axios.

findings.title: Unauthenticated OAuth callback overwrites any credential via attacker-controlled state
findings.description:
Entry: packages/server/src/routes/oauth2/index.ts:157 (router.get('/callback'))
Attacker: an unauthenticated outsider (or a cross-site page), crossing the boundary that should bind an OAuth authorization to the user who initiated it.
The callback reads code and state straight from req.query (line 159) and uses state as the credential primary key at lines 183-185, then exchanges the attacker-supplied code for tokens (line 240) and writes the resulting token data into that credential (lines 271-274). The path is whitelisted ('/api/v1/oauth2-credential/callback', constants.ts:39) so the global middleware never authenticates it, and the route performs no authentication or ownership check of its own.
Nothing on the path stops it: state is only used as the credential id and is never validated as a value the server issued (no signed/random state, no session binding), and the repository contains no CSRF middleware at all (a search for csrf across packages/server/src returns nothing), so an attacker who knows or observes a credential id can drive the callback with their own authorization code. The token endpoint URL cannot be redirected (it comes from the stored credential), but the code and state are fully attacker-controlled.
Impact: OAuth login/account-binding CSRF against the integration — the victim's credential is silently overwritten with tokens minted for the attacker's account, so subsequent Flowise flows run with the attacker's identity (data exfiltration or poisoned upstream account).
Fix: generate a cryptographically random, single-use state value bound to the initiating authenticated session and verify it in the callback before exchanging the code; require authentication/authorization on the callback path or otherwise tie it to the user who started the flow.

findings.title: Unauthenticated OAuth callback allows unbounded axios request, DoSing server
findings.description:
Entry: packages/server/src/routes/oauth2/index.ts:157 (router.get('/callback')) — the axios.post at line 240 is the dangerous operation.
Attacker: an unauthenticated caller (the route is whitelisted), crossing the authentication boundary; the code/state query values are attacker-supplied.
Path: GET /api/v1/oauth2-credential/callback is in WHITELIST_URLS (packages/server/src/utils/constants.ts:39) so the global middleware at packages/server/src/index.ts:215-285 calls next() without any API-key/JWT check. The handler reads req.query.code and req.query.state (line 159), looks up the credential by state (line 183), decrypts it (line 198) and then calls axios.post(tokenUrl, ...) at line 240.
Why nothing stops it: the axios call passes only headers — no timeout (axios default 0 = no timeout) and no maxContentLength (axios default -1 = unlimited). There are no axios.defaults, no interceptors and no maxContentLength anywhere in packages/server (verified by grep), and the oauth2 router has no rate limiting, timeout or size guard. Nothing between the request and the call bounds the outbound operation.
Impact: a token endpoint that never responds holds the connection (and the request's socket and memory) open indefinitely; one that returns a multi-GB JSON body is buffered entirely into memory via tokenResponse.data and then re-encrypted and written to the DB. Repeating the request (or a provider that hangs) exhausts server sockets/file descriptors and can OOM the Node process, denying service to every tenant. Because the endpoint is unauthenticated, it is reachable by any caller who can present a credentialId.
Fix: pass an explicit timeout (e.g. { timeout: 15000 }) and a response size cap (e.g. maxContentLength/maxBodyLength of a few hundred KB) to both axios.post calls, and add a per-source rate limit or attempt throttle to the whitelisted callback/refresh routes.

findings.title: Unauthenticated read of any chatflow's lead PII via whitelisted /api/v1/leads/<id>
findings.description: Entry: packages/server/src/index.ts:221 (whitelist bypass) -> packages/server/src/routes/leads/index.ts:9 -> packages/server/src/controllers/leads/index.ts:14. Attacker: an unauthenticated internet caller, crossing the tenant boundary into another organization's chatflow lead data. The request path /api/v1/leads/<id> starts with the whitelisted '/api/v1/leads' (utils/constants.ts:19), so the global middleware in index.ts:215-285 calls next() without ever invoking verifyToken or validateAPIKey; the leads router (routes/leads/index.ts:9) has no auth middleware of its own, and the controller passes req.params.id verbatim into leadsService.getAllLeads. The service then runs AppDataSource.getRepository(Lead).find({ where: { chatflowid } }) with no workspaceId, organizationId or ownership predicate, so any chatflow id (which is exposed publicly via the chatbot embed/URL) returns every Lead row for that chatflow. Nothing on the path stops it: there is no token check, no permission check, no scoping of the query. Impact: unauthenticated disclosure of PII (name, email, phone, chatId) captured by every chatflow in the deployment, across all workspaces and organizations. Fix: remove '/api/v1/leads' from WHITELIST_URLS for the read route (keep it public only for the POST create), add verifyToken/checkPermission('leads:view') to the GET route, and scope the query by the caller's activeWorkspaceId (join Lead -> ChatFlow and filter by workspaceId).

findings.title: Known default TOKEN_HASH_SECRET lets attacker forge JWT identity meta
findings.description:
Entry: packages/server/src/enterprise/utils/tempTokenUtils.ts:33 (encryptToken key derivation) and the matching decrypt at line 52.
Attacker: an outside caller who knows the shipped default hash secret, crossing the token-integrity boundary by crafting the JWT meta field.
Both encryptToken and decryptToken derive the AES-256-CBC key with sha256(process.env.TOKEN_HASH_SECRET || 'Secre$t'). The default 'Secre$t' is hardcoded in the repository and .env.example leaves TOKEN_HASH_SECRET commented out, so deployments that do not override it encrypt with a publicly known key. This value is the only thing protecting the meta field of the auth/refresh JWT (passport/index.ts:394 encryptToken(user.id + ':' + activeWorkspaceId)) and the AuthStrategy check at AuthStrategy.ts:30-37 trusts the decrypted result as the identity to compare against req.user.id.
Nothing on the path stops it: no check that TOKEN_HASH_SECRET was set, no authenticated encryption (raw CBC with no MAC), and no additional signature over meta.
Impact for this application: an attacker can encrypt an arbitrary 'id:workspaceId' string with the known default key and place it in a token meta so it decrypts to whatever identity they choose, defeating the id-matching control in AuthStrategy and enabling cross-user/cross-workspace access.
Fix: remove the 'Secre$t' fallback, require a random TOKEN_HASH_SECRET at startup, and switch to an authenticated mode (AES-256-GCM) or HMAC the meta so it cannot be forged even if the key leaks.

findings.title: MITM can impersonate the Flowise database and read/modify all DB traffic
findings.description:
Entry: packages/server/src/DataSource.ts:114 (rejectUnauthorized: process.env.DATABASE_REJECT_UNAUTHORIZED === 'true'), reached from getDatabaseSSLFromEnv used by the postgres session store (SessionPersistance.ts:78) and the app DataSource.
Attacker: an outsider positioned on the network path between Flowise and its database, crossing the boundary by impersonating the database server.
The option is written so that any value other than the exact string 'true' yields rejectUnauthorized:false, i.e. TLS certificate verification is disabled by default whenever DATABASE_SSL_KEY_BASE64 is provided and the operator has not explicitly set DATABASE_REJECT_UNAUTHORIZED=true. The value is passed straight into the pg pool / TypeORM ssl config with no other validation.
Nothing on the path stops it: there is no secure-by-default here and no warning, and the .env.example does not force the flag to be set.
Impact for this application: a man-in-the-middle can present any certificate to the Flowise database connection, read and modify database traffic including credentials, chat flows, API keys and user sessions, because the client accepts the attacker's certificate.
Fix: default to verification on (e.g. rejectUnauthorized: process.env.DATABASE_REJECT_UNAUTHORIZED !== 'false'), and require an explicit opt-out plus a CA to be configured.

findings.title: Redis TLS certificate verification disabled for rediss:// connections
findings.description:
Entry: packages/server/src/utils/rateLimit.ts:60-63 (rediss:// branch sets tls = { rejectUnauthorized: false }).
Attacker: an outsider on the network path to the Redis server, crossing the boundary by impersonating Redis.
When REDIS_URL starts with rediss:// the code hardcodes rejectUnauthorized:false and passes it to the ioredis client (new Redis({... tls: tlsOpts})) with no way to enable verification, unlike the REDIS_TLS branch which accepts cert/key/ca. Nothing on the path checks the server certificate or offers an override.
Impact for this application: a man-in-the-middle can terminate the TLS session and read or tamper with everything stored in Redis, including rate-limit state and cached session data, and can impersonate the Redis endpoint to the app.
Fix: remove the hardcoded false, verify certificates by default, and allow a CA/cert/key (or an explicit, logged opt-out) for rediss:// connections.

findings.title: Auth cookies lack Secure flag, exposing session to plaintext HTTP capture
findings.description:
Entry: packages/server/src/enterprise/middleware/passport/index.ts:38-45 (secureCookie defaults to false), applied to the session cookie at line 59 and to the token/refreshToken cookies at lines 325-347.
Attacker: a network attacker on a plaintext HTTP leg, crossing the confidentiality boundary of the authentication cookie.
secureCookie is true only when SECURE_COOKIES==='true' or APP_URL starts with 'https'; otherwise, including the default where APP_URL is unset, it is false, and the same value is used for the session cookie (line 59), the 'token' cookie (lines 325, 338) and the 'refreshToken' cookie (lines 330, 343). SameSite is 'lax' and httpOnly is set, but the Secure attribute is missing whenever APP_URL is not set to an https URL, which is the shipped default (see .env.example line 102 where SECURE_COOKIES is commented out).
Nothing on the path forces Secure: there is no check that APP_URL was configured, and a reverse proxy terminating TLS in front of the app is explicitly the case the comment mentions.
Impact for this application: the bearer authentication cookie can be sent over an HTTP request, so a network attacker or a downgrade/HTTP subresource request can capture the session or token cookie and replay it to become the user.
Fix: default Secure to true and only disable it through an explicit, documented opt-out, and require APP_URL to be set for cookie issuance.

findings.title: Authenticated user can invite accounts into any workspace via body-supplied workspace id
findings.description:
Entry: packages/server/src/enterprise/routes/account.route.ts:12 (POST /account/invite)
Attacker: an authenticated low-privilege member of one workspace, crossing the workspace authorization boundary by adding users into a workspace they do not administer.
The caller supplies workspace.id and role.id in the request body. The controller (account.controller.ts:20) passes req.body to accountService.invite -> saveInviteAccount, which reads the target workspace with workspaceService.readWorkspaceById(data.workspace.id) (line 290) and the role with roleService.readRoleByRoleIdOrganizationId(data.role.id, data.workspace.organizationId) (line 297) purely from those body values.
Nothing on the path stops it: the only guards are IdentityManager.checkFeatureByPlan('feat:workspaces') and checkAnyPermission('workspace:add-user,users:manage') in account.route.ts:14-15. PermissionCheck.checkAnyPermission only checks that the caller's own permission list contains the string; the permission list is built from the caller's role in their own activeWorkspaceId (middleware/passport/index.ts:182). The service never compares the caller's activeWorkspaceId/activeOrganizationId to the target workspace's id/organizationId, and the role lookup only scopes the role to the target organization, not to the caller.
Impact for this application: any user who has workspace:add-user in any one workspace can invite users into any other workspace in the organization, granting them any role of that organization (including a high-privilege role) via data.role.id, escalating access and polluting/joining workspaces they were never granted.
Fix: before acting, verify the caller is a member/admin of the target workspace (e.g. look up a WorkspaceUser row for req.user.id + data.workspace.id, or require req.user.activeWorkspaceId === data.workspace.id), and restrict the assignable role to roles the caller is permitted to grant.

findings.title: Wildcard CORS with credentials lets any site read authenticated data
findings.description:
Entry: packages/server/src/index.ts:177 (this.app.use(cors(getCorsOptions()))) together with the header at line 204; the account/auth routes under /api/v1/account and /api/v1/auth are then reachable cross-origin with the caller's cookies.
Attacker: a malicious website visited by a logged-in Flowise user, crossing the same-origin boundary to read authenticated responses and drive state-changing account/auth endpoints.
getCorsOptions (utils/XSS.ts:41-78) returns `globallyAllowed = allowedOrigins === '*' || allowedList.includes(originLc)` and calls `originCallback(null, true)` for any origin when CORS_ORIGINS='*' (parseAllowedOrigins, line 32-34); index.ts:204 then unconditionally sets `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true` on every response regardless of the resolved origin. The cors middleware reflects the request's Origin back in Access-Control-Allow-Origin when the callback allows it, so with CORS_ORIGINS='*' the server answers Access-Control-Allow-Origin: <attacker origin> plus Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true. Nothing on the path ties the allowed origin to the requesting user's workspace, and the '*' mode is a documented configuration. Impact: any website can make credentialed cross-origin requests to this Flowise instance and read the responses, e.g. enumerate workspaces/chatflows and invoke account endpoints with the victim's session. Fix: never combine '*' with credentials — reject a wildcard when Access-Control-Allow-Credentials is 'true', set credentials only in the cors options for explicitly allow-listed origins, and emit Access-Control-Allow-Credentials from the cors middleware rather than unconditionally on every response.

findings.title: Any authenticated user can read another tenant's organization record by id or name
findings.description: Entry: packages/server/src/enterprise/routes/organization.route.ts:7 (router.get('/', organizationController.read)). Attacker: any authenticated user or API key holder, crossing the tenant boundary into another organization's data. Path: req.query.id / req.query.name flows from the query straight into organizationService.readOrganizationById(query.id, queryRunner) (line 32) / readOrganizationByName(query.name, queryRunner) (line 35), which run findOneBy(Organization, { id }) / { name } with no predicate limiting to the caller. Nothing on the path stops it: the router has no checkPermission (unlike role.route.ts:10-14, workspace.route.ts, organization-user.route.ts), and the global middleware in packages/server/src/index.ts:215-277 only establishes that a valid JWT or API key exists, never that it belongs to the requested org. The controller never compares query.id/query.name to req.user.activeOrganizationId. Impact: an ordinary member (or any workspace API key, whose req.user.isOrganizationAdmin is hard-coded false at index.ts:272) can enumerate/read any other tenant's organization record, including customerId and subscriptionId, which then feed the billing routes below. Fix: ignore the client id for self-scoped reads and resolve the organization from req.user.activeOrganizationId, or gate the route with checkPermission('organization:view') plus an explicit ownership/tenant check.

findings.title: Any authenticated user can read another tenant's Stripe customer and card data
findings.description: Entry: packages/server/src/enterprise/routes/organization.route.ts:15 (router.get('/customer-default-source', organizationController.getCustomerWithDefaultSource)). Attacker: any authenticated user, crossing the tenant boundary to read another organization's payment information. Path: customerId is read from req.query (organization.controller.ts:79) and passed to identityManager.getCustomerWithDefaultSource(customerId) (line 84), which calls stripeManager.getCustomerWithDefaultSource (IdentityManager.ts:312) and stripe.customers.retrieve(customerId, { expand: ['default_source', 'invoice_settings.default_payment_method'] }) (StripeManager.ts:262-264), returning the full Stripe customer object. Nothing stops it: no comparison to req.user.activeOrganizationCustomerId and no route guard. Impact: disclosure of another tenant's Stripe customer record including the default payment method / card details (the UI consumes invoice_settings.default_payment_method, PricingDialog.jsx:461-490), plus the customer's balance and metadata. Fix: use req.user.activeOrganizationCustomerId instead of the query parameter and add an admin/billing permission check.

findings.title: Any authenticated user can read another org's billing proration by subscriptionId
findings.description: Entry: packages/server/src/enterprise/routes/organization.route.ts:21 (router.get('/plan-proration', organizationController.getPlanProration)). Attacker: any authenticated user, crossing the tenant boundary to read another organization's billing/plan data. Path: subscriptionId and newPlanId are read from req.query (organization.controller.ts:112) and passed to identityManager.getPlanProration(subscriptionId, newPlanId) (line 120) -> stripeManager.getPlanProration -> stripe.subscriptions.retrieve(subscriptionId) and stripe.customers.retrieve(subscription.customer) (StripeManager.ts:435-439), which returns proration amounts and the customer's credit balance. Nothing stops it: no comparison to req.user.activeOrganizationSubscriptionId and no route guard. Impact: disclosure of arbitrary subscriptions' plan change proration and associated customer balance, i.e. another tenant's billing posture. Fix: use the caller's own subscription id from req.user and enforce an admin permission on the route.

findings.title: Invite token reused for password reset enables unauthenticated account takeover
findings.description:
Entry: packages/server/src/enterprise/routes/account.route.ts:29 (POST /reset-password, unauthenticated) -> account.controller.ts:70 -> account.service.ts:563 resetPassword.
Attacker: an unauthenticated caller holding a workspace-invite link, crossing from 'may join a workspace' to 'owns the target account's password'.
Path: the invite flow stores an invite token in the SAME User.tempToken column (account.service.ts:305 for a new user, and account.service.ts:378 for an EXISTING user who already has a password and is being invited to another workspace), and emails it as `${APP_URL}/register?token=<tempToken>` (account.service.ts:315/384 -> sendEmail.ts sendWorkspaceInvite). resetPassword looks the user up by email (line 568), then at line 570 accepts any value equal to user.tempToken and, with no check that the token was issued for PASSWORD_RESET, writes a new bcrypt hash (line 589-591) and destroys the user's sessions (line 601).
Nothing on the path stops it: there is no token-purpose/type binding anywhere; TokenType and isTokenValid exist in tempTokenUtils.ts but are never called. The token column is shared by invite, verification and reset flows, and the reset path only compares the raw token string and its expiry.
Impact: an invite email link (forwarded, shared inbox, chat, logs, browser history) becomes a full account-takeover credential for an existing user, not merely a workspace-join link, letting the holder log in as that user with all their permissions.
Fix: store a separate, purpose-scoped, single-use token (or embed a token type/audience in the token) for password resets, and have resetPassword verify the token's purpose and expiry before changing the credential; never reuse the invite token for password changes.

findings.title: verify() response leaks bcrypt password hash and tempToken to unauthenticated caller
findings.description:
Entry: packages/server/src/enterprise/routes/account.route.ts:23 (POST /verify, unauthenticated) -> account.controller.ts:41 `res.status(201).json(data)` -> account.service.ts:507 verify.
Attacker: an unauthenticated caller who possesses a tempToken, crossing into read access of another user's stored credential hash.
Path: verify() assigns the full User entity to data.user (line 516) and reassigns it from saveUser at line 520, then returns `data`; the controller serializes it directly. Unlike the register flow (account.service.ts:267-269) and the login middleware (generateSafeCopy in middleware/passport/index.ts:311), verify() applies no sanitization.
Nothing on the path stops it: there is no serializer or field allow-list on the response, and generateSafeCopy is not used on this path, so `credential` (the bcrypt password hash), `tempToken` and `tokenExpiry` are all included in the JSON body.
Impact: any holder of a token obtains the victim's bcrypt password hash (and the token) in the HTTP response, enabling offline password cracking and further token reuse.
Fix: return only a safe subset of the user (use generateSafeCopy or an explicit DTO) from verify(), never the credential hash or tempToken.

findings.title: Any workspace member can read another workspace's document store via storeId
findings.description:
Entry: packages/server/src/controllers/documentstore/index.ts:495 (queryVectorStore), reached via routes/documentstore/index.ts:70 (POST /vectorstore/query, checkPermission('documentStores:view')).
Attacker: an authenticated API-key holder in one workspace, crossing the workspace/tenant boundary into another workspace's document store data.
The body's data.storeId is taken straight from the request body and passed to appServer.AppDataSource.getRepository(DocumentStore).findOneBy({ id: data.storeId }) with NO workspaceId filter, then the store's embedding/vector-store config is used to run retriever.invoke(data.query) and the matching DocumentStoreFileChunk rows are returned. Every sibling operation (getDocumentStoreById:179, deleteDocumentStore:321, saveVectorStoreConfig:1181, updateVectorStoreConfigOnly:1142, saveProcessingLoader:748, processLoader:837, deleteVectorStoreFromStore:400) filters findOneBy by { id, workspaceId }, but this one does not. Nothing on the path re-checks ownership after the lookup; the only guard is the generic documentStores:view permission, which every workspace member holds.
Impact: any user with documentStores:view can enumerate store ids and read the full pageContent/metadata of any other workspace's (and organization's) document store by querying with its id, exposing confidential uploaded documents.
Fix: pass workspaceId into queryVectorStore and filter the lookup with findOneBy({ id: data.storeId, workspaceId }), mirroring the other service functions.

findings.title: Authenticated user deletes other workspaces' document chunks by chunkId
findings.description:
Entry: packages/server/src/controllers/documentstore/index.ts:197 (deleteDocumentStoreFileChunk), reached via routes/documentstore/index.ts:49-53 (DELETE /chunks/:storeId/:loaderId/:chunkId).
Attacker: an authenticated API-key holder, crossing into another workspace's chunks.
The DocumentStore lookup IS scoped by workspaceId (lines 362-365), but the chunk is then fetched and deleted by chunkId alone: findOneBy({ id: chunkId }) at 375-377 and .delete(chunkId) at 381, with no verification that the chunk's storeId equals the scoped storeId. A caller supplies their own in-workspace storeId (passing the scoped lookup) and an arbitrary chunkId belonging to another workspace's store; the chunk is deleted regardless of owner. The same unchecked chunkId is used at line 383 to decrement counts.
Impact: cross-tenant destruction of another workspace's document chunks (data loss), and the existence of any chunk id is confirmed.
Fix: fetch the chunk with findOneBy({ id: chunkId, storeId }) (or verify tbdChunk.storeId === storeId) before deleting.

findings.title: Any authenticated API key can read other workspaces' document chunks via tool-desc route
findings.description:
Entry: packages/server/src/routes/documentstore/index.ts:82 (POST /generate-tool-desc/:id).
Attacker: any authenticated API-key holder, including one with no document-store permissions, crossing the permission boundary and the workspace boundary.
This is the only document-store route with no checkPermission/checkAnyPermission middleware; every sibling route (lines 14-79) has one. It reaches controllers/documentstore/index.ts:700 generateDocStoreToolDesc -> services/documentstore/index.ts:2141-2143, which loads DocumentStoreFileChunk.findBy({ storeId: docStoreId }) using the raw :id path parameter with no workspaceId scoping, then feeds the first four chunks' pageContent into the LLM prompt. Nothing on the path checks the caller's permissions or that the store belongs to the caller's workspace.
Impact: an API key lacking documentStores permissions can read the content of any other workspace's document chunks (via the LLM response) and invoke an arbitrary configured chat model, both a permission bypass and a cross-tenant data leak.
Fix: add checkPermission('documentStores:view') (or similar) to the route and scope the chunk lookup by the caller's workspaceId.

findings.title: Authenticated user exhausts server memory via tiny text-splitter chunkSize
findings.description: Entry: packages/server/src/routes/documentstore/index.ts:41 (POST /loader/preview, also /loader/save:43 and /loader/process/:loaderId:45). Attacker: an authenticated user with documentStores:preview-process, crossing the boundary of a small request causing server-side memory exhaustion. Path: req.body.splitterConfig is taken verbatim in previewFileChunks/processLoader (controllers/documentstore/index.ts:423, 311), passed to documentStoreService.previewChunksMiddleware/processLoaderMiddleware (services/documentstore/index.ts:664, 861), into _splitIntoChunks (services/documentstore/index.ts:565) where nodeData.inputs = {...data.splitterConfig} (line 578), and finally the splitter node's init parses chunkSize/chunkOverlap with parseInt and constructs RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter (lines 62-72) with no lower bound. Nothing on the path validates chunkSize/chunkOverlap; checkPermission only gates access. Impact: chunkSize=1 (or 0) against a multi-MB loaded document produces millions of document objects that are all materialized in memory and returned, exhausting the Node heap and taking down the server for all tenants. Fix: enforce a sane minimum and maximum for chunkSize/chunkOverlap in the splitter node (and reject non-positive/absurdly small values) before constructing the splitter, and cap the total number of chunks the preview/process path will build.

findings.title: Authenticated user can DoS server via unbounded recursive web crawl
findings.description: Entry: packages/server/src/routes/documentstore/index.ts:43 (POST /loader/save, also /loader/process/:loaderId:45). Attacker: an authenticated user with documentStores:preview-process, crossing the boundary of a single small request triggering an unbounded server-side crawl/download. Path: req.body.loaderConfig flows unchanged through saveProcessingLoader/processLoader (controllers/documentstore/index.ts:311, 274) into documentStoreService.processLoaderMiddleware -> _saveChunksToStorage -> previewChunks (services/documentstore/index.ts:936, 710). previewChunks only clamps the crawler limit to 3 when data.preview is true (lines 712-720), and data.preview is never set on the save/process endpoints, so the caller's loaderConfig.limit reaches the loader node untouched. In the Cheerio/Playwright/Puppeteer loaders limit===0 means "fetch all links" and is passed to webCrawl (utils.ts:456), whose recursive crawl() only stops at `pages.length === limit` (utils.ts:413) - with limit 0 it never stops, fetching and parsing every same-host page it can reach. Nothing on the path bounds the number of pages fetched, the bytes downloaded, or the time spent. Impact: one request makes the server recursively crawl and load an entire target site into memory (headless-browser loads for Playwright/Puppeteer), pinning CPU/memory and effectively DoSing the instance. Fix: apply the same limit clamp used for preview to the save/process paths, replace limit===0 "fetch all" with a hard maximum page count, and cap total bytes/time for a crawl.

findings.title: Unauthenticated users can upload files into any organization's chatflow storage
findings.description: Entry: packages/server/src/routes/attachments/index.ts:8 (POST /api/v1/attachments/:chatflowId/:chatId), whitelisted at packages/server/src/utils/constants.ts:24 so the global auth middleware in packages/server/src/index.ts:221 skips it. Attacker: an unauthenticated caller, crossing the organization/tenant boundary by writing files into another tenant's storage. Path: req.params.chatflowId/chatId -> attachmentsController.createAttachment -> attachmentsService.createAttachment -> createFileAttachment: it looks up ChatFlow by the attacker-supplied chatflowid and, because req.user is absent for a whitelisted request, derives orgId/workspaceId from that chatflow's workspace (lines 50-74) and then writes the uploaded files via addArrayFilesToStorage under orgId/chatflowid/chatId (lines 158-167), charging quota to that org. Nothing stops it: there is no check that the chatflow isPublic and no check that the caller is a member of the owning workspace/organization; the only gate is that the target chatflow happens to have fullFileUpload enabled. Impact: any unauthenticated caller can upload arbitrary files into any chatflow's (any organization's) storage folder and consume that organization's storage quota, with the files later retrievable via the equally unauthenticated /api/v1/get-upload-file route. Fix: before writing, require the chatflow to be isPublic (or the caller to be an authenticated member of the owning workspace) and reject uploads to non-public chatflows owned by another tenant.

findings.title: Any authenticated user can start arbitrary containers on the Flowise host
findings.description:
Entry: packages/server/src/routes/nvidia-nim/index.ts:11 (POST /api/v1/nvidia-nim/start-container -> nimController.startContainer)
Attacker: an authenticated but low-privileged user (e.g. a workspace member with no permissions), crossing the boundary from "can log in" to "can start arbitrary containers on the Flowise host".
Path: the request body fields imageTag, apiKey and hostPort are read directly at controller lines 56-58 and passed unchanged to NimContainerManager.startContainer(imageTag, apiKey, hostPort, nimRelaxMemConstraints) at line 64. The only validation is that nimRelaxMemConstraints is 0 or 1 (line 61); imageTag, apiKey and hostPort are never validated, never checked against any allow-list, and never checked against the caller.
Why nothing stops it: the route registers no checkPermission/checkAnyPermission middleware, unlike every comparable router (packages/server/src/routes/chatflows/index.ts:9 etc.). The global middleware in packages/server/src/index.ts:215-285 only requires the `x-request-from: internal` header plus verifyToken, and verifyToken (packages/server/src/enterprise/middleware/passport/index.ts:404-430) merely validates the JWT session — it does not check role or permissions. The UI sends that header (packages/ui/src/api/client.js:9), so any logged-in user passes.
Impact: a non-privileged user can start containers on the host with an arbitrary image and arbitrary host port, consuming host resources, exposing ports, and potentially running untrusted images outside any Flowise authorization boundary.
Fix: add an authorization guard to the route (e.g. router.post('/start-container', checkPermission('<admin/nim permission>'), ...)) and/or an explicit admin check, and validate imageTag/hostPort against an allow-list server-side.

findings.title: Predictable, world-readable temp file exposes downloaded Google Drive docs
findings.description:
Entry: packages/components/nodes/documentloaders/GoogleDrive/GoogleDrive.ts:596 (createTempFile called from processBinaryFile) — reached from init() at line 342 via processFile -> processBinaryFile, with the buffer coming from downloadBinaryFile (line 590) or exportGoogleWorkspaceFileAsBuffer (line 584), i.e. the contents of a private Google Drive file fetched with the user's access token.
Attacker: an unprivileged local OS user on the same host as the Flowise server, crossing the boundary from "no access to another Flowise user's Google Drive data" to "can read that downloaded document content" (and, via symlink pre-creation, can influence where the write lands).
Path: init() (line 277) -> processFile (line 522) -> processBinaryFile (line 574) -> createTempFile (line 680). At line 698 tempDir is os.tmpdir() (typically world-writable /tmp) and at line 699 the name is `gdrive_${Date.now()}_${Math.random().toString(36).substring(7)}${extension}`; line 702 calls fs.writeFileSync(tempFilePath, buffer) with no mode option.
Why nothing stops it: Math.random() is not a cryptographically secure source, and Date.now() is predictable to the second, so the filename has low entropy and can be guessed or brute-forced by a local process watching /tmp. fs.writeFileSync is called with the default mode (0666 masked by umask, normally 0644), so the file is world-readable; it is also followed if an attacker has pre-created that path as a symlink, letting the write target an arbitrary file the server user can write. The file is only removed in the finally block at lines 670-676, so it also persists on disk if the process crashes or is killed mid-load.
Impact for this application: any private document pulled from Google Drive (including Google Docs/Sheets/Slides exported to PDF/DOCX/XLSX and PDF/DOCX/CSV binaries) is briefly, and sometimes permanently, readable by any other local user, and can be redirected to an attacker-chosen path via a symlink race.
Fix: create the temp file with a cryptographically random name (crypto.randomBytes / fs.mkdtemp with mode 0o700) inside a per-run private directory, open it with the exclusive 'wx' flag and mode 0o600 so a pre-existing path or symlink causes an error instead of being followed, and keep the existing cleanup (ideally also on process exit).

findings.title: Admin with sso:manage can force server-side HTTPS requests to arbitrary internal hosts
findings.description: Entry: packages/server/src/enterprise/routes/login-method.route.ts:16 -> LoginMethodController.testConfig (packages/server/src/enterprise/controllers/login-method.controller.ts:143) -> Auth0SSO.testSetup(providers[0].config) (Auth0SSO.ts:113). Attacker: an authenticated user holding the sso:manage permission (admin-category permission, Permissions.ts:132), crossing from 'configure SSO' into 'make the Flowise server issue HTTP requests to arbitrary internal hosts'. The value `domain` is taken unvalidated from req.body.providers[0].config and destructured at Auth0SSO.ts:114, then interpolated directly into the request URL host at line 118: `https://${domain}/oauth/token`. The route is guarded only by checkPermission('sso:manage') (PermissionCheck.ts:5), and neither the controller (login-method.controller.ts:133-150) nor testSetup performs any allow-list, host validation, scheme check, or DNS/private-address filtering. Because `domain` controls the authority component, a caller can set it to an internal target such as `169.254.169.254`, `localhost:8080`, `10.0.0.5`, or `[::1]` (e.g. domain = '169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials' or 'internal-service.local'), and axios will connect to that host over HTTPS on the server's behalf. The response status/statusText is returned to the caller (Auth0SSO.ts:129), and the same interpolation is used for the `audience` field, giving status/error disclosure and blind SSRF against cloud metadata endpoints, internal admin panels, and services bound to loopback that are unreachable from outside. Fix: do not build the URL from raw input — validate `domain` against an allow-list of Auth0 tenant domains (or at minimum a strict hostname regex that forbids IP literals, localhost, and private/link-local ranges), resolve the hostname and reject private/link-local/loopback addresses before the request, and restrict the scheme to https.

findings.title: Authenticated user can bulk-delete evaluations in any workspace
findings.description: Entry: packages/server/src/routes/evaluations/index.ts:13 (PATCH /, checkPermission('evaluations:delete'), body.ids) -> controllers/evaluations/index.ts:170 -> services/evaluations/index.ts:619. Attacker: an authenticated user with evaluations:delete in workspace A, crossing the tenant boundary by sending ids belonging to workspace B in the request body. The service first runs a workspace-scoped `find` into evalsToBeDeleted (line 613-618) but then performs the actual deletion with `.getRepository(Evaluation).delete(ids)` on the raw ids array from the body, with no workspaceId in the criteria. TypeORM treats a string array as primary-key criteria, so the delete removes every matching row in every workspace regardless of the earlier find. The controller copies `req.body.ids` straight through, and the only guard is the permission string; nothing ties the ids to the caller's workspace. The impact is a cross-tenant bulk delete of arbitrary evaluations (and, via the loop, their runs). Fix: delete using ids filtered to the caller's workspace, e.g. `delete({ id: In(evalsToBeDeleted.map(e => e.id)) })` using the already-scoped list, or include workspaceId in the delete criteria.

findings.title: Cross-workspace evaluation versions leaked by unscoped name query
findings.description: Entry: packages/server/src/routes/evaluations/index.ts:12 (GET /versions/:id, checkPermission('evaluations:view')) -> controllers/evaluations/index.ts:152 -> services/evaluations/index.ts:586. Attacker: an authenticated user with evaluations:view in workspace A, crossing the tenant boundary to read workspace B's data. getVersions first validates the requested id belongs to the caller's workspace (line 581-585), but then loads versions with `.getRepository(Evaluation).find({ where: { name: evaluation.name } })` with no workspaceId, and returns each row's `id`, `runDate` and `version`. Any evaluation in another workspace that shares the name is included, so the caller learns other tenants' evaluation ids and run timestamps. Nothing on the path scopes this query to the workspace; the route guard only checks the permission string. Besides the direct metadata leak, this is what makes the unscoped delete operations (deleteEvaluation line 431 and patchDeleteEvaluations line 619) practically exploitable, because it hands the attacker valid cross-workspace ids. Fix: add `workspaceId: workspaceId` to the where clause so only the caller's workspace versions are returned.

findings.title: Missing permission check lets any user read evaluation outdated status
findings.description: The /is-outdated route is missing a permission check, so it can be reached without the required authorization. Add the appropriate permission/authorization check to the route handler.

findings.title: Authenticated user can queue unbounded chatflow prediction executions
findings.description: Entry: packages/server/src/routes/evaluations/index.ts:9 (POST /api/v1/evaluations -> evaluationsController.createEvaluation) and :11 (POST /run-again/:id). Attacker: an authenticated workspace user with evaluations:create/run, crossing the boundary that one HTTP request should not be able to force unbounded server-side work. Path: controller passes req.body straight to evaluationsService.createEvaluation (packages/server/src/controllers/evaluations/index.ts:29-34); the service at line 125 does `const chatflowIds = JSON.parse(body.chatflowId)` with no length check, loops every id doing a DB lookup (lines 126-143), then calls evalRunner.runEvaluations(data) (line 159) which is NOT awaited. In packages/components/evaluation/EvaluationRunner.ts runEvaluations (line 104) loops over chatflowIds and evaluateChatflow (line 112) loops over data.dataset.rows, and for every pair issues axios.post(`${this.baseURL}/api/v1/prediction/${chatflowId}`) at line 135, i.e. a full chatflow/agent/LLM execution. Nothing caps chatflowIds.length (the body is a short JSON array, so the express.json size limit does not help) and nothing caps the product chatflowIds.length x dataset.rows.length; runAgain (service lines 24-63) re-enters the same path for an existing evaluation. Impact: a single small request can queue an arbitrarily large number of concurrent prediction executions on the server, exhausting CPU, memory, outbound connections and LLM quota, and each request is fire-and-forget so they stack. Fix: enforce a hard maximum on the number of chatflow ids per evaluation and on total iterations (chatflows x rows), reject arrays above it before the loop, and serialize/limit concurrency of runEvaluations.

findings.title: Authenticated user can send unbounded ids array to evaluations delete, exhausting DB
findings.description: Entry: packages/server/src/routes/evaluations/index.ts:13 (PATCH /api/v1/evaluations -> evaluationsController.patchDeleteEvaluations). Attacker: an authenticated workspace user with evaluations:delete, crossing the boundary that a caller-supplied array must not translate into unbounded SQL work. Path: controller reads `const ids = req.body.ids ?? []` with no validation or length cap (packages/server/src/controllers/evaluations/index.ts:161) and passes it to evaluationsService.patchDeleteEvaluations; the service builds `where: { id: In(ids), workspaceId: activeWorkspaceId }` at lines 613-618 and then `delete(ids)` at line 619. Nothing bounds ids.length. Impact: an attacker can send an array of tens of thousands of ids, producing a huge parameterized IN clause and delete statement that the database must parse and execute, pinning DB CPU and memory; combined with isDeleteAllVersion (lines 624-640) each matched evaluation also triggers further per-row find/delete loops. Fix: cap the accepted array length (e.g. a few hundred ids) and reject anything larger with 400 before building the query.

findings.title: Unbounded evaluations list query loads entire table into memory
findings.description: Entry: packages/server/src/routes/evaluations/index.ts:6 (GET /api/v1/evaluations -> evaluationsController.getAllEvaluations). Attacker: an authenticated workspace user with evaluations:view, crossing the boundary that a list endpoint must not be able to load the whole table into memory on demand. Path: controller calls getPageAndLimitParams (packages/server/src/utils/pagination.ts:10) which defaults page and limit to -1 when the query params are absent and only rejects negative values, then calls evaluationsService.getAllEvaluations(workspaceId, page, limit). In the service, when `page > 0 && limit > 0` is false (the default), the namesQueryBuilder at lines 360-374 has no skip/take, and line 381-387 runs `where ev.name IN (:...names)` with no limit, loading every Evaluation row for every distinct name in the workspace via getMany() and then building the full returnResults array in memory (lines 390-408). Nothing caps the number of distinct names or rows returned. Impact: a workspace with many evaluations (or an attacker who first creates many versions) can make a single unauthenticated-cost GET materialize and JSON-serialize the entire evaluations table, exhausting server memory and DB bandwidth. Fix: always apply a bounded default limit/take (and reject absurd limits) instead of returning the unbounded result set when pagination is omitted.

findings.title: Authenticated user can exhaust server memory via unbounded version query
findings.description: Entry: packages/server/src/routes/evaluations/index.ts:12 (GET /api/v1/evaluations/versions/:id -> evaluationsController.getVersions), also reached indirectly from getEvaluation (service line 565). Attacker: an authenticated workspace user with evaluations:view, crossing the boundary that a caller-triggered lookup must not scale with unbounded stored rows. Path: controller passes req.params.id to evaluationsService.getVersions; the service loads the target Evaluation, then at lines 586-593 does `find({ where: { name: evaluation.name }, order: { runDate: 'ASC' } })` with no take/limit, pulling every evaluation sharing that name into memory, and then maps them all into returnResults (lines 594-601). The name is attacker-controlled in the sense that they can create many versions of an evaluation with the same name, making the result set grow without bound; getEvaluation calls this same function and additionally loads all EvaluationRun rows for the id (lines 562-564). Impact: repeated calls force the server to read and serialize an ever-growing set of rows, driving memory and DB load. Fix: bound getVersions with a take/limit and paginate, and avoid the unbounded EvaluationRun.find in getEvaluation.

findings.title: Authenticated user can delete any workspace's evaluation by UUID
findings.description:
Entry: packages/server/src/controllers/evaluations/index.ts:97 (deleteEvaluation), route packages/server/src/routes/evaluations/index.ts:8 guarded only by checkPermission('evaluations:delete').
Attacker: An authenticated user in workspace A, crossing the workspace boundary to destroy data in workspace B.
Path: The controller reads req.params.id and passes it plus the caller's own workspaceId into evaluationsService.deleteEvaluation(id, workspaceId). At line 431 the service runs AppDataSource.getRepository(Evaluation).delete({ id: id }) with NO workspaceId predicate, and line 432 deletes EvaluationRun rows by evaluationId: id. The activeWorkspaceId argument is only used afterward, at line 433, to re-list the caller's own evaluations — it never constrains the delete.
Why nothing stops it: checkPermission('evaluations:delete') only tests a permission string in req.user.permissions (PermissionCheck.ts:14); it does not verify that the target evaluation belongs to the caller's workspace. getWorkspaceSearchOptions is available and is used elsewhere, but not here.
Impact: Any user holding evaluations:delete in any workspace can permanently delete any evaluation and all its run rows in every other workspace/tenant simply by sending that evaluation's UUID, since ids are returned by the workspace-scoped listing endpoints and are thus enumerable/discoverable. The sibling datasetService.deleteDataset (services/dataset/index.ts:239) correctly does delete({ id: id, workspaceId: workspaceId }), showing this is an oversight, not a design choice.
Fix: Delete with both keys — getRepository(Evaluation).delete({ id, workspaceId: activeWorkspaceId }) — and likewise scope the EvaluationRun cleanup to the rows that belong to that evaluation, so a non-matching id deletes nothing.

findings.title: Authenticated user can read any account's record via GET /api/v1/user?id=<uuid>
findings.description: Entry: packages/ui/src/api/user.js:4 (getUserById) -> GET /api/v1/user?id=<uuid>. Attacker: any authenticated user, crossing the user boundary to read another account's record. req.query.id (controller line 25) goes to userService.readUserById(query.id) (line 30), which does findOneBy(User, { id }) (user.service.ts line 46) with no check that the id belongs to the caller. The controller only deletes credential/tempToken/tokenExpiry (lines 40-42) and returns the rest, so email, name, status, createdBy and timestamps of an arbitrary user id are returned. The /user router (enterprise/routes/user.route.ts line 7) has no checkPermission and the controller has no id===req.user.id comparison (only the PUT handler, line 60, has that check). Impact: an attacker enumerates user ids to harvest emails and account metadata for any user in the deployment, including other tenants. Fix: require query.id === req.user.id (or an admin/appropriate permission) before returning the record, and return only a minimal self-profile shape.

findings.title: Any authenticated user can read members and roles of any workspace by ID
findings.description: Entry: packages/ui/src/api/user.js:30,31,33,35 (getAllUsersByWorkspaceId/getUserByRoleId/getWorkspacesByUserId/getWorkspacesByOrganizationIdUserId) -> GET /api/v1/workspaceuser?... Attacker: any authenticated user, crossing the tenant/workspace boundary. The handler branches on query.workspaceId / query.userId / query.roleId / query.organizationId (lines 30-47) and passes them unchecked to WorkspaceUserService methods that build queries like WHERE workspaceUser.workspaceId = :workspaceId (workspace-user.service.ts lines 84-89) or WHERE workspace.organizationId = :organizationId AND workspaceUser.userId = :userId (lines 131-137), returning member/user/workspace/role rows. The route (enterprise/routes/workspace-user.route.ts line 10) has no checkPermission or feature guard and the controller never compares the supplied ids to req.user.activeWorkspaceId/activeOrganizationId. Impact: an attacker enumerates any workspace or organization id to dump its members, roles and associated users across tenants. Fix: validate that the requested workspace/organization belongs to req.user's active scope before querying, or require a permission such as workspace:read.

findings.title: Any authenticated user can read another tenant's billing via subscriptionId
findings.description: Entry: packages/ui/src/api/user.js:16 (getAdditionalSeatsQuantity) -> GET /api/v1/organization/additional-seats-quantity?subscriptionId=<id>. Attacker: any authenticated user, crossing the billing tenant boundary. req.query.subscriptionId is taken from the caller (line 61) and passed to identityManager.getAdditionalSeatsQuantity(subscriptionId) (line 69) with no check that this subscription belongs to req.user.activeOrganizationSubscriptionId. Only req.user.activeOrganizationId is used, and only for the unrelated seat count. The route has no authorization middleware. Impact: an attacker supplies another tenant's subscriptionId to read that tenant's billing/seat details. Fix: compare the supplied subscriptionId against req.user.activeOrganizationSubscriptionId and reject mismatches before calling the identity manager.

findings.title: Any authenticated user can change another tenant's subscription seats and billing
findings.description: Entry: packages/ui/src/api/user.js:21 (updateAdditionalSeats) -> POST /api/v1/organization/update-additional-seats. Attacker: any authenticated user, crossing the billing boundary to mutate another tenant's subscription. req.body.subscriptionId, quantity and prorationDate are read from the caller (line 130) and passed to identityManager.updateAdditionalSeats(subscriptionId, quantity, prorationDate) (line 141) with no verification that subscriptionId belongs to the caller's organization; the route (organization.route.ts line 19) has no checkPermission and no feature guard, and the controller never uses req.user.activeOrganizationSubscriptionId. Impact: an attacker changes the seat quantity (and therefore billing) of any tenant by supplying that tenant's subscriptionId, and can trigger proration charges. Fix: ignore the client-supplied subscriptionId and use req.user.activeOrganizationSubscriptionId, and gate the route with the appropriate admin permission.

findings.title: Any authenticated user can change another tenant's subscription plan by ID
findings.description: Entry: packages/ui/src/api/user.js:25 (updateSubscriptionPlan) -> POST /api/v1/organization/update-subscription-plan. Attacker: any authenticated user, crossing the billing boundary to change another tenant's plan. req.body.subscriptionId/newPlanId/prorationDate are read from the caller (line 151) and passed to identityManager.updateSubscriptionPlan(req, subscriptionId, newPlanId, prorationDate) (line 162) with no check that the subscription belongs to the caller. The route (organization.route.ts line 23) has no authorization middleware and the controller does not use req.user.activeOrganizationSubscriptionId. Impact: an attacker moves any tenant to an arbitrary plan (downgrade/upgrade) and incurs proration charges by supplying that tenant's subscriptionId. Fix: derive the subscription from req.user.activeOrganizationSubscriptionId and require an admin permission on the route.

findings.title: Unset HTTP_DENY_LIST lets any flow author SSRF the server into internal networks
findings.description: Entry: packages/server/.env.example:174 (HTTP_DENY_LIST ships commented out, i.e. unset) reaching the fetch sinks at packages/components/src/utils.ts:426 / 482 (secureFetch), utils.ts:1658-1661 (the node-fetch mock used inside tool code), packages/components/nodes/tools/RequestsGet/core.ts:170, RequestsPost/core.ts:130, RequestsPut/core.ts:130, RequestsDelete/core.ts:170, WebScraperTool/WebScraperTool.ts:62 and packages/components/nodes/chains/ApiChain/postCore.ts:95. Attacker: a user of a Flowise instance who can build/run a flow (or drive an agent that holds one of these tools), crossing from the application sandbox into the server's own internal network and cloud metadata endpoint. The path: the caller supplies the request URL (tool argument or flow configuration), it flows to the tool's _call, into secureFetch/secureAxiosRequest, into resolveAndValidate(url) at packages/components/src/httpSecurity.ts:188, where the code reads `const denyListString = process.env.HTTP_DENY_LIST` and sets `denyList = denyListString ? ... : null`; when the variable is unset, the `if (denyList)` guards at lines 197 and 214 are skipped entirely and the function simply returns the resolved target, so `createPinnedAgent` happily pins the connection to `127.0.0.1`, `10.x.x.x`, `192.168.x.x` or `169.254.169.254`. Nothing else on the path stops it: there is no hostname allow-list, no protocol restriction (plain http to an internal port is fine), and because the socket is pinned to the resolved IP there is no way for a later check to catch it. checkDenyList (line 40) has the same `if (!httpDenyListString) return` early exit, so the fetch-links crawler at packages/server/src/services/fetch-links/index.ts:9 is equally unprotected. Impact for this application: on any default install (the variable is commented out in packages/server/.env.example and in all three docker .env.example files, and only surfaced as an optional CLI flag at packages/server/src/commands/base.ts:103), any user who can configure a flow turns the Flowise server into an internal-network proxy — reading cloud instance metadata credentials (169.254.169.254), hitting unauthenticated internal services, Redis/Postgres admin ports and Kubernetes APIs from inside the trust boundary — with the response body returned to them. Fix: invert the default so the deny list always exists (seed it with loopback, link-local, and all RFC1918/CGNAT/ULA ranges unless the operator explicitly widens it), perform the check in resolveAndValidate unconditionally rather than behind `if (denyList)`, and additionally reject non-http(s) schemes.

findings.title: Unauthenticated attacker can dump any tenant's private chatflow flowData
findings.description: Entry: packages/server/src/controllers/chatflows/index.ts:246 (getSinglePublicChatbotConfig -> chatflowsService.getSinglePublicChatbotConfig(req.params.id)). Attacker: an unauthenticated caller, crossing the login boundary and the tenant boundary. The route /api/v1/public-chatbotConfig/:id (routes/public-chatbots/index.ts:8, mounted at routes/index.ts:110) is in WHITELIST_URLS (utils/constants.ts:10), so index.ts:215-223 calls next() without verifyToken or API-key validation and req.user is never required. The controller passes req.params.id straight through with only a presence check, and the service does ChatFlow.findOneBy({ id: chatflowId }) (line 366) with no workspaceId filter and, unlike getSinglePublicChatflow, with no isPublic check at all. If the row has any chatbotConfig or uploads enabled, line 391 returns { ...parsedConfig, uploads, flowData, isTTSEnabled } - i.e. the entire flowData node graph for a flow in any workspace/organization, plus the chatbot config. Nothing on the path stops it: the only guard that exists elsewhere (getSinglePublicChatflow's isPublic/membership check) is not applied here, and the comment claiming it is safe only reasons about chatbotConfig, not about flowData, which is returned unconditionally. Impact: anyone on the network can enumerate chatflow UUIDs and dump the full flow definition (node parameters, embedded file paths/credential ids, system prompts, internal endpoints) of every tenant's private flows. Fix: require the chatflow to be isPublic before returning anything, and never include flowData in this public response; scope the lookup to the caller's workspace for non-public flows.

findings.title: API key listing returns chatflows from other workspaces
findings.description: Entry: packages/server/src/routes/chatflows/index.ts:24 (GET /api/v1/chatflows/apikey/:apikey -> chatflowsController.getChatflowByApiKey), controller at controllers/chatflows/index.ts:97-101. Attacker: any holder of one valid API key (or, because the route is whitelisted at utils/constants.ts:8, anyone who obtains/guesses a key), crossing the tenant boundary. The controller validates only that the string matches a row via apiKeyService.getApiKey(apiKey) (services/apikey/index.ts:144-157, findOneBy({apiKey}) with no workspace scoping), then calls getChatflowByApiKey(apikey.id). The query at lines 225-232 filters only on cf.apikeyid = :apikeyid, and when keyonly is undefined it ORs in cf.apikeyid IS NULL and cf.apikeyid = '', with no workspaceId/organizationId predicate. Nothing restricts the result to the key's workspace: an API key scoped to workspace A returns every unbound chatflow across all workspaces in the deployment. Impact: cross-tenant disclosure of other organizations' flows (names, flowData, chatbot/api config) to any API key holder, plus a listing primitive for the id-based endpoints. Fix: join workspace and constrain cf.workspaceId to apiKey.workspaceId (and the workspace's organization) before applying the apikeyid/IS NULL conditions.

findings.title: Authenticated user can move chatflows into any other workspace via mass assignment
findings.description: Entry: packages/server/src/routes/chatflows/index.ts:27-31 (PUT /api/v1/chatflows/:id -> updateChatflow). Attacker: an authenticated low-privileged user with chatflows:update, crossing the workspace/tenant boundary and the field-level authorization boundary. The handler loads the chatflow scoped to req.user.activeWorkspaceId (line 182, correct), but then does const updateChatFlow = new ChatFlow(); Object.assign(updateChatFlow, body) (lines 195-196) and only forces updateChatFlow.id = chatflow.id (line 198) - it never clears workspaceId. The service then runs getRepository(ChatFlow).merge(chatflow, updateChatFlow) (services/chatflows/index.ts:354) and save, and TypeORM merge copies every defined body property, so workspaceId from the request body overrides the loaded chatflow's workspace. Nothing validates or strips workspaceId (or isPublic/apikeyid/type) from the body. Impact: a user can move a flow out of their workspace into any other workspace id, and can flip isPublic/apikeyid on their own flows, breaking workspace isolation and data ownership. Fix: whitelist the fields that may be updated (name, flowData, chatbotConfig, apiConfig, etc.) instead of Object.assign-ing the whole body, or explicitly re-assert updateChatFlow.workspaceId = workspaceId (and reject body-supplied workspaceId/id/isPublic/apikeyid) before merge.

findings.title: Unauthenticated attacker can read decrypted SSO client secrets via GET /api/v1/loginmethod
findings.description:
Entry: packages/server/src/routes/index.ts:221 (whitelist check) -> packages/server/src/enterprise/routes/login-method.route.ts:8 (router.get('/', loginMethodController.read)) -> login-method.controller.ts:72 (read).
Attacker: an unauthenticated remote caller, crossing the authentication boundary to reach another tenant's/client's SSO provider secrets.
The path: GET /api/v1/loginmethod is whitelisted in packages/server/src/utils/constants.ts:36 (WHITELIST_URLS), so the global middleware in packages/server/src/index.ts:215-285 calls next() without running verifyToken or validateAPIKey. The route (login-method.route.ts:8) has no checkPermission guard (unlike the sibling POST/PUT/'/test' routes, which require 'sso:manage'). The read controller then selects the LoginMethod row by the attacker-supplied query.id or query.organizationId (login-method.service.ts:36-58) and, at lines 94 and 99, does `loginMethod.config = JSON.parse(await decrypt(loginMethod.config))` and returns it in the JSON response. Nothing on the path restricts who may call it or which organization's row is returned.
Why nothing stops it: the whitelist bypasses all auth for any path starting with '/api/v1/loginmethod'; the route defines no verifyToken and no checkPermission; the service only validates that the id is a UUID, never that the requester owns it. decrypt() succeeds for any stored config.
Impact: the decrypted config is exactly the object AzureSSO.setSSOConfig / AzureSSO.refreshToken and the other providers consume — tenantID, clientID and clientSecret (and Auth0/GitHub/Google equivalents).
