An unauthenticated attacker enumerates login-method rows and exfiltrates the OAuth client secrets used to authenticate users to the organization's identity provider, enabling account takeover and impersonation against Azure AD/Google/Auth0/GitHub.
Fix: remove '/api/v1/loginmethod' from WHITELIST_URLS and add an explicit auth guard, and add checkPermission('sso:manage') to the GET '/' route; never return clientSecret in the read response (mask it), and scope the query to the caller's organization.

findings.title: Missing authz on /assistants/generate/instruction lets any user use others' LLM credentials
findings.description:
Entry: packages/server/src/routes/assistants/index.ts:25 (router.post('/generate/instruction', assistantsController.generateAssistantInstruction) - no checkPermission, unlike every other route in this router).
Attacker: an authenticated user or API key that holds no assistants:* permission, crossing into another workspace's/organization's LLM credential.
The controller (packages/server/src/controllers/assistants/index.ts:178) forwards req.body.task and req.body.selectedChatModel unchanged into generateAssistantInstruction. The service resolves the node class from the caller-controlled name (appServer.nodesPool.componentNodes[selectedChatModel.name].filePath), instantiates it, and sets nodeData.credential = selectedChatModel.credential, then newNodeInstance.init(nodeData, '', options). The node's init calls getCredentialData(nodeData.credential) (packages/components/src/utils.ts:621-643), which does appDataSource.getRepository(Credential).findOneBy({ id: selectedCredentialId }) with no workspaceId or organization filter, decrypts the secret and uses it for the outbound model call.
Nothing on the path stops it: the route has no permission middleware (contrast lines 8, 11, 12, 15, 18 of the same file), the controller performs only a presence check on req.body, and the credential lookup is by primary key alone. Because the global /api/v1 middleware (packages/server/src/index.ts:215-285) only establishes that the caller is authenticated and copies apiKey.permissions into req.user, a caller with a read-only or empty permission set still reaches this handler.
Impact: any authenticated tenant can drive an LLM node with another workspace's credential, consuming the victim's quota/billing and using their provider account; the selected node name is also attacker-chosen, so any chat-model node (including ones that reach an attacker-chosen base URL) can be invoked server-side.
Fix: add checkPermission('assistants:create') (or a dedicated permission) to the /generate/instruction route, and make getCredentialData/credential lookups filter by the caller's workspaceId (e.g. findOneBy({ id, workspaceId })), rejecting credentials that do not belong to req.user.activeWorkspaceId.

findings.title: Cross-tenant assistant move via mass-assignable workspaceId
findings.description:
Entry: packages/server/src/routes/assistants/index.ts:15 (router.put(['/', '/:id'], checkAnyPermission('assistants:create,assistants:update'), assistantsController.updateAssistant)) -> packages/server/src/controllers/assistants/index.ts:129, which passes req.body unfiltered.
Attacker: a user holding assistants:update in their own workspace, crossing into another tenant's workspace by rewriting the assistant's workspaceId.
In the CUSTOM branch the service does const body = requestBody; const updateAssistant = new Assistant(); Object.assign(updateAssistant, body); repository.merge(assistant, updateAssistant); repository.save(assistant). The non-CUSTOM branch (lines 379-384) does the same. Assistant.workspaceId is a plain non-nullable text column (packages/server/src/database/entities/Assistant.ts:30-31), so any workspaceId present in the request body overwrites the stored one.
Nothing on the path stops it: the only authorization is the assistants:create/update permission, which is workspace-agnostic; the controller never pins workspaceId, and createAssistant does pin it (packages/server/src/controllers/assistants/index.ts:38 sets body.workspaceId = workspaceId before the service call), showing the update path simply forgot it. The existing row is fetched with workspaceId = req.user.activeWorkspaceId, so the attacker can only move their own assistant, but the destination is fully caller-chosen.
Impact: an assistant (and its details, which embed the OpenAI assistant id and tool_resources) is transplanted into a workspace the caller does not belong to, corrupting another tenant's assistant listing and making their records editable/visible through that tenant's assistants:view endpoints.
Fix: build the update payload from an allow-list of fields (details, credential, type, iconSrc) instead of Object.assign of the raw body, or explicitly set updateAssistant.workspaceId = workspaceId after the assign and validate that the target workspace exists and the caller is a member of it.

findings.title: Users lacking assistants permission can read chat models, tools and doc stores
findings.description:
Entry: packages/server/src/routes/assistants/index.ts:20-22 (router.get('/components/chatmodels'|'/components/docstores'|'/components/tools', <handler>) - no checkPermission).
Attacker: an authenticated user or API key whose role grants no assistants permissions, crossing the role/permission boundary the rest of this router enforces.
These three routes call assistantsController.getChatModels, getDocumentStores and getTools, which require no permission at all; every other route in the same file (lines 8, 11, 12, 15, 18) is wrapped in checkPermission/checkAnyPermission. The global /api/v1 middleware (packages/server/src/index.ts:215-285) only authenticates the caller and copies apiKey.permissions into req.user, so a key with an empty or unrelated permission set reaches these handlers.
Nothing on the path stops it: no permission middleware is attached and no in-controller role check exists (packages/server/src/controllers/assistants/index.ts:136-168). getDocumentStores does scope its query by the caller's workspace (getWorkspaceSearchOptions), so no cross-tenant rows leak, but the permission gate itself is absent for all three.
Impact: the assistants component catalog (chat models, tools, MCP tools) and the caller's own document-store list are exposed to principals the RBAC configuration deliberately excluded from the assistants module; this is a straightforward RBAC bypass, and it is the same missing-guard pattern that leaves /generate/instruction open (see the first finding).
Fix: wrap each of these three routes in checkPermission('assistants:view') (or checkAnyPermission('assistants:view,assistants:create')) so they match their siblings.

findings.title: Authenticated user can reassign document store workspaceId via PUT body, crossing tenants
findings.description:
Entry: packages/server/src/controllers/documentstore/index.ts:358 (PUT /api/v1/document-store/store/:id), routed at packages/server/src/routes/documentstore/index.ts:24.
Attacker: an authenticated user with documentStores:create/update in their workspace, crossing the tenant boundary by setting the record's workspaceId from the request body.
The path: req.body -> const updateDocStore = new DocumentStore(); Object.assign(updateDocStore, body) -> documentStoreService.updateDocumentStore(store, updateDocStore) -> repository.merge(store, updatedDocumentStore) then repository.save. workspaceId is a writable column on DocumentStore (packages/server/src/database/entities/DocumentStore.ts:41), and unlike createDocumentStore (which pins body.workspaceId = req.user.activeWorkspaceId), this controller never overrides it, so a client-supplied workspaceId in the JSON body is merged onto the entity and persisted.
Why nothing stops it: there is no allow-list of updatable fields and no removal/override of the tenant field before the merge; the store being updated is correctly fetched for the caller's workspace, but the body then reassigns its workspaceId.
Impact: a user can move their document store into an arbitrary (foreign) workspace id, injecting/relocating a record into another tenant's data set, and can also overwrite other sensitive fields (status, loaders, whereUsed) directly from the body.
Fix: whitelist the updatable fields (e.g. name, description) instead of Object.assign of the whole body, and explicitly delete/ignore body.workspaceId, id, status and other server-managed fields before merging.

findings.title: Unauthenticated caller can read a tenant's enabled SSO providers
findings.description: Entry: packages/server/src/enterprise/controllers/login-method.controller.ts:45 (organizationService.readOrganization) reached from router.get('/default', loginMethodController.defaultMethods) in packages/server/src/enterprise/routes/login-method.route.ts:10. Attacker: an unauthenticated remote caller, crossing the authentication boundary to learn another tenant's SSO configuration. Path: GET /api/v1/loginmethod/default -> defaultMethods reads the first organization (organizations[0].id, controller line 47) and then readLoginMethodByOrganizationId returns its login methods, from which the enabled provider names are collected and returned as { providers }. Nothing stops it: the route is whitelisted (constants.ts:36), so index.ts:221-223 bypasses authentication and req.user is undefined, and the handler has no checkPermission; it uses the first organization unconditionally rather than the caller's organization. Impact: an unauthenticated attacker can discover which SSO providers (azure/google/auth0/github) are enabled for the tenant, exposing the identity-provider surface for targeted attacks. Fix: keep only a strictly public subset (provider names) if the sign-in page needs it, but scope it to the intended organization and require authentication for anything beyond the minimum the login page requires; do not select organizations[0] blindly for anonymous callers.

findings.title: Chatflow author can force Flowise server to POST to arbitrary internal hosts
findings.description:
Entry: packages/components/nodes/documentloaders/FireCrawl/FireCrawl.ts:943 (firecrawlApiUrl = getCredentialParam('firecrawlApiUrl', credentialData, nodeData, 'https://api.firecrawl.dev')), consumed via this.apiUrl at line 191/293/405/444.
Attacker: a chatflow author/editor (a workspace user holding chatflows:create/update) crossing into the server's internal network by making the Flowise server issue an outbound HTTP POST to a host of their choosing.
Path: the chatflow JSON is stored verbatim and, at execution, buildFlow clones reactFlowNode.data (packages/server/src/utils/index.ts:588) and resolveVariables iterates every key in flowNodeData['inputs'] (packages/server/src/utils/index.ts:1076) with no filtering against the node's declared input params. getCredentialParam (packages/components/src/utils.ts:656-658) evaluates nodeData.inputs['firecrawlApiUrl'] BEFORE credentialData['firecrawlApiUrl'], so an injected input overrides the admin-set credential URL. That value becomes this.apiUrl (FireCrawl.ts:571, 139) and is concatenated as this.apiUrl + '/v1/scrape' etc., then passed as the url argument to postRequest, which calls raw axios.post(url, data, { headers }) at line 469.
Why nothing stops it: the FireCrawl node declares no firecrawlApiUrl input, so the only intended source is the credential; but getCredentialParam's node-input-first precedence lets a flow author bypass that. The request uses plain axios with no allow-list, no scheme check, no DNS pinning and no HTTP_DENY_LIST enforcement, and axios follows redirects by default. The codebase already ships secureAxiosRequest/checkDenyList in packages/components/src/httpSecurity.ts and uses it in RequestsGet/RequestsPost/WebScraperTool/HTTP/fetch-links, but this node does not.
Impact: the Flowise server performs POST requests (with the Firecrawl API key in the Authorization header, and attacker-chosen JSON body) to arbitrary internal endpoints — cloud metadata (169.254.169.254), localhost admin ports, internal microservices, or other tenants' internal hosts — enabling internal port scanning, credential/metadata theft and interaction with unauthenticated internal APIs, with the server's own response content returned to the caller.
Fix: stop reading the API URL from nodeData.inputs (use only the credential value), and route this call through secureAxiosRequest so the resolved host is validated against an allow-list and HTTP_DENY_LIST before the request is sent, with redirects disabled or re-validated.

findings.title: Any authenticated user can read another organization's user directory
findings.description: Entry: packages/server/src/enterprise/routes/organization-user.route.ts:9 (router.get('/', organizationUserController.read)). Attacker: any authenticated user (a non-admin workspace member with no users:manage permission, or an API-key caller) crossing the tenant boundary to read another organization's user directory. The GET route has no checkPermission middleware while its POST/PUT/DELETE siblings all require checkPermission('users:manage'); the request reaches OrganizationUserController.read (organization-user.controller.ts:35-80), which reads req.query.organizationId and calls OrganizationUserService.readOrganizationUserByOrganizationId (organization-user.service.ts:86-126), returning every user's email, name, role and last-login for whatever organizationId the caller supplies. Nothing on the path stops it: /api/v1/organizationuser is not in WHITELIST_URLS (utils/constants.ts:6-55) so only a login is required, req.user is set but the handler never consults req.user.activeOrganizationId, and no middleware compares the query organizationId to the caller's org. Impact: any authenticated tenant can enumerate another tenant's users (emails, roles, statuses), enabling targeted phishing and account-takeover reconnaissance. Fix: add checkPermission('users:manage') to the GET route and, in the controller, reject any organizationId that is not req.user.activeOrganizationId (or resolve the org from req.user instead of from the query).

findings.title: Org admin can add users to any other organization via client-supplied organizationId
findings.description: Entry: packages/server/src/enterprise/controllers/organization-user.controller.ts:28 (createOrganizationUser(req.body)). Attacker: an organization admin/member holding users:manage in org A crossing into org B to add users there. POST /organizationuser is guarded only by checkFeatureByPlan('feat:users') and checkPermission('users:manage'), which test the caller's own permission string, not the target; the handler passes the whole req.body straight to OrganizationUserService.createOrganizationUser (organization-user.service.ts:212-243), which uses data.organizationId, data.userId, data.roleId and data.createdBy exactly as the client sent them. Nothing compares req.body.organizationId to req.user.activeOrganizationId (grep confirms no such check exists anywhere), and createdBy is taken from the body rather than req.user.id. Impact: a tenant can inject/attach arbitrary users (including itself) into another organization with an attacker-chosen roleId, escalating into a foreign tenant. Fix: ignore client organizationId/createdBy and use req.user.activeOrganizationId and req.user.id, rejecting any mismatch.

findings.title: Cross-tenant user role change via mass-assigned organizationId in PUT /organizationuser
findings.description: Entry: packages/server/src/enterprise/controllers/organization-user.controller.ts:85 (updateOrganizationUser(req.body)). Attacker: a users:manage holder in org A crossing into org B to modify membership/roles. PUT /organizationuser is guarded only by checkFeatureByPlan('feat:users') and checkPermission('users:manage'); the entire req.body is mass-assigned to the record in OrganizationUserService.updateOrganizationUser (organization-user.service.ts:278-311), where queryRunner.manager.merge(OrganizationUser, organizationUser, newOrganizationUser) copies any client-supplied fields, including roleId, status, organizationId and userId. The lookup uses the client's organizationId+userId and nothing validates that organizationId belongs to the caller's organization (no comparison to req.user.activeOrganizationId anywhere). Impact: an attacker can change another tenant's user role to owner or alter membership, gaining administrative control of a foreign organization. Fix: derive organizationId from req.user.activeOrganizationId, whitelist the updatable fields (do not merge raw body), and re-check the caller's role against the target org.

findings.title: users:manage holder can delete members and accounts of any organization
findings.description: Entry: packages/server/src/enterprise/controllers/organization-user.controller.ts:98-134 (req.query.organizationId and req.query.userId). Attacker: a users:manage holder in org A crossing into org B to delete membership and, on Enterprise, the user account itself. DELETE /organizationuser is guarded only by checkFeatureByPlan('feat:users') and checkPermission('users:manage'); the handler reads organizationId and userId from the query and calls OrganizationUserService.deleteOrganizationUser (organization-user.service.ts:314-335), which deletes OrganizationUser and WorkspaceUser rows for that organizationId/userId; on Platform.ENTERPRISE it also soft-deletes the global User record (renames email, clears credential/tokenExpiry/tempToken at organization-user.controller.ts:124-132). Nothing checks that the query organizationId equals req.user.activeOrganizationId, so any users:manage caller can delete users from any organization and, in Enterprise, destroy the victim's account globally. Fix: validate organizationId against req.user.activeOrganizationId and restrict deletion to the caller's own organization.

findings.title: Any authenticated user can read other tenants' role definitions via GET /role
findings.description: Entry: packages/server/src/enterprise/routes/role.route.ts:8 (router.get('/', roleController.read)). Attacker: any authenticated user (or API-key holder) in an organization with the roles feature, crossing from their own account into other users'/other tenants' role data. The route is mounted at /api/v1/role (routes/index.ts:132) behind only IdentityManager.checkFeatureByPlan('feat:roles'), which merely requires the caller to be logged in and the plan to include the roles feature; unlike the sibling POST/PUT/DELETE on lines 10/12/14 it has no checkPermission('roles:manage'). roleController.read (role.controller.ts:19-42) then runs for any caller and, with query.id, calls roleService.readRoleById, or with query.organizationId calls readRoleByOrganizationId, or with no params returns all general roles. Nothing on the path verifies the caller holds roles:manage or that the requested role belongs to the caller's organization; readRoleById (role.service.ts:35-38) queries by {id} alone and readRoleByOrganizationId (role.service.ts:44-56) queries by the client-supplied organizationId alone. Impact: a low-privileged member of one tenant can enumerate and read the full role definitions, permission sets and member counts of any other tenant simply by supplying its organizationId or a role id, and can read general (owner/admin) role definitions. Fix: add checkPermission('roles:manage') (or a read-specific permission) to the GET route and scope every read to req.user.activeOrganizationId, rejecting ids/organizationIds that do not belong to the caller's organization.

findings.title: Org admin can overwrite roles in other organizations by id
findings.description: Entry: packages/server/src/enterprise/controllers/role.controller.ts:47 (roleService.updateRole(req.body)), reached from router.put('/') at packages/server/src/enterprise/routes/role.route.ts:12 with checkPermission('roles:manage'). Attacker: an organization administrator of tenant A crossing into tenant B by writing a role that belongs to B. checkPermission (PermissionCheck.ts:5-21) only confirms the caller is an org admin or holds roles:manage in their own organization; it does not scope the target. updateRole loads the victim role via readRoleById(newRole.id) (no organizationId filter, line 123), then sets newRole.organizationId = oldRole.organizationId and newRole.createdBy = oldRole.createdBy (lines 128-129) and merges/saves. Nothing compares the loaded role's organizationId to the caller's activeOrganizationId, so an admin in one organization can overwrite the name/permissions of any role in any other organization by passing that role's id in the request body. Impact: cross-tenant privilege escalation — an attacker can widen another tenant's role permissions or rename its roles, and because workspace users reference roleId, the change takes effect for that tenant's members. Fix: after loading oldRole, verify oldRole.organizationId === req.user.activeOrganizationId (and that the role is not a general/system role) before merging, and derive organizationId from the authenticated session instead of copying it from the loaded record.

findings.title: Cross-tenant role deletion via attacker-controlled organizationId
findings.description: Entry: packages/server/src/enterprise/controllers/role.controller.ts:56-64 (query.organizationId and query.id passed to roleService.deleteRole), reached from router.delete('/') at packages/server/src/enterprise/routes/role.route.ts:14 with checkPermission('roles:manage'). Attacker: an organization administrator of tenant A crossing into tenant B by deleting a role in another organization. The controller only checks that both query params are present; it never compares query.organizationId with req.user.activeOrganizationId. deleteRole then calls readRoleByRoleIdOrganizationId(roleId, organizationId) (role.service.ts:58-64), which looks up the role using the client-supplied organizationId, and on match deletes every WorkspaceUser row referencing that roleId (line 156) and the Role row itself (line 157). Because organizationId is attacker-controlled and unscoped, an admin can pass any other tenant's organizationId together with a role id from that tenant and delete it. Impact: cross-tenant destructive write — removal of another organization's roles and the unlinking of all its workspace members' role assignments, breaking that tenant's access control configuration. Fix: reject the request unless query.organizationId equals req.user.activeOrganizationId (or derive the organization from the session and ignore the query value), and re-verify the role belongs to that organization before deleting.

findings.title: Authenticated member can create users via unguarded POST /api/v1/user
findings.description:
Entry: packages/server/src/enterprise/routes/user.route.ts:10 (POST /api/v1/user).
Attacker: any authenticated caller with no user-management role — a plain workspace member or any API-key holder — crossing into an administrator-only operation.
Path: router.post('/', userController.create) with no middleware -> UserController.create (user.controller.ts:13) -> userService.createUser(req.body) -> createNewUser/saveUser, which persists a User row built from the whole request body (name, email, status, credential hashed, createdBy). The global middleware (index.ts:215-285) only authenticates; checkPermission is never applied on this route. The equivalent create on the sibling router, organization-user.route.ts:11, is guarded by IdentityManager.checkFeatureByPlan('feat:users') + checkPermission('users:manage'), so the permission that is supposed to gate user creation is simply absent here.
Impact: an ordinary member or API key can create arbitrary User records in the instance, bypassing the users:manage permission the application otherwise enforces, and can seed records with a chosen status/createdBy — data pollution and a foothold for later account/tenant manipulation. createUser also allows a caller-supplied createdBy (validated only as an existing user), letting the attacker attribute the record to someone else.
Fix: add IdentityManager.checkFeatureByPlan('feat:users') and checkPermission('users:manage') (or isOrganizationAdmin) to the POST route, and force createdBy to req.user.id server-side instead of trusting the body.

findings.title: Mass assignment in updateUser lets a user overwrite own credential and status
findings.description:
Entry: packages/server/src/enterprise/controllers/user.controller.ts:63 (PUT /api/v1/user, body copied from req.body after only an id-equality check at lines 59-62).
Attacker: an authenticated user crossing the field-level boundary on their own account, setting fields the update flow is supposed to control.
Path: req.body -> UserController.update (only checks currentUser.id === req.body.id, i.e. self) -> userService.updateUser(req.body) -> queryRunner.manager.merge(User, oldUserData, newUserData) then saveUser. updateUser copies every body field onto the record; the only fields it guards are name/status (enum validation) and createdBy (forced back to the old value at line 152). It does NOT re-hash a body-supplied credential: credential is hashed only inside the oldPassword/newPassword/confirmPassword branch (line 173), so a body field credential is merged and stored verbatim, and tempToken/tokenExpiry can be set to arbitrary values.
Impact: a user can overwrite their own credential with an arbitrary unhashed string (self-lockout / credential-store poisoning and a way to break the password-hash invariant the login path relies on, account.service.ts:476), and can set status to any valid enum value (active/invited/unverified/deleted) and tempToken to any value without going through verify()/reset flows. The controller's own id check is the only barrier, and it is a self-check, not an allow-list of writable fields.
Fix: build the update payload from an explicit allow-list (name, and password fields only through the existing hashing branch), never merge the raw request body; re-hash any accepted credential and drop status/tempToken/tokenExpiry/createdBy/updatedBy from client input.

cases.checks: Of 1 published vulnerability in langflow-ai/langflow@73c1f203, how many does a scan capped at $3 report?

detail.what: GHSA-8C4J-F57C-35CF (authz) Langflow flow API 水平越权（CVE-2026-34046 / GHSA-8c4j-f57c-35cf） - flows.py

findings.title: Authenticated user can execute any other user's flow by UUID
findings.description: Entry: src/backend/base/langflow/api/v1/voice_mode.py:702 (WebSocket /ws/flow_as_tool/{flow_id}, and /ws/flow_as_tool/{flow_id}/{session_id} at line 719). Attacker: any authenticated Langflow user (valid JWT cookie/query token or API key) crossing into another user's flow data and execution. The client-supplied flow_id path parameter is accepted by flow_as_tool_websocket, stored on FunctionCall (flow_id=flow_id, line 1040), and passed to handle_function_call (line 689), which calls build_flow_and_stream(flow_id=UUID(flow_id), inputs=..., background_tasks=..., current_user=current_user) at line 431. build_flow_and_stream -> build_flow (chat.py:143) -> start_flow_build (api/build.py:41) -> generate_flow_events -> create_graph -> build_graph_from_db_no_cache (api/utils.py:185-198), which does session.get(Flow, flow_id) and builds the graph with no Flow.user_id check. Nothing on the path verifies ownership: get_current_user_for_websocket (services/auth/utils.py:221) only proves the caller is some valid user, and build_flow only checks that the flow row exists (chat.py:180-184). Additionally get_flow_desc_from_db (voice_mode.py:524-532) reads any flow's description by id alone. Impact: an authenticated user can execute any other user's flow by guessing/knowing its UUID, causing the flow's components to run with the victim's stored flow data and returning the flow's output (and its description) to the attacker — a full cross-tenant IDOR over flow execution. Fix: load the flow scoped to the caller (e.g. select(Flow).where(Flow.id == flow_id, Flow.user_id == current_user.id) or reuse get_flow_by_id_or_endpoint_name with user_id) and reject with a policy violation before building the graph; apply the same ownership check in get_flow_desc_from_db.

findings.title: Authenticated user can use another user's ElevenLabs key and voices
findings.description:
Entry: src/backend/base/langflow/api/v1/voice_mode.py:1346 (GET /voice/elevenlabs/voice_ids), also reached from voice_mode.py:1283 and voice_mode.py:875.
Attacker: any authenticated user, crossing into another user's ElevenLabs account and decrypted API key.
Path: get_elevenlabs_voice_ids (1346) → get_or_create_elevenlabs_client(current_user.id, session) (1354) → ElevenLabsClientManager.get_client(user_id, session) (175). The first caller populates the class attributes cls._api_key and cls._instance from that caller's own user-scoped secret (variable_service.get_variable filters Variable.user_id == user_id, confirmed at services/variable/service.py:65). Every later caller — a different user with a different user_id — is served the cached cls._instance because the `if cls._instance is None` guard on line 177 is already False, so their user_id is never used.
Why nothing stops it: get_client is a class-level singleton and the user_id argument is ignored once _instance is set; there is no per-user keying of the cached client. The endpoint requires only a valid login (CurrentActiveUser), not ownership of the key.
Impact: user B's requests are billed to and executed under user A's ElevenLabs API key, and GET /voice/elevenlabs/voice_ids returns user A's account-specific voice list to user B — a credential and account-data exposure across users.
Fix: cache the ElevenLabs client per user (e.g. key the cache by user_id, or store it on request/app state keyed by user_id) instead of in class-level attributes, and never share a decrypted secret between users.

findings.title: Cross-site WebSocket hijacking drives victim's authenticated voice sockets
findings.description:
Entry: src/backend/base/langflow/api/v1/voice_mode.py:702 (and 719, 1130, 1147) — @router.websocket endpoints that call client_websocket.accept() at line 729 and then get_current_user_for_websocket at line 735.
Attacker: An unauthenticated external website the victim merely visits, crossing the origin boundary into the victim's authenticated Langflow session.
The websocket authenticates via services/auth/utils.py:225, which reads the access_token_lf cookie (or a token query param), and the endpoints accept the socket before/without ever validating the Origin header. A grep of the whole backend shows no Origin/check_origin/trusted-origin validation anywhere (main.py registers only CORSMiddleware, which does not apply to WebSocket handshakes).
Nothing on the path stops it: browsers automatically attach cookies to cross-origin WebSocket handshakes, WebSockets are not subject to CORS preflight, and no code inspects the Origin or Host of the handshake, so the server accepts the socket as the victim and the attacker page can send arbitrary JSON frames (e.g. langflow.elevenlabs.config, session.update, audio/response frames) to it.
Impact for this application: a malicious page can drive the victim's authenticated voice sockets — running the victim's flows through execute_flow, streaming audio and flow output back to the attacker's script, and consuming the victim's OpenAI/ElevenLabs keys — all without the victim's knowledge.
Fix: validate the Origin header on every websocket handshake against an allow-list of trusted frontend origins before calling accept(), and reject the connection otherwise (or move to a non-cookie credential, e.g. a short-lived one-time websocket ticket).

findings.title: Authenticated user exhausts server memory via unbounded session_id cache
findings.description:
Entry: src/backend/base/langflow/api/v1/voice_mode.py:1212 (`get_tts_config(session_id, openai_key)` inside the websocket handler /ws/flow_tts/{flow_id}/{session_id} at line 1147); the same pattern exists at line 734 (`get_voice_config(session_id)`) for /ws/flow_as_tool/{flow_id}/{session_id}.
Attacker: an authenticated low-privilege user, crossing the boundary from "my own short-lived session" to "process-global state I can grow without limit"; any flow_id is accepted because the handler only reads the flow description.
Path: `session_id` arrives as a client-controlled path parameter (line 1153) or is generated only when the no-session route is used (line 1137); it is passed straight to `get_tts_config` at 1212, which does `if session_id not in tts_config_cache: tts_config_cache[session_id] = TTSConfig(session_id, openai_key)` at 255-256. `get_voice_config` at 203-209 does the identical thing for `voice_config_cache`.
Why nothing stops it: both caches are plain module-level dicts declared at lines 513-514 with no size limit, no TTL and no eviction path — I grepped the file and the only writes are lines 207-208 and 255-256, with no delete, pop, clear or expiry anywhere. Authentication happens before the insert but does not constrain the key, so a user can supply an unlimited number of distinct session_ids.
Impact: each entry is a live Python object (TTSConfig at line 238 constructs and retains an OpenAI client; VoiceConfig holds a full session dict), so a loop that opens `ws/flow_tts/{flow_id}/{random_uuid}` grows the dictionary without bound and pins memory for the lifetime of the process, exhausting it and denying service to all users.
Fix: key the cache by user id and evict entries on websocket disconnect (or use an LRU/TTL cache such as cachetools.TTLCache with a hard maxsize), and reject or ignore a client-supplied session_id that the caller did not just create.

findings.title: Authenticated user grows unbounded per-connection response dict, exhausting memory
findings.description:
Entry: src/backend/base/langflow/api/v1/voice_mode.py:1000 (`responses[response_id] = Response(...)` inside forward_to_client, reached from the websocket /ws/flow_as_tool/{flow_id}/{session_id} at line 719).
Attacker: an authenticated low-privilege user, crossing the boundary from "one response at a time" to "an unbounded per-connection structure"; they simply use the voice feature normally and can make OpenAI emit many responses.
Path: `response_id` comes from the OpenAI event at line 991; on `response.created` the code inserts `responses[response_id] = Response(response_id, voice_config.use_elevenlabs)` at line 1000. When ElevenLabs is enabled the constructor additionally spawns a `process_text_deltas` task and an `asyncio.Queue` (lines 863-865).
Why nothing stops it: the only removal is `responses.pop(response_id)` at line 1017, which sits inside the `response.text.done` branch and is further gated by `if voice_config.use_elevenlabs:` at line 1013. Responses that never emit `response.text.done` (audio-only responses, cancellations via the barge-in `response.cancel` at line 800, or any session where the user has not enabled ElevenLabs) leave their entry in the dict for the whole connection, and nothing else ever clears it (grep shows line 1017 as the sole pop).
Impact: a user who keeps a single websocket open and triggers many responses accumulates Response objects — each potentially holding a queue and a background task — for the connection's lifetime, driving the process toward memory exhaustion.
Fix: remove the `responses[response_id]` entry on `response.done` (or on every terminal event) regardless of the ElevenLabs flag, and cancel the associated `text_delta_task` when the response ends.

findings.title: Any authenticated user can build and run another user's flow by ID
findings.description:
Entry: src/backend/base/langflow/api/v1/chat.py:142 (POST /api/v1/build/{flow_id}/flow, flow_id from the path).
Attacker: any authenticated user (or any holder of an API key) crossing into another user's flow data and running it with the owner's identity.
Path: flow_id -> build_flow checks only `flow = await session.get(Flow, flow_id)` and rejects only when the row is absent (lines 182-184); the check never compares flow.user_id to current_user.id. flow_id is then passed to start_flow_build -> generate_flow_events -> create_graph -> build_graph_from_db -> build_graph_from_db_no_cache (api/utils.py:185-192), which does `flow = await session.get(Flow, flow_id)` for any id and then sets `kwargs['user_id'] = kwargs.get('user_id') or str(flow.user_id)`, and the caller passes user_id=str(current_user.id) at api/build.py:264, so the graph executes the victim's stored flow data (including its embedded component credentials/API keys) under the attacker's request.
Why nothing stops it: build_flow has an auth dependency (CurrentActiveUser) but no ownership predicate anywhere on the path; the sibling endpoint POST /run/{flow_id} in api/v1/endpoints.py:547 filters `select(Flow).where(Flow.id == flow_id).where(Flow.user_id == api_key_user.id)` and api/v1/flows.py:277-284 filters on Flow.user_id, proving the missing check is an oversight, not policy.
Impact: horizontal privilege escalation / IDOR — one tenant or user can enumerate flow UUIDs and execute, inspect outputs of, and consume the credentials configured in any other user's flow.
Fix: after loading the flow, reject unless flow.user_id == current_user.id (or the flow is public and the request came through the public endpoint), matching the predicate used in endpoints.py and flows.py.

findings.title: Unauthenticated stream endpoint exposes any user's flow results
findings.description:
Entry: src/backend/base/langflow/api/v1/chat.py:500 (GET /api/v1/build/{flow_id}/{vertex_id}/stream).
Attacker: an unauthenticated caller crossing the login boundary to read another user's flow execution results.
Path: build_vertex_stream takes only flow_id and vertex_id (no current_user dependency) and returns StreamingResponse(_stream_vertex(str(flow_id), vertex_id, get_chat_service())); _stream_vertex (lines 418-497) reads `chat_service.get_cache(flow_id)`, pulls `graph = cache.get('result')` and yields the vertex's built_result/result chunks.
Why nothing stops it: no auth dependency on the handler, no router-level dependency, no auth middleware; the cache is keyed by flow_id alone and is populated by the other chat endpoints (including the unauthenticated retrieve_vertices_order) with no per-user scoping.
Impact: unauthenticated disclosure of another user's flow outputs — built_result/result chunks can contain LLM completions, retrieved documents and tool outputs — and it also leaks internal exception text via StreamData error events.
Fix: require CurrentActiveUser on this deprecated endpoint and verify the flow belongs to the caller (or is public) before streaming, and scope the graph cache per user.

findings.title: Unauthenticated RCE via /build/{flow_id}/vertices code injection
findings.description:
Entry: src/backend/base/langflow/api/v1/chat.py:106 (and :272-278 in api/build.py, reachable from chat.py:186 build_flow and chat.py:614 build_public_tmp).
Attacker: an unauthenticated caller crossing into server-side code execution, because /build/{flow_id}/vertices has no authentication dependency at all yet accepts a full caller-supplied flow graph.
Path: chat.py retrieve_vertices_order takes `data: FlowDataRequest` and calls build_and_cache_graph_from_data(flow_id, data.model_dump(), chat_service) (chat.py:106-108). That calls Graph.from_payload(payload, ...) (api/utils.py:201-211) which stores the payload's nodes/edges verbatim. Each node's data.node.template.code.value is copied unchanged into vertex params by ParameterHandler._handle_code_field (graph/vertex/param_handler.py:192-202). When the vertex is built, instantiate_class pops that `code` and calls eval_custom_component_code(code) (interface/initialize/loading.py:38-47), which calls validate.create_class(code, class_name), which compiles and execs the attacker's source (custom/eval.py:9-12 -> utils/validate.py:172-202).
Why nothing stops it: /build/{flow_id}/vertices (chat.py:71-80) has no current_user dependency and no other auth middleware on the chat router (router.py only includes chat_router without a guard); the `code` field is never validated against an allow-list, the component registry, or the flow's stored data, and no ownership check ties the supplied graph to the flow_id. The endpoint caches the attacker's graph under the attacker-chosen flow_id, so a subsequent vertex build of that flow executes the injected code.
Impact: arbitrary Python execution with the server process's privileges and network/file access on any Langflow deployment that exposes this deprecated route.
Fix: require authentication and authorization on /build/{flow_id}/vertices, and refuse to execute `code` taken from a request body unless it matches the code already stored for that component/flow in the database (validate the graph against the persisted flow rather than trusting the payload).

findings.title: Unauthenticated callers can stream any build job's events by job_id
findings.description:
Entry: src/backend/base/langflow/api/v1/chat.py:210 (@router.get("/build/{job_id}/events"))
Attacker: an unauthenticated caller (or any user who obtains a job_id) crossing into another user's flow-build data, which requires authentication to start.
Path: the request reaches get_build_events, which has no CurrentActiveUser dependency (unlike build_flow at chat.py:153, which does). It calls get_flow_events_response (api/build.py:83), which calls queue_service.get_queue_data(job_id) (services/job_queue/service.py:187). get_queue_data looks the job up in a global dict by job_id with no ownership or user check, and the queue it returns is streamed straight back to the caller (api/build.py:149-178 and the polling branch at api/build.py:104-131). The queue is populated by EventManager.send_event (events/event_manager.py:68-80) from generate_flow_events/_build_vertex (api/build.py:287-397), which serializes the entire VertexBuildResponse into the end_vertex event (api/build.py:419-425).
Why nothing stops it: there is no router-level or app-level authentication (api/router.py:34 includes chat_router with no dependencies; main.py:287-301 registers only CORS/content-size/JS-MIME middleware), the endpoint declares no current_user parameter, and get_queue_data performs no per-user authorization. Any caller who presents the job_id — the id appears in the build/events URL and is handed out by the unauthenticated /build_public_tmp/{flow_id}/flow endpoint (chat.py:632-633) — receives the whole stream.
Impact: full read of another party's flow build output: component/LLM results, chat message content, artifacts, and, on component failure, the raw traceback built at api/build.py:319 (tb = traceback.format_exc()) and api/build.py:322, which exposes server file paths, internal module names and query/parameter details.
Fix: add an authentication dependency to get_build_events and cancel_build, and store the owning user id alongside each job in JobQueueService so get_queue_data (or a wrapper) rejects a job_id whose owner does not match the authenticated caller.

findings.title: Any website can make credentialed cross-origin requests to the Langflow API
findings.description:
Entry: src/backend/base/langflow/main.py:292 (origins = ["*"] passed to CORSMiddleware with allow_credentials=True)
Attacker: any website the victim visits, crossing the same-origin boundary to read responses from the Langflow API.
The app is created in create_app() and unconditionally adds CORSMiddleware with allow_origins=["*"], allow_credentials=True, allow_methods=["*"], allow_headers=["*"]. Starlette's CORSMiddleware, when allow_origins is the literal "*" and allow_credentials is True, reflects the request's Origin back in Access-Control-Allow-Origin and sends Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true, so any origin is treated as trusted for credentialed requests. Nothing overrides `origins` anywhere else in the backend (the only other references are the unrelated chroma component).
This is a shipped default, not operator configuration: every deployment that does not replace create_app() is exposed. It lets a malicious page issue credentialed cross-origin requests and read the responses, and it removes the origin barrier around the API (including the endpoints that accept the session cookie used by the websocket auth path in services/auth/utils.py:225).
Fix: replace the wildcard with an explicit allow-list of trusted frontend origins, and do not combine allow_origins=["*"] with allow_credentials=True.

findings.title: Access and API-key cookies shipped without HttpOnly and Secure flags
findings.description:
Entry: src/backend/base/langflow/services/settings/auth.py:46-51 (ACCESS_SAME_SITE="lax", ACCESS_SECURE=False, ACCESS_HTTPONLY=False)
Attacker: a network attacker or any script running in the victim's browser, crossing the transport/script-isolation boundary to steal or replay the session token.
These shipped defaults are consumed by login.py (lines 51-59, 86-94, 144-152) and api_key.py:75-80, which pass secure=auth_settings.ACCESS_SECURE and httponly=auth_settings.ACCESS_HTTPONLY to response.set_cookie for the access_token_lf and apikey_tkn_lflw cookies. With HttpOnly=False the token is readable by JavaScript (so any XSS or a script on a trusted-but-compromised origin can exfiltrate it), and with Secure=False the cookie is transmitted over plain HTTP where a network attacker can capture it. The refresh cookie is hardened by default, but the access token and API-key cookies are not.
Nothing in the path re-hardens these; they are the code's own defaults and every deployment that does not override LANGFLOW_ACCESS_HTTPONLY / LANGFLOW_ACCESS_SECURE is affected.
Fix: default ACCESS_HTTPONLY and ACCESS_SECURE to True so the access token and API-key cookies are not readable by script and are only sent over TLS.

findings.title: Unauthenticated caller can exhaust server memory via unbounded chat cache
findings.description:
Entry: src/backend/base/langflow/api/v1/chat.py:71 (POST /api/v1/build/{flow_id}/vertices -> retrieve_vertices_order)
Attacker: an unauthenticated outside caller, crossing the authentication boundary (this route has no CurrentActiveUser dependency while its siblings build_flow/build_vertex do).
Path: the caller posts a body with an arbitrary `data` (FlowDataRequest: nodes[], edges[]) and an arbitrary `flow_id` path segment. Line 103-108 takes the `else` branch and calls build_and_cache_graph_from_data(flow_id=flow_id, graph_data=data.model_dump(), chat_service=chat_service), which (api/utils.py:201-211) does Graph.from_payload(...) and chat_service.set_cache(str_flow_id, graph); line 116 then sets the cache again under the same caller-chosen key.
Why nothing stops it: no auth dependency, no ownership check on flow_id, and no size cap on `data` other than the global 100MB body limit. ChatService.set_cache writes into the process-wide cache service, and CacheServiceFactory.create builds AsyncInMemoryCache(expiration_time=...) / ThreadingInMemoryCache(expiration_time=...) with max_size unset, so both cache implementations skip eviction (services/cache/service.py:96 and :324 guard eviction behind `if self.max_size`). Entries only expire after cache_expire (default 3600s). Each request therefore retains one attacker-sized Graph object for an hour, and the attacker can use a different flow_id each time to insert unlimited distinct entries.
Impact: anonymous callers can grow the shared chat cache without bound (up to ~100MB per request, retained for an hour) until the server process exhausts memory and is killed, taking down all tenants.
Fix: add the CurrentActiveUser dependency (and an ownership check on flow_id) to retrieve_vertices_order, and construct the in-memory cache services with a real max_size so the cache is LRU-bounded instead of unbounded.

findings.title: Unauthenticated caller can start unlimited concurrent public flow builds
findings.description:
Entry: src/backend/base/langflow/api/v1/chat.py:561 (POST /api/v1/build_public_tmp/{flow_id}/flow -> build_public_tmp)
Attacker: an unauthenticated outside caller, crossing the authentication boundary (this route is intentionally public, but nothing limits how much work one anonymous source can start).
Path: the caller supplies a client_id cookie and a public flow_id; verify_public_flow_and_get_user (api/utils.py:324-381) only checks that the flow exists and is AccessTypeEnum.PUBLIC, then line 614-626 calls start_flow_build, which (api/build.py:41-80) unconditionally queue_service.create_queue(job_id) and queue_service.start_job(job_id, task_coro) with a fresh random job_id, then generate_flow_events builds the entire graph and build_vertices (api/build.py:399-457) spawns one asyncio.create_task per successor vertex, recursing through the DAG with no depth or breadth cap.
Why nothing stops it: there is no authentication, no per-client or per-flow rate limit, no attempt counter, and no cap on concurrent jobs. JobQueueService.create_queue registers every job in an unbounded dict (services/job_queue/service.py:145-151) and start_job launches each as a free-running asyncio task; nothing rejects a new job when many are already running, and each job performs real component work (LLM calls, code execution, DB writes) using the flow owner's credentials.
Impact: one anonymous caller can loop this endpoint to start unlimited concurrent graph builds, saturating CPU, memory, DB connections and any downstream model provider, and starving legitimate users (a classic unauthenticated application-layer DoS on a public deployment).
Fix: bound the public endpoint with a per-client/per-IP rate limit and a global maximum number of concurrently running build jobs (reject or queue beyond it), and cap the number of vertices/tasks a single build may spawn.

findings.title: Unauthenticated caller can read every user's chat messages via /monitor/messages
findings.description:
Entry: src/backend/base/langflow/api/v1/monitor.py:61 (GET /api/v1/monitor/messages).
Attacker: an unauthenticated caller (or any lower-privileged user), crossing the login boundary and then the per-user data boundary.
Path: the route has no dependencies=[Depends(get_current_active_user)] (unlike its siblings on lines 43, 92, 101, 130), so get_current_user is never invoked; flow_id/session_id/sender are taken straight from the query string and used to build select(MessageTable) with no user or flow-ownership filter, then every matching MessageTable row is serialized into MessageResponse (text, files, properties, content_blocks).
Why nothing stops it: there is no global auth middleware (api/router.py includes monitor_router with no dependencies; main.py adds only CORS/size/MIME middleware), the handler never receives a current_user, and the query only filters by flow_id/session_id, never by owner. MessageTable has no user_id, and every other flow-scoped endpoint (e.g. flows.py:489, endpoints.py:547) adds Flow.user_id == user.id — this one does not.
Impact: anyone who can reach the server reads every chat message of every flow, including message text, file references and properties payloads belonging to other users, and can enumerate all flows by guessing/knowing flow_id.
Fix: add dependencies=[Depends(get_current_active_user)], inject the current user, and constrain the query to messages whose flow belongs to the caller (join Flow and filter Flow.user_id == current_user.id), returning 403/404 otherwise.

findings.title: Authenticated user can delete any other user's messages by UUID
findings.description:
Entry: src/backend/base/langflow/api/v1/monitor.py:92 (DELETE /api/v1/monitor/messages).
Attacker: any authenticated user, crossing into other users' message data.
Path: message_ids is a request body list of UUIDs; the handler runs delete(MessageTable).where(MessageTable.id.in_(message_ids)) with no join to Flow and no ownership check. The login dependency only proves the caller is *a* user, not that they own these messages.
Why nothing stops it: get_current_active_user checks only that the user exists and is active (services/auth/utils.py:247); no code on this path compares message flow ownership to the caller. Sibling flow endpoints scope deletes by Flow.user_id (flows.py:489).
Impact: a user can permanently delete arbitrary messages of any other user by supplying their message UUIDs (obtainable via the unauthenticated GET /monitor/messages).
Fix: resolve the caller's user id, join MessageTable to Flow, and delete only rows whose Flow.user_id == current_user.id; reject the request if any supplied id is not owned.

findings.title: Unauthenticated attacker can delete any session's message history
findings.description:
Entry: src/backend/base/langflow/api/v1/monitor.py:165 (DELETE /api/v1/monitor/messages/session/{session_id}).
Attacker: an unauthenticated caller, crossing the login boundary.
Path: this handler has no dependencies=[Depends(get_current_active_user)] (its siblings on lines 43/92/101/130 do), so get_current_user is never run; session_id from the path is used directly in delete(MessageTable).where(col(MessageTable.session_id) == session_id) and committed.
Why nothing stops it: no global auth middleware exists (router.py/main.py add none), and there is no ownership filter on session_id — any session string deletes every matching message regardless of owner.
Impact: an unauthenticated attacker deletes the entire message history of any session, for any user, by supplying or guessing the session id (session ids are also enumerable via the unauthenticated GET /monitor/messages/sessions).
Fix: add dependencies=[Depends(get_current_active_user)] and delete only messages whose Flow.user_id == current_user.id; 404 when the session is not the caller's.

findings.title: Any authenticated user can reassign another user's chat session messages
findings.description:
Entry: src/backend/base/langflow/api/v1/monitor.py:128 (PATCH /api/v1/monitor/messages/session/{old_session_id}).
Attacker: any authenticated user, crossing into other users' message data.
Path: old_session_id (path) and new_session_id (query) are caller-controlled; select(MessageTable).where(MessageTable.session_id == old_session_id) (line 139) loads messages with no ownership filter, then every message.session_id is set to new_session_id (line 150) and committed.
Why nothing stops it: get_current_active_user only proves login; no code checks that the messages' flow belongs to the caller, and there is no filter on flow or user anywhere on this path.
Impact: any user can rename/reassign another user's chat sessions, injecting their own messages into someone else's session or hijacking a session id.
Fix: filter the select by the caller's owned flows (join Flow where Flow.user_id == current_user.id) and only update messages that belong to the caller.

findings.title: Unauthenticated attacker reads any flow's build logs via /monitor/builds
findings.description:
Entry: src/backend/base/langflow/api/v1/monitor.py:25 (GET /api/v1/monitor/builds).
Attacker: an unauthenticated caller, crossing the login boundary and the per-user data boundary.
Path: the handler has no dependencies=[Depends(get_current_active_user)], so get_current_user is never invoked; flow_id from the query string is passed to get_vertex_builds_by_flow_id (services/database/models/vertex_builds/crud.py:10), which selects VertexBuildTable rows filtered only by flow_id and returns them as VertexBuildMapModel.
Why nothing stops it: no auth middleware exists (router.py includes monitor_router without dependencies; main.py adds none), and the crud function has no owner filter — it matches purely on flow_id.
Impact: an unauthenticated attacker reads the build logs/outputs of any flow (including other users' flows) by supplying its flow_id.
Fix: add dependencies=[Depends(get_current_active_user)] and verify the flow belongs to the caller before returning builds.

findings.title: Unauthenticated attacker can delete any flow's vertex build history
findings.description:
Entry: src/backend/base/langflow/api/v1/monitor.py:34 (DELETE /api/v1/monitor/builds).
Attacker: an unauthenticated caller, crossing the login boundary.
Path: no dependencies=[Depends(get_current_active_user)] on this route; flow_id from the query is passed to delete_vertex_builds_by_flow_id (crud.py:133), which executes delete(VertexBuildTable).where(VertexBuildTable.flow_id == flow_id) and commits.
Why nothing stops it: no global auth middleware, and the delete statement has no owner/flow-ownership condition — it deletes on flow_id alone.
Impact: an unauthenticated attacker deletes the vertex build history of any flow, for any user, by supplying its flow_id.
Fix: require authentication and delete only builds of flows owned by the caller (verify Flow.user_id == current_user.id first).

findings.title: Unauthenticated attacker reads any flow's transaction inputs and outputs
findings.description:
Entry: src/backend/base/langflow/api/v1/monitor.py:183 (GET /api/v1/monitor/transactions).
Attacker: an unauthenticated caller, crossing the login boundary and the per-user data boundary.
Path: this route declares no dependencies=[Depends(get_current_active_user)]; flow_id from the query builds select(TransactionTable).where(TransactionTable.flow_id == flow_id) and paginates the result, serializing TransactionTable including the inputs/outputs JSON columns.
Why nothing stops it: no global auth middleware exists, and the query filters only by flow_id with no ownership check against the caller (who is never even resolved).
Impact: an unauthenticated attacker reads the transaction inputs and outputs of any flow — including user prompts, component inputs and results, which can contain secrets/personal data belonging to other users.
Fix: add dependencies=[Depends(get_current_active_user)] and constrain the query to transactions of flows owned by the caller (join Flow where Flow.user_id == current_user.id).

findings.title: Authenticated user can dump every tenant's session IDs via monitor endpoint
findings.description: Entry: src/backend/base/langflow/api/v1/monitor.py:43 (GET /api/v1/monitor/messages/sessions). Attacker: any authenticated user (including the default AUTO_LOGIN superuser, or any user holding an API key/JWT), crossing the tenant boundary by reading identifiers from every other user's conversations. The input arrives as the optional flow_id query param and flows into `stmt = select(MessageTable.session_id).distinct()` with `where session_id is not null` and an optional `where flow_id == flow_id`, executed by `await session.exec(stmt)` and materialized with `list(session_ids)` at lines 55-56. Nothing on the path stops it: get_current_active_user only proves the caller is a logged-in active user (services/auth/utils.py:247, reached via get_current_user at :142-157 which accepts a valid JWT or API key), it never checks that the caller owns the flow or the messages, and the handler does not call custom_params, so there is no pagination, LIMIT, or per-user predicate on this query. Impact for this application: the response is a DISTINCT over the entire shared MessageTable, so on a multi-tenant or multi-user deployment one cheap GET forces a full table scan plus a sort/hash of every message row in the database and returns the complete list of every session_id in the system, disclosing other tenants' session identifiers and exhausting database and server memory as the table grows; the flow_id filter cannot be used to scope the query to the caller's own data. Fix: join MessageTable to Flow and constrain the query to flows owned by the current user (or filter by the caller's flow/user_id), and cap the number of returned session ids with a limit/pagination.

findings.title: Any authenticated user can overwrite another tenant's message by UUID
findings.description: Entry: src/backend/base/langflow/api/v1/monitor.py:101 (PUT /api/v1/monitor/messages/{message_id}). Attacker: any authenticated user crossing the tenant boundary into another user's message row; the UUID in the path is the only thing needed and it is a value the attacker can obtain or guess/observe from session listings. The path is: message_id (UUID path param) and the MessageUpdate body -> `db_message = await session.get(MessageTable, message_id)` at line 108 -> `message.model_dump(exclude_unset=True, exclude_none=True)` at line 116 -> `db_message.sqlmodel_update(message_dict)` and `session.add(db_message)` at lines 119-120 -> `await session.commit()`. Nothing on the path stops it: the only dependency is get_current_active_user (monitor.py:101), which merely verifies the caller is an active logged-in user (services/auth/utils.py:247); there is no check that db_message.flow_id/session_id belongs to a flow owned by the caller, and no per-user scoping is applied to the lookup at line 108, so the UPDATE writes to whatever row the UUID names. Impact for this application: the MessageUpdate fields (including the free-text `text` column, stored unbounded up to the deployment's max_file_size_upload cap) are written into another tenant's conversation, so an attacker can use one small request to inject arbitrarily large text into rows that the victim later loads through /monitor/messages, corrupting their chat history, and can rewrite session_id to move another user's messages into a session the attacker controls; the message row is returned in the response, so the write is also a cross-tenant data modification primitive. Fix: after fetching the message, verify that its flow belongs to the current user (join to Flow and compare user_id, or reject when the caller is not the owner) and reject the update with 404/403 otherwise; also bound the size of the accepted `text` field.

findings.title: Unauthenticated attacker can download any flow's stored files by ID
findings.description:
Entry: src/backend/base/langflow/api/v1/files.py:74 (GET /api/v1/files/download/{flow_id}/{file_name}).
Attacker: an unauthenticated network caller, crossing the login boundary into any user's private flow storage.
The route handler download_file (line 75) declares only file_name, flow_id and a StorageService dependency — no CurrentActiveUser, no get_flow. flow_id comes straight from the path and file_name from the path, and both are passed to storage_service.get_file (line 92) which resolves to LocalStorageService.get_file (services/storage/local.py:58) and reads data_dir/flow_id/file_name with no ownership check. The files router is included with no dependencies in api/router.py:43 and main.py installs no auth middleware (only CORS/content-size/MIME/Sentry and a multipart boundary check), so nothing on the path authenticates the caller or verifies the flow belongs to them. The sibling routes upload_file/list_files/delete_file and the whole v2 files API (api/v2/files.py) do enforce flow.user_id == current_user.id, proving the guard was simply omitted here. Impact: anyone who can reach the server can read any file stored under any flow (uploaded datasets, secrets in attached files) if they know or can guess the flow UUID and file name, and the Content-Disposition header confirms it is a raw file download. Fix: add current_user: CurrentActiveUser and flow: Annotated[Flow, Depends(get_flow)] (or an equivalent ownership check against the flow_id path param) to this route.

findings.title: Unauthenticated read of any user's flow image files
findings.description:
Entry: src/backend/base/langflow/api/v1/files.py:103 (GET /api/v1/files/images/{flow_id}/{file_name}).
Attacker: an unauthenticated network caller, crossing the login boundary into any user's flow image storage.
The handler download_image (line 104) takes only file_name and flow_id from the path and obtains the storage service directly via get_storage_service() (line 105); it declares no current_user and no get_flow dependency. The attacker-controlled flow_id and file_name are passed to storage_service.get_file (line 122), which reads data_dir/flow_id/file_name from local storage with no ownership check. No auth dependency exists on the route, on the files router (api/router.py:43), or in main.py middleware, so an unauthenticated request reaches the read. Impact: anyone can retrieve image files belonging to any user's flow by supplying that flow's UUID and file name. Fix: require CurrentActiveUser and validate the flow with the get_flow dependency (or an equivalent flow.user_id == current_user.id check) before serving the file.

findings.title: Unauthenticated callers can read any stored profile picture by path
findings.description:
Entry: src/backend/base/langflow/api/v1/files.py:128 (GET /api/v1/files/profile_pictures/{folder_name}/{file_name}).
Attacker: an unauthenticated network caller, crossing the login boundary into the server's profile-picture storage.
The handler download_profile_picture (line 129) takes folder_name and file_name as plain path strings with no user dependency, builds folder_path = config_dir/profile_pictures/folder_name (line 138) and calls storage_service.get_file(flow_id=folder_path, file_name=file_name) (line 140), which reads the file directly from disk. Neither the route, the files router, nor any main.py middleware authenticates the caller, so anyone can fetch profile pictures by path. Because both path segments are unconstrained strings they also widen the readable surface beyond a single user's pictures. Impact: unauthenticated disclosure of profile pictures stored on the server. Fix: add a CurrentActiveUser (or equivalent) dependency to this route and constrain/validate folder_name and file_name.

findings.title: Unauthenticated callers can enumerate stored profile picture files
findings.description:
Entry: src/backend/base/langflow/api/v1/files.py:147 (GET /api/v1/files/profile_pictures/list).
Attacker: an unauthenticated network caller, crossing the login boundary into the server's file listing.
The handler list_profile_pictures (line 148) takes no parameters and no user dependency; it calls storage_service.list_files on config_dir/profile_pictures/People and config_dir/profile_pictures/Space (lines 157-158) and returns the resulting file names (lines 163-166). Nothing on the path authenticates the caller: the route has no auth dependency, the files router is included without dependencies in api/router.py:43, and main.py adds no auth middleware. Impact: an unauthenticated caller can enumerate the server's stored profile-picture files, giving the file names needed to retrieve them via the download routes. Fix: require CurrentActiveUser (or an equivalent authenticated dependency) on this route.

findings.title: Unauthenticated path traversal reads secret_key and langflow.db
findings.description:
Entry: src/backend/base/langflow/api/v1/files.py:128 (`@router.get("/profile_pictures/{folder_name}/{file_name}")`).
Attacker: an unauthenticated outsider, crossing the login boundary into the server's config directory (this route has no Depends at all, so no user, token or API key is required, and it reaches files the caller is never allowed to read).
Path: `folder_name` and `file_name` come straight from the URL path into `download_profile_picture`. Line 138 builds `folder_path = config_path / "profile_pictures" / folder_name` and line 140 calls `storage_service.get_file(flow_id=folder_path, file_name=file_name)`. LocalStorageService.get_file (services/storage/local.py:58) then does `file_path = self.data_dir / flow_id / file_name` and opens it. `data_dir` is `settings_service.settings.config_dir` (services/storage/service.py:21), and config_dir defaults to the platformdirs user cache dir (services/settings/base.py:315-337) or whatever LANGFLOW_CONFIG_DIR is set to. Nothing on the path normalizes or contains the value: the only inspection of `file_name` is `file_name.split(".")[-1]` for the media type, and `folder_name` is not looked at at all. Passing `folder_name=..` and `file_name=..%2Fsecret_key` (or `..%2Flangflow.db`) resolves outside the profile_pictures directory. The generic `except` at 143 returns the error text but does not stop a successful read. With storage_type=s3 the same value lands in `Key=f"{folder}/{file_name}"` (services/storage/s3.py:53), so it is a cross-prefix read there too.
Impact: full unauthenticated read of `<config_dir>/secret_key`, the HS256 signing secret created at services/settings/auth.py:92, which lets the attacker forge JWTs for any user including the superuser, plus the SQLite `langflow.db` holding every user, flow, credential and API key, and any other file the server process can read.
Fix: resolve the path and require containment, e.g. `resolved = (base / "profile_pictures" / folder_name / file_name).resolve()` and reject unless `resolved.is_relative_to(base.resolve())`, validate `file_name` against `^[A-Za-z0-9._-]+$`, and add the same authentication dependency the other file routes use.

findings.title: Authenticated user writes arbitrary files outside flow folder via upload filename
findings.description:
Entry: src/backend/base/langflow/api/v1/files.py:40 (`@router.post("/upload/{flow_id}")`).
Attacker: an authenticated user who owns at least one flow, crossing into the server's config directory and gaining code execution / integrity control over files that belong to the deployment.
Path: the multipart part's filename is read at line 65 (`file_name = file.filename or hashlib.sha256(...)`) and only prefixed with a timestamp at line 66; it is never sanitized. Line 67 sets `folder = str(flow.id)` (the flow is fetched and ownership-checked by `get_flow` at line 32-37, so the attacker must own a flow, which is trivially satisfied) and line 68 calls `storage_service.save_file(flow_id=folder, file_name=full_file_name, data=file_content)`. LocalStorageService.save_file (services/storage/local.py:33-39) does `folder_path = self.data_dir / flow_id; file_path = folder_path / file_name` and `async_open(str(file_path), "wb")`. Because `file_name` may contain `../` sequences (multipart filenames are attacker-controlled and are not path-normalized by Starlette), `../../../<config_dir>/evil.py` writes outside the flow folder. The only limit on the path is `max_file_size_upload` (line 54) and nothing restricts the target location or extension. `build_content_type_from_extension`/`UploadFileResponse` do not constrain it. With storage_type=s3 the same unsanitized value goes into `Key=f"{folder}/{file_name}"` (services/storage/s3.py:30).
Impact: attacker-controlled bytes written to an arbitrary path the server process can write, e.g. a `.py` file inside an importable package or a sitecustomize-style path for code execution on the next restart, an overwrite of `langflow.db`, or of the JWT `secret_key` file in config_dir, giving persistent takeover rather than just a stored file.
Fix: reduce the upload name to `os.path.basename(file_name)`, reject names containing path separators or `..`, and enforce containment on the resolved destination inside `LocalStorageService.save_file` before writing.

findings.title: Authenticated path traversal in file delete allows arbitrary server file deletion
findings.description:
Entry: src/backend/base/langflow/api/v1/files.py:182 (`@router.delete("/delete/{flow_id}/{file_name}")`).
Attacker: an authenticated user who owns a flow, crossing the per-flow boundary to delete arbitrary files on the server.
Path: `file_name` is the raw URL path segment in `delete_file` (v1/files.py:184) and is passed straight to `storage_service.delete_file(flow_id=str(flow.id), file_name=file_name)` at line 189 with no validation; `get_flow` checks only that the flow exists and belongs to the caller (lines 32-37), never the filename. LocalStorageService.delete_file at this location does `file_path = self.data_dir / flow_id / file_name`, and if `await file_path.exists()` it calls `await file_path.unlink()`. A `file_name` such as `../../secret_key` or `../../langflow.db` resolves outside the flow folder, and `flow_id` need not be a real directory for the traversal to work. The S3 backend has the same gap (`Key=f"{folder}/{file_name}"`, services/storage/s3.py:93). Nothing on the path normalizes or contains the value, and the response echoes the caller's string in a plain JSON message (line 193), which is not an HTML sink.
Impact: authenticated arbitrary file deletion inside the config directory, most damagingly `langflow.db` (destroys all flows, users and credentials) and the JWT `secret_key` file; a missing `secret_key` also causes the app to regenerate it, invalidating every session.
Fix: reject `file_name` values containing `/`, `\` or `..` (allow-list `^[A-Za-z0-9._-]+$`) and enforce containment on the resolved path inside `LocalStorageService.delete_file`.

findings.title: Unauthenticated profile-picture GET loads arbitrary file into RAM, enabling DoS
findings.description:
Entry: src/backend/base/langflow/api/v1/files.py:128 (GET /api/v1/files/profile_pictures/{folder_name}/{file_name})
Attacker: an unauthenticated internet caller, crossing the login boundary (this route has no CurrentActiveUser dependency, unlike the upload/list/delete routes in the same file).
Path: folder_name and file_name are plain str path params with no validation. They flow into folder_path = config_path / "profile_pictures" / folder_name (line 138) and then storage_service.get_file(flow_id=folder_path, file_name=file_name) (line 140). LocalStorageService.get_file does file_path = self.data_dir / flow_id / file_name and then `content = await f.read()` (local.py:58-65), loading the whole file into memory; line 141 then copies it again into BytesIO for the StreamingResponse.
Why nothing stops it: there is no auth dependency on this route, no allow-list or normalization of folder_name/file_name, and no size cap on the read (max_file_size_upload is only enforced on the upload path and by ContentSizeLimitMiddleware, which limits the request body, not the response read). ".." components in folder_name/file_name traverse out of the config dir, so the attacker chooses which server file is read.
Impact: a tiny unauthenticated GET makes the server read an arbitrarily large file fully into RAM (twice, via BytesIO). Repeated in parallel this exhausts process memory and takes the Langflow server down for all users.
Fix: require CurrentActiveUser on this route, validate/normalize folder_name and file_name (reject "..", absolute paths and separators), confine the resolved path to the profile_pictures directory, and stream the file in bounded chunks with a maximum size instead of reading it whole into memory.

findings.title: Unauthenticated caller exhausts server memory via download path traversal
findings.description:
Entry: src/backend/base/langflow/api/v1/files.py:74 (GET /api/v1/files/download/{flow_id}/{file_name})
Attacker: an unauthenticated internet caller, crossing the login boundary (this route has no CurrentActiveUser dependency; the tests even pass an API key that the handler never checks).
Path: file_name is a raw str path param with no validation; flow_id is a UUID but file_name can contain "../" segments. It flows into storage_service.get_file(flow_id=flow_id_str, file_name=file_name) (line 92). LocalStorageService.get_file builds data_dir / flow_id / file_name and does `content = await f.read()` (local.py:58-65), loading the entire file into memory; line 98 then wraps it in BytesIO (a second full copy).
Why nothing stops it: no auth dependency, no allow-list/normalization of file_name, no response-side size limit. The extension/content-type check (lines 79-89) only requires the last dot-segment to be non-empty and build_content_type_from_extension returns a truthy default for unknown extensions, so it never blocks the read. The upload-time max_file_size_upload does not apply to files reached via traversal.
Impact: an unauthenticated caller can force the server to read an arbitrarily large file into memory (doubled by BytesIO) with a single small request; repeated requests exhaust memory and deny service to all users.
Fix: require CurrentActiveUser and an ownership check, validate file_name against path traversal (resolve and confine to the flow directory, reject ".."), and stream the file in bounded chunks with an explicit maximum size instead of reading it whole into memory.

findings.title: Unauthenticated callers exhaust server memory via unbounded file read
findings.description:
Entry: src/backend/base/langflow/api/v1/files.py:103 (GET /api/v1/files/images/{flow_id}/{file_name})
Attacker: an unauthenticated internet caller, crossing the login boundary (no CurrentActiveUser dependency on this route).
Path: file_name is a raw str path param; the extension is taken as file_name.split(".")[-1] and only used to pick a content type. It flows into storage_service.get_file(flow_id=flow_id_str, file_name=file_name) (line 122), which in LocalStorageService does `content = await f.read()` (local.py:65) loading the entire file into memory, then line 123 copies it into BytesIO.
Why nothing stops it: the only guard is that the content type derived from the extension must start with "image" (lines 112-119), which is satisfied by any name ending in .png/.jpg/.jpeg/.gif/.svg; it says nothing about the actual file being read or its size. There is no auth, no path normalization, and no size cap on the read, so file_name with "../" segments lets the caller select an arbitrarily large server file.
Impact: an unauthenticated request with a crafted file_name (e.g. ending in .png but resolving to a large file) makes the server load that file entirely into memory, twice; repeated in parallel it exhausts memory and denies service.
Fix: require CurrentActiveUser, validate/normalize file_name and confine the resolved path to the flow directory, and stream the file in bounded chunks with a maximum size instead of reading it whole into memory.

findings.title: Unauthenticated attacker logs in as superuser using shipped default password
findings.description:
Entry: src/backend/base/langflow/api/v1/login.py:31 (POST /api/v1/login, unauthenticated).
Attacker: an unauthenticated network caller, crossing the login boundary into the superuser account.
Path: login_to_get_access_token -> authenticate_user(username, password) -> get_user_by_username + verify_password(password, user.password) (services/auth/utils.py:407-418). The password stored for the superuser comes from SUPERUSER_PASSWORD, whose default here is DEFAULT_SUPERUSER_PASSWORD = "langflow" (services/settings/constants.py:2). AUTO_LOGIN defaults to True, so setup_superuser/initialize_super_user_if_needed create the superuser with that literal password (services/utils.py:86-94, initial_setup/setup.py:1009-1016). The /login route is registered publicly in api/router.py:41 and never consults AUTO_LOGIN before verifying credentials.
Why nothing stops it: authenticate_user is called for every login request regardless of AUTO_LOGIN; the superuser account is created is_active=True and is_superuser=True; the password is a fixed, guessable literal committed to the repository. There is no forced password change and no rate limit on this route.
Impact: any remote caller can POST username=langflow&password=langflow and receive a full superuser access/refresh token pair, giving them every flow, credential and API key in the deployment. Whoever reads the source holds this password.
Fix: do not ship a working default password. Require the operator to set LANGFLOW_SUPERUSER_PASSWORD (fail startup if unset), or generate a random password at first run and print it once, and force a change on first login.

findings.title: Unauthenticated attacker gets superuser via forced default 'langflow' password
findings.description:
Entry: AuthSettings field_validator validate_superuser, invoked at settings construction (services/settings/manager.py:46, service.py:25).
